We also treat our community members to special offers, promotions, and adverts from us and our partners. If you don’t like our community, you can check out any time you like. If you’re curious, you can read our Privacy Notice. NEWSLETTER: Or sign up to the Mirror's Money newsletter here for all the best advice and shopping deals straight to your inbox.

Attendance Allowance is paid every four weeks, which means you could receive either £306.80 or £458.40 every pay period. It is not a means-tested benefit there is no limit on how much money you can have in savings.

It is also tax-free and you will be exempt from the benefit cap. If you claim other benefits, these might increase if you get Attendance Allowance.

Article continues below

You won't be able to Attendance Allowance if you already get Personal Independence Payment (PIP) or Disability Living Allowance (DLA). Attendance Allowance has been replaced in Scotland with Pension Age Disability Payment.

There are potentially up to one million eligible pensioners missing out on Attendance Allowance, according to research firm Policy in Practice.

News.title: Eclipse - live: Stunning solar eclipse reaches peak over UK in dramatic images
News.content:
Darkness descends upon Land's End as sky watchers dazzled by eclipse

The Mirror's Saskia Rowlands was among the crowds wowed by the solar eclipse tonight. She says the sjy went from bright sunshine to darkness.

In Land's End, the UK's most southerly point, crowds fell silent in awe as 98.5% of the sun became covered by the moon.

Hundreds excitedly gathered on a cliff top overlooking the Channel and Celtic sea ahead of the phenomenon.

Many had travelled from far and wide to catch a glimpse of the first eclipse in nearly three decades.

Susan Carpenter, 70, drove down to Cornwall from Newbury, Berks, on Wednesday morning with her husband, daughter and grandson.

She told the Mirror: "For the last eclipse in 1999, we took our children to Devon and we’ve brought our grandson so he can experience an eclipse.

"The last one [eclipse] was phenomenal —it was at 11 in the morning.

"Everything went black and the birds went to sleep and as it went over the birds started to wake and you get the dawn chorus. The children couldn’t believe it. It’s a really good experience."

Steve Lipscombe, from Mitcham, South London, watched the 1999 eclipse from Devon, but last minute cloud cover obscured his view.

He said: "I was in Penzance with the Radio 1 roadshow they did back then.

"It was a lovely day like today, but it went cloudy just as the eclipse was starting to happen, so we basically missed it, which was terrible — I’d travelled 300 miles there and back, so I’m back again today for take two.

"I like celestial things, I’ve seen many shooting star showers - but there’s not another eclipse for 65 years in this country."

Shop Judy’s Body Art, a shack next to the infamous Land’s End sign, had sold over 140 pairs of eclipse glasses in just two hours.

Owner Judith Dyulaine Buskas, who sold our reporter one of her last pairs, said: "We have been very busy today, and only have a few pairs left.

"We are very excited for tonight - it will be the last eclipse in my lifetime."

News.title: 'Dozens of women come forward' to police over serial sex attacker Simon Levy
News.content:
'Dozens of women come forward' to police over serial sex attacker Simon Levy

EXCLUSIVE: The Metropolitan Police is understood to be considering forming a special team to deal with a flood of reports following previous errors that left Levy free to kill

View 5 Images Simon Levy in the dock on Wednesday (Image: Julia Quenzler / SWNS)

Dozens of women have come forward to say they may been targeted by serial sex attacker Simon Levy, a source has revealed.

The Metropolitan Police is understood to be thinking about forming a special team to deal with the flood of reports in an effort to avoid any further failings in investigating the double killer. It comes after a series of disastrous decisions previously left Levy free kill and assault women.

The predator was given a rare whole-life order on Wednesday at the Old Bailey, meaning he will never be released. Levy, 40, was last week found guilty of smothering grandmother Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March last year and mum-of-four Sheryl Wilkins, 39, five months later.

He was also convicted of raping another woman and leaving her for dead in January 2025 in the same north London car park where Sheryl’s body was later found. Levy was convicted following a trial earlier this year of attacking 10 women on public transport in London, seeking out busy carriages to assault women aged between 18 and 32.

Killer Simon Levy used bus driver's stolen travelcard to move around London after police repeatedly returned it READ MORE :

5 View 5 Images Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53 5 View 5 Images Sheryl Wilkins was murdered by Levy (Image: Metropolitan Police/PA Wire)

BTP said more women "may recognise [Levy] and have not yet reported what has happened to them".

British Transport Police said women who think Levy attacked them should report it, while the Met Police said it had investigated whether he had more victims, including further murders.

A source said on Wednesday that dozens of women had come forward to the Met while a number have also contacted the BTP over concerns they were targeted by Levy. It is unclear how many will prove to be Levy and officers are now in the process of investigating the reports in an effort to substantiate them.

Levy was first convicted of sexually assaulting two women in 2018, which he was jailed for in 2021.

View 5 Images Levy is being probed over dozens of cases (Image: Metropolitan Police/PA Wire)

BTP has confirmed two officers have been moved to other roles due to "incompetence" in handling investigations into the assaults.

Lisa Ramsarran, chief crown prosecutor for the CPS, said: "Our actions fell short of the standards that victims, families and the public are entitled to expect."

Deputy Assistant Commissioner, Kevin Southworth, said: “We know that this case has raised questions around the way Levy was handled and we have carefully reflected on the opportunities missed to prevent his violent offending. It highlighted that improvements needed to be made and we have not waited for the outcome of the IOPC’s report to implement change.

“As the Commissioner recently said, we are concerned by the fragility of the criminal justice system. As we have seen in Levy’s case, despite clear risk and rapid escalation, the courts defaulted to bail on two occasions. We now need to work together, with other judicial partners, to create and implement a plan of action which sees repeat offenders – like Levy – automatically placed on remand to protect the wider public.

View 5 Images Moment Simon Levy was arrested (Image: Metropolitan Police/PA Wire)

The Met said in a statement on Wednesday: "Since the launch of the investigation, detectives have exhausted numerous lines of enquiry – including working with coroners – to identify whether Levy is responsible for any similar, unsolved incidents, including deaths.

"While they are yet to find anything they believe to be linked to Levy, they are urging anyone who believes they may be a victim of his to contact police.

Article continues below

"Reporting rape or sexual assault can be daunting and many victim-survivors will have concerns about speaking to the police."

Those with information about Levy who are yet to speak to police can do so via 101, quoting 4779/7AUG. People can also contact the incident room directly on 07751 700 330 or anonymously via Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Barmy pop videos exposed from Freddie Mercury's giant  prawn to Neil Young's boxing fiasco
News.content:
From dressing Freddie Mercury as a giant Mediterranean prawn to accidentally prompting Neil Young to punch himself unconscious, director Tim Pope knew no bounds when turning pop videos into art. During the 1980s and 1990s, the maverick’s iconic videos made him a leading light for the MTV generation.

Now 70 and casting for a movie, The Photographer's Assistant, as well as working on commercials and a cinema documentary project for The Cure, he says: “It was a very free-spirited period, before the rulebook was written. “There was no health and safety. I was always causing as much trouble as I could.” This included putting The Cure in a wardrobe and throwing them off a cliff for their hit Close To Me. But it’s the Neil Young incident that still preys on his mind. He says: “I tied Neil Young to a redwood tree when shooting Pressure.

“There were these beats in the music which were like doom, doom. So I got Neil to put on a boxing glove and punch himself in the face. He was so committed to it that he actually - and this is not made up - knocked himself out! “There he was, unconscious, tied to a redwood tree as this character. I thought, ‘oh, my god, I've just killed Neil Young.’ Or rather, ‘Neil Young has just killed Neil Young.’ The entire crew and I were like, ‘oh my god’. Then he came to. He stayed in character, and just went, ‘do you want me to hit it harder, Tim?’ I thought it was brilliant.”

Record label that made The Smiths spills 50 years of secrets READ MORE :

View 5 Images Maverick director Tim Pope, whose pop music videos dominated MTV (Image: Andy Vella)

Born and raised in Enfield, North London, to banker parents, Tim’s inventive, surreal, and darkly playful videos led the way across two decades. But, as his new book, I Shoot Rock Stars, reveals, for a long time he feared it would never happen. He says: “I had no contacts. So I wrote thousands of letters to the BBC saying, ‘just let me in, let me in!’ No one would. Eventually, I found my way through music videos.

“My first music video was with a band called Soft Cell, for a song called Bedsitter (1982). I came up with a concept, and me and my old production designer, Alex McDowell, tried to storyboard loads of videos. We couldn't get a foot in the door. But through telling lies, that I'd made this and that, I got myself into a room with Marc Almond, the Soft Cell vocalist… and the rest was history. I was a bit like a kid let loose in a sweet shop. Suddenly, there I was working with all my heroes.”

Tim went on to make over 200 music videos. Thirty seven were for The Cure, including Close to Me and Lullaby, and there were creations for David Bowie, Queen, Iggy Pop, Siouxsie & the Banshees, Talk Talk, and Neil Young. Choosing a favourite is tough for Tim.

View 5 Images The Cure perform in a Tim Pope video

He says: “It’s like choosing between my children. love The Cure’s Lullaby, where Robert [Smith, lead singer] is a spider man. He's this creepy character. And the Neil Young ones are great - he embraced characters that I created for him, such as The Pig Farmer. He's completely demented and just wonderful. Then I think some of The The’s videos, for the sheer danger of how we filmed them. We worked underneath a moving steam train. We filmed in a working brothel in Harlem in the '80s. That was completely crazy.”

Tim, who lives in Brighton with his wife Victoria, who he has two adult children with, says not all stars liked his direction. He found a DVD commentary by Queen’s Roger Taylor and Brian May and says: “They were moaning about the video I made for It’s a Hard Life, saying they didn't like Freddie's Mediterranean prawn costume, which I loved. Freddie loved it too. Freddie designed it. So blame him, don't blame me. Robert Smith never said no. That included tracking a huge camera into his mouth and making him wear a mite-infested polar bear suit.”

In the forward to the book, Robert recalls making videos with Tim. He says: “The hours left hanging in midair by very painful wires, the hours spent drowning in filthy water, the hours spent being asphyxiated by strong glue, the hours spent being asphyxiated by snakes, the hours being fed into a giant spider’s mouth, being chucked off a pier…”

Tim was inspired to write his book by a rediscovered 1990s’ answerphone message from David Bowie. Reflecting on the eclectic characters he’d met, he felt compelled to share his experiences. One of the stand out characters was Freddie Mercury.

View 5 Images David Bowie, who worked with Tim Pope for 12 years (Image: Getty Images)

Describing Freddie as “really very sweet, down-to-earth,” he recalls one incident, saying: “I went to meet him in Munich. He kept making sure I had cups of tea, which he referred to as ‘a builder’s.’ There was a Mirror photographer there. Freddie flounced into the room wearing a big orange dress with breasts larger than Dolly Parton's. He draped himself over my knee and he was like, ‘ooh, darling!’ This Mirror photographer went click, click, click. I pushed Freddie to the floor and sort of clambered aboard him for a joke, to pay him back. The manager of the band came and pulled the 35mm film out of the camera, took Freddie away!”

Tim also worked with David Bowie for 12 years. He says: “I christened him ‘The Governor.’ He was just a bloke underneath - albeit a bloke who was quite amazing. He was always the biggest name-dropper I've ever heard. He was always like ‘this person’ and ‘that person’. He was wonderful. I just remember laughing around him a lot. He had this particular laugh, like a Marlborough laugh, very much made from cigarettes. Bowie really liked to be directed. He liked to be told what to do. He was always such a great intellect and a mind to work with. Although he would put his intellect ahead of his heart sometimes.”

Tim, who is working on a cinema documentary project for The Cure to celebrate their 50th anniversary, says: “Robert Smith has got 50 boxes of film that nobody has ever seen, which I'm hoping to cut into something special.” But his filmmaking experiences have not always been good.

View 5 Images Tim Pope's book I Shoot Rock Stars

He says: “I made an independent movie called Phone at the start of the '90s, and Martin Scorsese wrote to me to say he loved it. I subsequently went to Hollywood, and I made a film - the sequel to The Crow - under the eyes of the Weinstein brothers. The infamous Harvey Weinstein. Harvey Weinstein told me he owned me, which were the worst three words anyone has ever said to me.

“He wanted me to cut a film. I went to supper with him and his brother and he said, ‘Just cut the f***ing film how we want it you b******, we own you.’ To be owned by Harvey Weinstein was not great and put me off making movies for an awful amount of time. Part of the reason I wrote the book was to let that go, cathartically. I look forward to him reading it in Rikers Island jail.”

*I Shoot Rock Stars: The Wild Adventures of a Music Video Director by Tim Pope publishes 13th August in Hardback, priced £25.00 (Wildfire)’

News.title: Andy Burnham urges shops to pause disposable barbecue sales after Cobra heatwave meeting
News.content:
Andy Burnham urges shops to pause disposable barbecue sales after Cobra heatwave meeting

Prime Minister Andy Burnham convened ministers, officials and agencies as scorching temperatures persist across the country in the fifth heatwave of the summer

View 2 Images The PM convened ministers, officials and agencies as scorching temperatures persist across in the fifth heatwave of the summer (Image: Getty Images)

Andy Burnham has urged all retailers to pause the sale of disposable barbecues in order to prevent more wildfires raging this summer.

‌



It came as the Prime Minister warned extreme heat conditions "could be with us for some weeks yet" after chairing an emergency Cobra meeting in response to the fifth heatwave this summer.

‌



Speaking on Wednesday evening, he said: "The big risk in terms of risk to the wider regions across the country is the risk of wildfires. What we are seeing is multiple serious incidents across the country.

‌



"Fire services by and large are supporting each other through mutual aid to deal with those incidents, but we are keeping a very close watching brief on them."

He added: "There is advice to the public here not to use disposable barbecues. We have today confirmed through the National Fire Chiefs Council that the framework restricting the retail sale of those disposable barbecues is being extended.

"Now I would ask all retailers big and small to adhere to that framework. Longer term we will look at whether a temporary ban in the summer months is justified." Most major UK supermarkets have already suspended sales of disposable barbecues in recent weeks in line with voluntary guidance from the NFCC.

‌



NHS must plan for heatwaves like winter crises to protect frail and vulnerable, Yvette Cooper says READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham is looking at whether a temporary ban of disposable barbecue in the summer months is justified (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

The message followed Wednesday's Cobra meeting with the PM convening ministers, officials and agencies as scorching temperatures persist across the country in the fifth heatwave of the summer. They included representatives from the Environment Agency, the Met Office, and the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

Earlier this week, the Environment Agency said 71.3% of England is now experiencing "flash drought", following the country's driest July on record.

‌



Before the Cobra meeting, Mr Burnham also said people should not be using single-use grills "at this time" amid a "significant problem" of wildfires in the south, where a blaze hit protected heathland in the New Forest, Hampshire.

The Prime Minister said he was "certainly going to consider" a ban, adding: "I do believe we need to get the message out loud and clear. People should not be using those barbecues outside at this moment in time."

On Tuesday, a firefighters' union sounded the alarm, warning that the country is facing a "national emergency" amid the ongoing wildfire crisis. General secretary Steve Wright said: "Lives are being put at risk. This is only going to get worse unless we get a grip of it now and put in place a proper national strategy".

Article continues below

The Cobra meeting on Wednesday was the second this summer on heatwaves after one took place amid high temperatures in June.

The Met Office has said the UK is on course for its hottest summer on record. Rare amber "extreme heat" warnings have been issued by the forecaster for London and parts of the South East, East Midlands, East of England, West Midlands and South Yorkshire from 9am to midnight on Thursday.

News.title: Bus driver, 25, shot dead outside London pub named as devastated family pay tribute
News.content:
Bus driver, 25, shot dead outside London pub named as devastated family pay tribute

Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa was described as an 'amazing person' and 'kind man' who died from being in 'the wrong place at the wrong time'

View 3 Images (Image: Metropolitan Police/PA Wire)

A 25-year-old bus driver who died after being shot outside a pub in Clapham, south London, on Monday has been named as Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa.

‌



The victim died after he was attacked outside a venue by an assailant who was also hospitalised with a gunshot wound and was arrested on suspicion of murder, according to the force.

‌



The suspect remains in hospital under police guard.

‌



Paramedics raced to the area outside the Landor Pub in Clapham North, within three minutes of the incident, but despite their best efforts, the man was pronounced dead at the scene, a London Ambulance Service spokesperson said.

View 3 Images Bile-aka Amoa was shot outside a pub in Clapham on Monday (Image: Jonathan Brady/PA Wire)

Speaking near the scene, a fried of Amoa described him as a "cool guy" who was "in the wrong place at the wrong time."

‌



“I don’t have bad things to say about him.

“He’s a cool guy, like I said, bus driver, hard-working.

“It’s shocking because of who he is and his character.”

‌



The man, who also works as a bus driver, said the death is “going to hurt a lot of people”.

Another friend of the victim, who asked to remain anonymous, said he was a “great guy”, adding: “It’s been hectic, everyone’s very hot-headed right now, everyone’s obviously grieving and I feel extremely bad for his mother as well, she’s in bits.

“It hurts me as well.”

‌



Prior to his death, Amoa also worked as a volunteer at a local school, and helped to mentor young people, a staff member told The Metro.

View 3 Images Friends described the victim as a 'kind man' who was 'in the wrong place at the wrong time' (Image: Jonathan Brady/PA Wire)

"He was a lovely kid; he had played around the area when he was young and wanted to give something back.

‌



"He was a lovely guy, great with the kids who would look up to him."

Another family member told the publication: "He was an amazing person and a best friend. He loved driving, so bus driver was the perfect job. He was living his dream.

"I have a daughter, and he would buy her gifts and was such a kind man.

‌



"He loved music and dancing; he was just wonderful. I heard about the shooting yesterday, and I know he is in that area.

"I texted him and got nothing back, then I found out the news. I’m heartbroken.’

Detective chief inspector Claire Guiver, who is leading the investigation, said: “Our thoughts remain with Bile-aka’s family as they come to terms with this tragic incident.

‌



“We continue to appeal for anyone with information to come forward.

“If you were in the area at the time of the shooting, witnessed anything suspicious or have any CCTV, dashcam or doorbell footage that could assist our investigation, we urge you to get in touch.

“Any piece of information could prove vital in helping us piece together the full circumstances.”

Article continues below

It is understood the alleged gunman was hospitalised by injury inflicted by his own gun.

News.title: Schoolboy, 9, dead in tragic Birmingham crash as devastated brother pays touching tribute
News.content:
Schoolboy, 9, dead in tragic Birmingham crash as devastated brother pays touching tribute

A nine-year-old schoolboy who 'loved Pokémon and dinosaurs' has died following a serious collision between two cars in Kings Norton

View Image A schoolboy has died following a serious crash at the end of last month. (Image: BPM Media)

A nine-year-old boy has tragically dried after being involved in a serious car crash.

‌



The schoolboy, named only as Kyron, was critically injured during a major collision between two cars on Masshouse Lane in Kings Norton on July 28.

‌



Police, paramedics and an off-duty nurse rushed to save the boy's life and restarted his heart, before he was taken to hospital in critical condition.

‌



But after an intense fight to save his life, Kyrom passed away in hospital on Wednesday, West Midlands Police confirmed.

"His family have asked for privacy at this tragic time, and we would ask that you respect their wishes at this time," they said in a statement.

In a heartbreaking tribute shared on GoFundMe, Kyron's brother Darnel Gittens has shared a tribute to his "happy, loving and special" sibling who was "always full of dreams and determination."

‌



"Kyron was such a happy, loving and special child," his older brother wrote. "He loved Pokémon and dinosaurs, and he was always full of dreams and determination.

"He had so much he wanted to achieve in life and was the kind of person who wanted to turn his dreams into reality. As his big brother, I could never have asked for a better little brother."

He added: "The thought of having to say goodbye to him is something I never imagined I would have to face, and our family is completely heartbroken."

‌



Darnel said he started the GoFundMe page in order to give his little brother the "beautiful and dignified funeral he deserves."

"We want to give him the best possible farewell and celebrate the wonderful little boy that he was," he said.

"Any donation, no matter how big or small, would mean so much to our family during this incredibly painful time.

Article continues below

"If you’re unable to donate, sharing this fundraiser would also be greatly appreciated.

"Kyron, I love you so much, You will always be my special little brother, and you will never be forgotten."

You can donate to Kyron's GoFundMe page here.

News.title: Mum's anger at groomed daughter's death after she was wrongly charged with terrorism
News.content:
Mum's anger at groomed daughter's death after she was wrongly charged with terrorism

Emily Rudd reported Rhianan, 16, to the government's anti-terror scheme - only for her daughter to die after she was charged with terrorism, despite evidence she was a victim

The Schoolgirl Terrorist

A mother who reported her daughter to the authorities has described her anger, after the groomed schoolgirl was wrongly charged with terrorism offences and later died.

‌



Rhianan Rudd, 16, plotted to blow up a synagogue and scratched a swastika into her forehead after being radicalised by an American white supremacist. Despite evidence clearly showing autistic Rhianan was a victim, she became the youngest girl ever to be charged with terror offences in the UK - only for the case to be dropped.

‌



Five months later, in May 2022, she was found dead at a Nottinghamshire children's home.

‌



Rhianan's friends and mother Emily Carter have revealed in a new documentary what led up to one of Britain's most controversial youth counter-terrorism cases. In Channel 4's "The Schoolgirl Terrorist?" Emily told of her shock when she realised her daughter had become obsessed with far-right ideology.

View 4 Images Rhianan died after being wrongly charged (Image: BBC)

She said: "She came down and went: 'I've downloaded "How to Make a Bomb'''. She came over and sat on my lap like a two-year-old, put her arms around me and cried."

‌



Emily added: "That afternoon I actually went online to a form and referred her to Prevent." She wrote: "I need help with my 15-year-old daughter. She has a very unhealthy outlook on fascism - she also has massive dislikes for certain races and creeds…I have done my best to deter her from any such ideologies, but it seems to be falling on deaf ears."

View 4 Images Rhianan and Emily (Image: BBC)

It emerged this month that the number of people being flagged to the government's anti-terrorism scheme rocketed 39% in a year to a record high, with one in five reported over fear of extreme right-wing ideology.

‌



Prevent received 10,293 referrals in the 12 months to September 2025. Half were under 18.

Chesterfield Coroner's Court heard Christopher Cook, from Ohio, first contacted Rhianan when she was 14. She had previously told detectives that she had exchanged explicit photographs with the neo-Nazi, adding: "I did love him." Cook, 23, was jailed in the US in 2023 over a plot to attack power grids.

View 4 Images Christopher Cook, from Ohio, first contacted Rhianan when she was 14 (Image: BBC)

‌



Emily said: "He had groomed Rhianon to the point where she had sent him sexual videos of herself nude."

The FBI had passed this evidence to the British authorities many months before she was charged showing he had groomed, coerced and exploited her. Emily, who admits she has made mistakes that adversely affected her children, added: "They knew Rhianon was being sexually exploited but they kept on treating her like a terror suspect."

She added: "I know a lot the mistakes I made have affected my kids but when I'm telling someone else I can see what you're doing is wrong, listen to me and they did f*** all." Rhianon also had direct contact with American white supremacist Dax Mallaburn, who came to the UK to live with Emily, who was vulnerable having previously been in a violent relationship.

‌



View 4 Images Emily is angry at the way her daughter was treated (Image: PA)

Mallaburn has since fled the UK. Emily said her daughter had an apprenticeship lined up as a jockey and was making costumes for charity when she was found hanged.

She wept as she said: "She had so much to offer the world and she had a good heart."

Article continues below

Rhianan, from Derbyshire, had gone from being a huge My Little Pony fan to obsessing about white supremacy. Rhianon's brother Brandon said: "It's clear that there were failings."

Rhianan was arrested in August 2020. The charges were eventually dropped in December 2021 after she told detectives that she had been coerced and groomed.

'The Schoolgirl Terrorist?' on Channel 4 on Thursday at 10pm.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe's loved ones gather for her funeral
News.content:
Police officers and sniffer dogs were in the grounds of the abbey ahead of the service, which lasted about 90 minutes.

The private requiem mass included a homily from the Rt Rev David Charlesworth, Abbot of Buckfast.

He said: "In the midst of the shock, clamour and sometimes unwarranted comment surrounding her death, our response is to pray for the repose of her soul, to give thanks for her fortitude, and offer Holy Mass in this Abbey Church which Ann called her safe haven."

A statement from the Abbey Church earlier said Widdecombe would be "missed and fondly remembered" and "many in our worshipping community knew her as a kind and warm character".

"Ann was a woman of profound faith, a faith which found expression in the public forum of politics," it said.

It added: "Ann was unafraid to express her unwavering convictions, formed through her Roman Catholic faith. She had a sharp intellect and was a dedicated public servant."

The order of service also included tributes paid by the Rev Roger Widdecombe, Widdecombe's nephew, and Sir Christian Sweeting, a close friend.

A public memorial for Widdecombe is due to be held later this year.

News.title: Double killer and rapist given whole life sentence
News.content:
A serial sex attacker who had a "morbid fascination" with sex has been jailed for the rest of his life after he was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third.

Simon Levy, 40, killed Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March 2025 and 39-year-old Sheryl Wilkins five months later. Earlier that year, he raped a third woman in the same Tottenham car park where Wilkins was later found dead.

At the Old Bailey on Wednesday, Judge Mark Lucraft KC sentenced Levy to a whole life order, meaning he will never be released.

The sentence comes after police and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) apologised over a series of disastrous decisions that left him free to roam the streets.

When Levy carried out the attacks, he was on bail and being monitored by the Met.

The police watchdog is currently examining how he was managed over a four-year period, from his first conviction in September 2021 for sexual assault up to his final arrest in September 2025.

Following Wednesday's sentencing, Met Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said the handling of Levy's case was a "whole system failing".

News.title: Burnham urges shops not to sell disposable BBQs over wildfire risks
News.content:
Andy Burnham has urged shops to stop selling disposable barbecues amid increased wildfire risk driven by this summer's droughts.

The prime minister said he was urging retailers "big and small" to adhere to voluntary guidance to suspend sales during extreme heat.

He added that in the "longer term" the government would look at potentially banning the single-use grills during summer months.

It comes after a potential ban was discussed at an emergency Cobra meeting on the government's response to record temperatures.

A number of large retailers and supermarkets have voluntarily stopped selling the devices under a framework, external agreed in 2023 between fire chiefs and the British Retail Consortium (BRC).

This says that retailers should suspend sales once an extreme heat event has been declared as imminent, or in response to "reasonable, evidence based" requests from local councils.

Earlier, Burnham told reporters single-use grills had been behind a number of recent blazes and people should not be using them "at this moment in time".

"We do want people to take the greatest possible care when they are out in the countryside, both in terms of cigarettes, but also those temporary barbecues that we know are causing risk of fires."

Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been officially declared in drought, creating conditions rife for fire to spread.

The Met Office has issued a rare amber extreme heat warning for Thursday, with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England, and a high of 38C possible.

News.title: Jasper Carrott says family is 'so proud' of Lucy Davis after cancer diagnosis
News.content:
Actor and comedian Jasper Carrott has spoken about his pride and love for daughter Lucy Davis after she announced she has incurable breast cancer.

The actress, best known for playing receptionist Dawn Tinsley in BBC sitcom The Office, has received an outpouring of support since she revealed her diagnosis on Tuesday.

Carrott, who was one of the most familiar faces on British television over several decades, told BBC News: "This is a very difficult time for the whole family and we have been supporting her in every way possible since her diagnosis.

"We are so grateful for all the support we have had over this trying time and we are very hopeful for her future being what she wants it to be."

He added: "We are so proud of our daughter and love her so much. The way she has conducted herself through many traumatic health issues is a lesson to us all.

"We would request privacy for the coming months, but thanks once again for the love and concern shown by so many people."

Carrott, whose real name is Robert Davis, became a household name in the 1970s thanks to his stand-up comedy and novelty songs.

He has presented programmes such as Canned Carrott, Golden Balls and Carrott's Commercial Breakdown, and acted in comedy series such as The Detectives.

News.title: PM warned of Iran war impact on UK growth next year
News.content:
Andy Burnham has been warned that the UK economy could barely grow next year if disruption in the Strait of Hormuz continues until the end of 2026.

Treasury sources have confirmed that internal modelling presented to the new prime minister and chancellor suggests UK GDP growth could be as low as 0.3% in 2027, as first reported by Bloomberg.

Government officials say they routinely plan for all possible scenarios.

The UK economy saw a strong start to the year, but growth then faltered with the conflict in the Middle East affecting some businesses. The Iran war has pushed up oil and fuel prices, and also disrupted supply chains.

On Thursday, official figures will show how much the economy grew between April and June of this year.

Economists are expecting growth of 0.4% for the three months.

Burnham and Chancellor John Healey were presented with a reasonable worst-case scenario of the Strait of Hormuz remaining effectively closed for the next five months, and no permanent US-Iran peace deal until the new year.

The Treasury modelling for that scenario was that the UK economy would grow by 0.9% over 2026 - slightly under the 1.1% forecast by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March.

The prospect was much dimmer for next year, with just 0.3% growth projected - much lower than the OBR's 1.6% forecast for 2027.

Under the modelling, inflation would peak at 4.3% in the first three months of next year. It currently stands at 2.6%, just above the Bank of England's 2% target.

The prime minister and chancellor will face pressure to use the upcoming Budget on 28 October to ease the financial burden on households and businesses.

Since taking office three weeks ago, Burnham has announced policies including the removal of VAT from domestic electricity bills and bringing forward an already planned end to "subscription traps".

But this week he told the BBC's Wake up to Money the announcements, aimed at tackling the cost of living, are not enough on their own, hinting at further support.

He has asked Healey to look at what more the government can do on the cost of living in the Budget, with the chancellor saying it will be his "main focus".

But Healey has said he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

Burnham has said his government will stick to the party's 2024 manifesto pledges not to increase people's income tax, VAT or National Insurance contributions.

He also promised to follow the fiscal rules imposed by former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, which include a pledge to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues by the end of the decade.

News.title: Trump sued over Truth Social's $100,000 early access service
News.content:
Donald Trump is being sued by two US media groups over a new Truth Social service that charges up to $100,000 a month for early access to his posts.

The lawsuit was filed on Wednesday in New York federal court by The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation.

The suit argues that selling priority access to the president's messages raises serious concerns, external, describing it as "extraordinary, corrupt and unconstitutional".

Trump Media & Technology Group (TMTG) said the lawsuit was brought by "left-wing activists" seeking to censor the president.

The BBC has approached the White House for comment. TMTG has previously dismissed concerns about the paid service.

The paid Truth Social service offers subscribers near-instant delivery of Trump's posts, arriving seconds before they appear for the general public. The plaintiffs say those moments matter because Trump often uses the platform to announce major developments, such as during the Iran war, that can move financial markets.

They argue the setup gives an unfair advantage to those who can afford it, creating a system where market-sensitive information reaches paying clients first.

More than 10 firms now pay up to $100,000 a month for fast access to Truth Social posts.

Trump Media and Technology Group has said the product is aimed at businesses seeking faster data feeds and has dismissed concerns about how the information is used.

The company unveiled the service, called Truth API, in mid-July and said it would deliver posts from Trump and other high-profile accounts in milliseconds.

Trump is the most followed person on the platform, with about 13 million followers, ahead of his eldest son Donald Trump Jr., who has around 7.5 million.

Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation's, said Trump selling priority access to news he generates, for the benefit of a private company he controls, is "so blatantly corrupt and unconstitutional that it would have been hard to even fathom just a few years ago".

And David Bralow, chief legal officer at The Intercept, said: "Nothing could be more antithetical to the free, independent press than the president charging for early access to his public announcements."

The lawsuit described Truth API as a "scheme" and a money-making opportunity, noting that Trump holds the largest stake in TMTG through a revocable trust that owns about 41% of the company â a stake worth more than $1 billion. He is the trust's sole beneficiary.

Responding to the lawsuit, a TMTG spokesperson said: "Information from President Trump is disseminated by countless platforms and news outlets, many of which offer subscription APIs.

"One of those channels is Truth Social, which was founded as an uncancellable haven for free speech after the President was unjustly de-platformed.

"Now, left-wing activists are trying to wrongfully weaponize the courts to censor him again and harm our shareholders."

The spokesperson also accused the Freedom of the Press Foundation of violating Truth Social's terms of service.

News.title: Eurovision Song Contest changes rules for countries at war
News.content:
Organisers of the Eurovision Song Contest have updated their rules to state that if a country involved in an armed conflict wins the competition, it will be ineligible to host it the following year.

The amendment was approved by the contest's governing body, following feedback from participating broadcasters after Eurovision 2026 in Vienna.

It states that winning countries will also be disqualified from hosting if a "sensitive geopolitical situation" affects the "security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region".

The update will be interpreted as a reaction to Israel's continued presence at the contest, amid criticism of its military actions in Gaza and the Middle East.

Last November, following a failed attempt to have Israel suspended, five broadcasters announced they were boycotting the competition - including Eurovision powerhouses Spain and Ireland.

Despite the protests, Israel's Noam Bettan ultimately took second place with his song Michelle.

It marked the second year in a row that Israel had taken the runners-up position - and some participating broadcasters have privately expressed safety concerns over the contest being staged in Jerusalem or Tel Aviv, should the country win in the future.

Although Israel will undoubtedly be seen as the target of the rule change, it will also affect Ukraine, which has been engaged in a protracted war since it was invaded by Russia in 2022.

Ukrainian group Kalush Orchestra went on to win Eurovision that same year, in a symbolic show of public support.

Following their victory, Eurovision organisers undertook a "full assessment and feasibility study" to decide whether the 2023 contest could proceed in Kyiv.

They ultimately decided the security risks were too great, and the UK stepped in to host the competition in Liverpool.

News.title: Lucy Davis urges women to check their breasts for cancer - here's how
News.content:
Signs of breast cancer are not always a lump in the traditional sense, so what should you look for?

Actress Lucy Davis, who played Dawn Tinsley in the original UK version of the popular TV series The Office, has revealed she has incurable breast cancer.

On Instagram, external, the 53-year-old said it had spread to her bones and it was too late for chemo.

She added: "The initial lump that I felt, wasn't a 'lump' as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny."

Here's how to check yourself at home.

News.title: Ministers push ahead with housing asylum seekers on ex-military sites
News.content:
Home Office minister Anna Turley has said the government is sticking with plans to accommodate asylum-seekers on former military bases despite protests from local residents.

She told the BBC the government's priority was to ensure asylum-seekers were looked after in a "secure" and "appropriate" place.

That included disused Ministry of Defence properties because they had on-site facilities and were "more contained," she added.

But campaigners in areas earmarked for asylum centres have said small communities with limited infrastructure would not be able to cope with large numbers of people.

There have been protests in Piddington, Oxfordshire, over plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers at a site near the village.

Mike Nixon, the vice-chairman of Piddington Parish Council, said there was a "huge amount of concern and worry" among residents and that an asylum centre would have a "dramatic effect" on the way they lived their lives.

The proposal has prompted Piddington to hold a symbolic independence referendum, asking its 400 or so residents if they want to remain part of the UK.

Nixon said: "We're still very frustrated. Andy Burnham did say that he's willing to listen, but we've had no formal contact. No consultation, nothing from the Home Office.

"We felt that the only way of making our views felt was to say 'well if we're not going to be listened to, what's the point of being a part of the country?'"

The government has promised to end the use of hotels for asylum seekers, announcing on Wednesday that a further 13 across England had been closed.

It plans to use former military sites instead with two already up and running - RAF Wethersfield in Essex, and Crowborough Training Camp in East Sussex.

In June, it announced proposals to open three more, including the site near Piddington.

The two other planned sites are a former RAF base in Barnham in Suffolk where there were protests last week and RAF Linton-on-Ouse in North Yorkshire where the area's Labour mayor said it was "simply the wrong place".

Defending the proposals on BBC Breakfast, Turley said the public wanted the government to end the use of hotels, pointing to how an "iconic" hotel in Blackpool, the Metropole, was no longer being used to accommodate asylum-seekers.

She said it sent "an important message" that the government wanted the hotel to be part of Blackpool's future.

"The priority is to ensure we look after asylum seekers in a secure place that is more appropriate and we limit the impact on communities."

Asked what she meant by secure, she said: "Examples we are looking at is former military bases and we have two up and running and possibly another three.

"They have have facilities on site and are more contained and it limits the impact on on communities.

"We are looking at other sites such as former industrial sites, student accommodation - accommodation that is more more appropriate than hotels."

News.title: New Forest wildfire continues as temperatures rise
News.content:
Firefighters on the fourth day of battling a wildfire in the New Forest are facing "challenging" weather conditions with temperatures set to rise again

The blaze began on Sunday 9 August when a van caught fire on the A31, with 23 drivers abandoning their vehicles as the fire took hold.

Hampshire & Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service (HIWFRS) said crews had implemented fire breaks and had a 'good hold' of the perimeter of the fire, while changing wind conditions were proving challenging.

National Highways said repairs to the A31 were not expected to be begin until Friday 14 August at the earliest.

News.title: Victim of fatal Clapham shooting named
News.content:
A man who was shot dead in south-west London has been named by police as Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa.

Officers and paramedics were called to Willington Road, Clapham, just before 22:00 BST on Monday following reports of gunshots near The Landor pub.

The 25-year-old, who worked as a bus driver, was pronounced dead at the scene, the Metropolitan Police said.

A 22-year-old man was later arrested on suspicion of murder after attending hospital with a gunshot wound on Tuesday. He remains in hospital under police guard.

Det Ch Insp Claire Guiver said her thoughts were with the victim's family as they "come to terms with this tragic incident".

News.title: Estonia rejects proposals to take prisoners from UK jails
News.content:
The Estonian government has rejected the idea of taking prisoners from the UK to help ease the overcrowding crisis in British jails.

Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta told the BBC Estonia would not rent jail cells to other countries while it was housing criminals from Sweden in its half-empty Tartu prison under a deal signed last week.

The Conservatives and Reform UK have both suggested renting cells in foreign prisons, including in Estonia, to free up space and prevent the early releases of some offenders in England and Wales.

The Labour government also explored the idea in 2024 but talks with Estonia came to nothing.

Pakosta said Estonia had received no proposals to rent its prison space from the UK, adding that if one was to be made "our answer would be unequivocal - in Margaret Thatcher's famous words: No. No. No."

She added: "Such a proposal would not merely be mistaken, misguided or unacceptable; it would deserve to be rejected outright."

Thatcher memorably repeated "no" three times in 1990 speech, as she fiercely rejected calls for deeper political and economic integration of the European Community, which later evolved into the European Union.

In 2024, the Labour government, when Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister, held talks with Estonia to discuss the Baltic state's policy to house some prisoners from abroad.

Pakosta previously told the BBC she had met then-UK Justice Secretary Shabana Mahmood in Lithuania.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government is planning to release thousands of prisoners early this October, as it scrambles to free up space in jails almost at 100% capacity.

On Monday, Downing Street did not rule out renting space in foreign prisons, when asked by reporters if the government was considering doing so.

A No 10 spokesperson said the government was focused on "creating that extra capacity within the system domestically".

"In terms of renting prison places abroad, it's just not a quick fix," the spokesperson added.

"It will require primary legislation underpinned by a complex international agreement which would take several years to agree."

A government source told the BBC that renting foreign prison space would not help with the short-term crisis in jails.

Burnham has ordered the justice secretary to come up with a plan to create more space in jails by September.

He said the plan would be based on removing more foreign national offenders from prisons, releasing some offenders on indefinite sentences, and using space in women's jails for male inmates.

News.title: Windermere signs to warn of algae poisoning risk
News.content:
Dozens of signs warning people about the dangers of algae poisoning are to be placed around England's largest lake.

About 40 notice boards alerting visitors to blue-green algae blooms, which can produce toxins that make humans ill and be fatal to pets, will be installed at Windermere, in the Lake District.

Blooms occur naturally but are more frequent during warm, dry weather and are exacerbated by nutrients from phosphate in pollutants such as sewage.

Funded by the Environment Agency (EA), a further 40 signs will be placed at other locations across Cumbria.

The Love Windermere Partnership, which includes organisations such as the EA, Lake District National Park Authority and United Utilities, said it was installing the permanent signs in response to requests for "clearer and more consistent public information".

As well as explaining what blue-green algae looks like, the notices will provide guidance on where to find current information about blooms and how to report suspected sightings using the Bloomin' Algae app, external.

The microscopic organisms can look like blue-green paint, scum or greenish-brown discolouration.

News.title: I share concerns over Arday appointment, says Cambridge University head
News.content:
The vice-chancellor of the University of Cambridge has said she understands the concerns raised by the appointment of Jason Arday and shares them too.

In a letter to staff, Prof Deborah Prentice acknowledged the "anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case".

The university head also announced Cambridge's investigation would be independent and carried out by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge and will begin "as soon as possible".

Arday resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education last week amid allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements.

The 41-year-old - who became Cambridge's youngest ever black professor in 2023 - denies any plagiarism and said the recent furore had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

In a letter to university staff, Prof Deborah Prentice said: "I fully understand the concerns being raised across the University and well beyond it, regarding Jason Arday's appointment and I share them...

"We will now investigate the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education back in 2022 and his time here in Cambridge since his appointment nearly four years ago.

"That investigation, as you say, should be thorough and transparent, and will be carried out independently by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge."

The findings of the investigation, previously announced on Friday, will inform a review into the process for the appointment of senior academic roles, the university has said.

Prentice added "our staff of colour are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements, and the contributions they make" and said the case "should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge".

Cambridge had previously said allegations of plagiarism regarding Arday's thesis and some journal publications had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University (LMJU) and the journals in question.

LJMU - which awarded his PhD in 2015 - had investigated the allegations that were made last year, and found he did not commit plagiarism.

In an interview with the Times, Arday defended himself by arguing that he had not received adequate supervision during his PhD given his autism and "learning disabilities".

The University of Cambridge said it had advised people to contact the relevant institution or pass on complaints.

But after Cambridge announced its own investigation, some academics pushed for the inquiry to be independent, questioning whether the university could adequately investigate its own processes.

It is not yet clear how the independent investigation will work or who will lead it. The university said it will look at the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education in 2022 and his time in Cambridge since his appointment.

Arday worked as a PE teacher before earning his doctorate at LMJU and going on to become an associate professor at Durham University and professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow.

Glasgow has also announced a review into Arday's previous academic post.

When he resigned from his post, Arday said he was not a "liar" and that his resignation "should not be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."

News.title: Man bled to death after being bitten by American XL Bully, court hears
News.content:
A man died from extreme blood loss after suffering "catastrophic injuries" when he was bitten on the leg by an American XL bully in his daughter-in-law's garden, a court has heard.

Keven Jones, 62, from Chester, who was in poor health, taking methadone and blood thinning medication, was staying at Chanel Fong's house at the time of the incident.

The incident took place before XL Bullies were added to the banned dog list in October 2023.

Fong, 33, denies being the owner of the dog, which the prosecution said was dangerously out of control at the time, and also denies an alternative charge of being the person in charge of a dog at the time of the attack.

Opening the case at Caernarfon Crown Court, prosecutor Mark Connor said it was a "sad and tragic case for everyone concerned" and told the jury they would be shown some "graphic images" of Jones' injuries during the trial.

He said it was not a case of whether the XL Bully, named Cookie, was a banned breed, but rather that the dog had been "dangerously out of control" and whether Fong was legally responsible for it, either as its owner or the person responsible for it at the time.

The court was told the dog was owned by Fong and her partner, Joshua Jones, the son of the victim, but that he was not present at the time of the attack.

Connor added that, in her police interview, Fong said on paper Cookie belonged to her partner.

He went on to describe how there were a number of dogs at the property on Holt Road in Wrexham, including Cookie and another XL Bully called Fire, who were in the back garden at the time.

Cookie's mother, an XL Bully called Rogue, was inside the property and was "in season" meaning she had been kept separate from the other dogs in the house.

News.title: Early release scheme risks more serious crimes, probation chief inspector warns
News.content:
The chief inspector of probation for England and Wales has told the BBC the early release of thousands of prisoners could lead to "a serious sexual or violent offence or even murder" because of the demands on probation staff to monitor offenders.

The government is set to release 5,000 offenders from October as part of new laws to create more space in overcrowded prisons.

Probation officers supervise offenders after prison sentences and check they follow the terms of their release, such as sticking to curfews and not taking drugs.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said "protecting the public is our top priority", adding it had invested in probation and hiring trainee officers.

But Martin Jones, His Majesty's Chief Inspector of probation for England and Wales, told the BBC that "ultimately I'm not fully confident that the probation system will be able to cope with this massive work and there's a risk that things will go wrong".

"Probation services are already under unprecedented pressure.

"I mean, they're managing a caseload of 258,000 cases, that's nearly three times the number that are in our prisons, and obviously the early release scheme will be increasing that pressure considerably."

On Tuesday, 50 police chiefs across the UK signed a letter to the prime minister urging him to pursue "every legal option" to prevent the early release of PC Andrew Harper's killers under the scheme.

They called for called for greater consideration of victims when prisoners have their sentences altered, adding: "Families across the country are now facing the distress of learning that offenders may be released earlier than they understood when sentence was passed."

They also welcomed Burnham's intervention on Tuesday, when he said he was "confident" the early release of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were jailed for 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, in January could be stopped.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp told BBC Breakfast the early release plans had "put public safety at risk as well as disrespecting victims and undermining confidence in the criminal justice system".

He urged Burnham to "pay attention and listen" to the senior police officers, adding he had "never seen every chief constable in the country write to the prime minister directly in this way".

Philip and Nick Timothy, the Conservative shadow justice secretary, wrote to Burnham on Tuesday urging him to introduce emergency primary legislation in September to amend the Sentencing Act 2026.

The letter said grooming gang perpetrators, including those convicted of indecent assault, and those convicted of the manslaughter of an emergency worker should be exempt from the early release scheme.

Stunning images show the solar eclipse as millions of people around the world gather to witness Europe's first total eclipse in 27 years.

Huge groups sat under clear skies in cities and towns across Spain Wednesday, equipped with folding lawn chairs, sun umbrellas, and hats eagerly waiting for the celestial spectacle.

Vast crowds across a wide band of northern and central Spain had front-row seats for some of mainland Europe's best viewing opportunities.

Narrow slivers of Iceland and Greenland were also positioned to observe the sun, moon, and Earth align, briefly casting portions of the planet into darkness.

open image in gallery A view of the total eclipse as seen from a cruise ship off the coast of Greenland ( Owen Humphreys/PA Wire )

open image in gallery The total eclipse seen from Iceland ( Sky News )

open image in gallery The moon completely covers the sun during a total solar eclipse as seen from Arija, Spain ( Reuters )

The period of totality — when the moon completely covers the sun’s light — was projected to last under 2 1/2 minutes, peaking off the western coast of Iceland.

As the alignment moves toward a small slice of Portugal and into Spain just prior to sunset, totality will shrink to around a minute or so before concluding over the Mediterranean.

The celestial event happens when the moon passes in front of the sun, obscuring its light.

That produces a stunning ring of fire around the lunar surface, as well as eerie events such as the day dramatically dimming and confused birds singing.

open image in gallery The sun emerging from the side of the moon after the total eclipse in Iceland ( Sky News )

open image in gallery The sun emerging from the side of the moon after the total eclipse in Iceland ( Sky News )

open image in gallery The solar eclipse seen from King's Stairs Gardens in Bermondsey, south London ( Aaron Chown/PA Wire )

The Iberian Peninsula last saw a total solar eclipse in 1912 and it is set to experience another on August 2, 2027, and an annular eclipse in January 2028, completing the so-called "Iberian Eclipse Trio."

U.S. space agency NASA plans to fly a high-altitude WB-57 aircraft from Iceland to follow the Moon's shadow, and NASA-funded teams will launch balloons to study how the sudden darkness and cooling affect the lower atmosphere.

open image in gallery The sun over Canary Wharf, London during the solar eclipse ( Ian West/PA Wire )

open image in gallery In Weymouth, Dorset, England ( The Independent )

open image in gallery The partial eclipse seen from Observatorielunden park in central Stockholm, Sweden ( TT NEWS AGENCY/AFP via Getty Ima )

open image in gallery A few of the moon partially covering the sun during a solar eclipse as seen from Arija, Spain ( REUTERS )

open image in gallery The Moon passes between the Earth and the Sun 6.38pm at the start of the solar eclipse as seen from King's Stairs Gardens in Bermondsey, south London ( Aaron Chown/PA Wire )

News.title: I’m a space expert. Here’s why the solar eclipse may leave you feeling ‘emotional’
News.content:

A space expert has suggested that onlookers might feel "emotional" while observing the finest solar eclipse in decades.

On Wednesday evening, gatherings formed at various vantage points across the country, including the Royal Observatory Greenwich in London, Calton Hill in Edinburgh, and outside Queen’s University in Belfast.

More than 90 per cent of the Sun was obscured by the Moon, marking the most significant solar coverage seen above UK skies since the total eclipse of 1999.

Spectators brought specialised or homemade viewing equipment, including devices crafted from cereal boxes and colanders.

open image in gallery More than 90 per cent of the Sun was obscured by the Moon, marking the most significant solar coverage seen above UK skies since the total eclipse of 1999 ( Getty )

Others carried their own chairs, while photographers gathered with cameras. Videos shared on social media showed a long queue in Goring, West Sussex, as people appeared to wait for protective glasses to be handed out for the event.

Queen guitarist and astrophysicist Sir Brian May posted a video of himself on Instagram waiting for the eclipse on a hillside in which he can be seen looking at an image on an iPad and asking a man nearby “how long ’til totality?”.

In an earlier post on his stories, the musician said he would be taking a white ceramic plate down to help him view the event.

Dhara Patel, who is a space expert at the National Space Centre, said some people may be overcome by emotion while watching the eclipse.

Speaking at the UK’s largest space attraction in Leicester, she told the Press Association: “For a lot of people, it can be a little bit of an emotional event.

“I’ve seen previously people being drawn to tears or just have a really good moment within themselves where they realise they’re seeing or witnessing something… you’ve never seen before in your life.”

She described it as “incredible” to be able to witness this eclipse, adding: “We’ve had solar eclipses over the last couple of years, about 30% coverage.

“They’ve been good, but this is definitely a different scale.

“And what’s really nice is it’s a way for lots of people to come together and connect with nature – looking up at the sky at objects that we typically tend to take for granted.”

open image in gallery People gather to watch the partial solar eclipse in Greenwich Park on August 12, 2026 in London, United Kingdom ( Getty )

Convenience stores, national parks and the Royal Greenwich Observatory all exhausted their glasses supplies ahead of the eclipse, which will be the country’s fullest for the next 54 years.

The Royal Greenwich Observatory said it had sold approximately 15,000 pairs of eclipse glasses, a sellout, in the last month.

John Lewis said colander sales have increased nearly 40% compared to last year, as Nasa recommends the kitchen item as a way to watch the eclipse by viewing the shadows it casts on the ground.

A spokesperson said: “Colander sales have surged nearly 40% compared to last year, as shoppers prepare for tonight’s eclipse.

“We’ve still got plenty of stock for anyone wanting to view this solar phenomenon safely, and, unlike eclipse glasses, you can use it to strain your spaghetti for dinner afterwards.”

Imo Bell, a planetarium astronomer at the Royal Greenwich Observatory, said: “You can project the image of the eclipse using a household item like a colander which has lots of holes in, point the colander towards the sun with your back facing it, and in the shadow of the colander you’ll be able to see the eclipse in the holes, which is really cool.”

Only special solar eclipse glasses that are ISO 12312-2 certified for the safest eye protection should be used and sunglasses are not sufficient, experts said.

Following the 1999 total solar eclipse, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists reported around 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems after watching the eclipse.

Around 40% had looked at it for less than a minute.

Devon, Cornwall and the westernmost parts of Pembrokeshire in Wales are set to see the eclipse at its fullest, with a range of 94% to 96% of the sun obscured by the Moon.

Plymouth in particular is forecast to see the Moon cover 94.66% of the sun at 7.16pm on Wednesday, according to the Met Office.

open image in gallery TWedding guests watch the solar eclipse at Alpheton in Suffolk ( PA )

The rest of Wales, Northern Ireland, parts of the West Midlands and the South West, and the westernmost parts of Scotland can expect to see 92% to 94% solar coverage.

In Cardiff, the Moon is forecast to obscure 93.24% of the sun at 7.13pm while in Belfast it will cover 93.09% of the sun at 7.08pm.

Skygazers in the rest of the UK will likely see the Moon obscure 90% to 92% of the sun, with 91.79% expected in Birmingham at 7.12pm, 91.41% in London at 7.13pm, 90.74% in Inverness at 7.03pm, 90.71% in Edinburgh at 7.06pm and 90.22% in Newcastle at 7.07pm.

Those most keen to catch a sight of the fullest possible solar eclipse should avoid the easternmost parts of the UK, where only 88% to 90% of solar coverage is expected.

These include the coasts of Norfolk, Yorkshire and Aberdeenshire, as well as the Orkney and Shetland Islands.

In an added bonus for stargazers, the annual Perseid meteor shower reaches its peak on the night of August 12-13, hours after the eclipse.

The shower is produced as Earth ploughs through a stream of dust left behind by Comet Swift–Tuttle.

Each tiny grain strikes Earth’s atmosphere at about 60 kilometres per second, burning up in a brief flash that takes the appearance of a shooting star.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso) has cancelled its call to the industry to generate more power during the eclipse.

A Neso spokesman said the notice had been issued “as a precautionary measure to the market due to the solar eclipse”.

He added: “Issuing an electricity margin notice gives the market a clear signal that additional capacity may be useful during this evening’s peak and helps us maintain the level of operating margin we expect to carry.

“To be clear, there is no risk to customer electricity supplies.”

Meanwhile, drivers are being warned they may need to turn on their headlights during the eclipse.

RAC head of policy Simon Williams said: “While total darkness is unlikely, those with vehicles that don’t have automatic headlights or daylight running lights may need to switch on their dipped beams to ensure they are easily visible to other road users.

“The best advice to enjoy this rare event is to pull over somewhere safe and watch with specialist glasses.”

News.title: Manchester United v Leeds LIVE: Zirkzee opens scoring as Carrick’s men take on old rivals in Dublin
News.content:
Carrick - the right man for right now

Leeds United and Manchester United continue their preparations for the new Premier League season as old foes renew their rivalry at Croke Park in Dublin.

This will be another chapter in a storied history between the pair as they collide at the home of Irish sport just 10 days before the start of their league campaigns. Michael Carrick’s side impressed in a 1-1 draw against Paris Saint-Germain at the weekend as Youri Tielemans made his bow for the club, though injury worries over Mason Mount may underline the need for more midfield reinforcements.

Leeds have had a relatively eye-catching summer with James Trafford, Tarik Muharemovic and Harry Wilson all high-profile additions. Wins over Liverpool and RB Leipzig have shown encouraging signs and Daniel Farke will be keen to keep the momentum rolling ahead of their Premier League opener against Nottingham Forest next Saturday.

Follow all of the latest from the pre-season friendly in Dublin with our live blog below:

The mayor of Portland has declared an emergency as city officials respond to a fire-damaged building that may collapse and impact operations at a nearby rail line.

A fire broke out in the Centennial Mills building earlier this month, leaving the building charred and exposing dangerous materials inside. Fire crews reportedly tested the debris from the building and found it contained asbestos and lead, according to KOIN.

The building is set to be demolished on Friday, but officials are concerned it may collapse due to the fire damage before it can be safely dismantled. City officials said the building is being constantly monitored.

Compounding the safety concerns is the building's proximity to an active rail line operated by Union Pacific.

The transportation company said it will continue to operate near the building to prevent supply chain disruptions. On Monday, a spokesperson told KATU that shuttering that section of the railroad would impact "regional industries, small businesses, ports and consumer goods."

The Centennial Mills building in northwest Portland. The building was damaged in a fire and is at risk of collapse, threatening the surrounding area as well as Union Pacific rail lines running near the structure ( M O Stevens )

The company said that trains will only move at 10 mph or less while passing by the building and only operate on the rail farthest from the building to protect the trains in the event of a collapse.

City officials warned that the vibrations caused by the passing rail cars could further erode the building's stability and trigger a collapse.

Portland City Administrator Raymond Lee said he has warned Union Pacific of the potential risks.

“I know this is constraining to their operations, but our first responsibility is community safety,” Lee said.

He noted that the "city has very limited authority to really stop the trains.”

Union Pacific issued a statement this week responding to concerns over its continued operation near the building.

"Union Pacific transports a broad array of commodities and products important to Oregon consumers, regional industries and businesses, with more than 400,000 rail cars either originating or arriving in the state," the statement said. "We are a critical link in the supply chain, and an important mode of transportation for businesses in Oregon to access both domestic and international markets."

The statement added that a "closure of a critical rail line such as the one in Portland for more than week – with no end in sight - has real-world impact on these businesses and a ripple effect that impacts the broader supply chain."

"One more thing: it’s fair to say there are few things that you can find on store shelves or in your own home that weren’t – at one time – transported by rail," the company said.

Members of the public have been advised to avoid the area until the building has been dismantled.

The building was used as a flour mill and was in operation between 1910 and 2000.

The Independent has requested comment from the city.

News.title: ‘Thank goodness!’: Builder almost misses out on £1m lottery win after ignoring ‘sales’ calls
News.content:

A Somerset family will claim a £1million lottery jackpot having very nearly missed out on the prize after ignoring calls and emails they thought were spam.

Mark Jefferson, who played with his wife Naomi and four children, said it was only by chance that he reluctantly answered a call from the National Lottery after nine days turning down their attempts to reach him.

“You get so many calls and emails these days – I just thought it was another sales call so it was only by chance I answered, thank goodness I did,” said the builder from Ilminster.

“When I was told I'd won a million pounds, I genuinely thought someone was winding me up. It sounded completely ridiculous. A builder from Somerset being told over the phone he'd won £1M? I wasn't convinced at all.”

open image in gallery The family from Somerset plan to spend the money on supporting the children and spending more time together ( The National Lottery )

The family syndicate matched five main numbers and the Bonus Ball in the Lotto draw on 24 June, winning a £1m prize that will be shared between Mark, Naomi, and their four adult children, Alexandra, Lily and Emily and Taylor.

Mark said he had already received a few notifications telling him to check his account and guessed he had probably won “a few pounds”.

But he said he was “absolutely floored” when he learned that he had won such a huge amount of money for his family.

“I was in tears,” he said. “To think I'd spent nine days ignoring emails about something so life-changing is incredible."

The family set up their syndicate less than a year ago, on 20 July 2025, to celebrate Mark’s birthday. Each member chose one Lotto line for each draw. The winning numbers were selected by daughter Alexandra.

open image in gallery Mark Jefferson, who played with his wife Naomi and four children, said it was only by chance that he reluctantly answered a call from the National Lottery after nine days turning down their attempts to reach him ( The National Lottery )

“I've played The National Lottery for years but we only started the family syndicate last summer,” said Mark.

“To win less than a year later feels incredible. You always hear about people winning and wonder what it would feel like. Now we're the family everyone talks about.”

Mark said it was not the first time that someone in the extended family had won big on the National Lottery.

“In 1995, a close relative shared a £16.2M Lotto jackpot...with 132 other winning ticket-holders!” he said.

While helping their children financially is a priority, the family is also planning to travel and spend time together making memories.

Among the first plans are a big family holiday abroad, a new convertible for Naomi and a caravan on the south coast where they can enjoy spontaneous weekends away together.

open image in gallery Mark said he had already received a few notifications telling him to check his account and guessed he had probably won “a few pounds”. ( The National Lottery )

“For us, it's all about making memories. Knowing the family has opportunities we never imagined before is the best feeling in the world,” Mark said.

More than 100 people have become millionaires through the National Lottery since the start of the year, operator Allwyn said.

It also emerged this week that a mother who says her winning lottery ticket was accidentally binned by a shopkeeper will be allowed to claim her £12million jackpot following an agonising wait.

Kath Main, 46, from Pontypridd in South Wales, appealed after the owner of the Londis in Abercynon threw out her ticket when his scanner failed to register her numbers as a win, according to The Sun.

National Lottery operator Allwyn launched a 30-day investigation and has now concluded that Ms Main will be able to claim her win - so long as nobody else comes forward by 3 December.

Ms Main, the secretary of a rugby club, previously said that she “feels sick all the time” waiting for the potential payout, and that she hopes to use some of the money on a Lions rugby tour of New Zealand.

News.title: Andy Burnham must be brave to tackle burning Britain
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum.
