The meeting follows two extraordinary seizures in the space of a few weeks. In July, security personnel intercepted six cargo boxes at Roberts International Airport disguised as textiles and seasoning cubes; inside were nearly 200 compressed blocks of cocaine, ultimately valued around $19 million — a case that drew public criticism after delays in identifying suspects raised fears that individuals connected to the shipment had already fled the country. Weeks later came a seizure of a different order of magnitude entirely: nearly four tonnes of cocaine, worth an estimated $317.7 million, recovered from what investigators described as an organized, sophisticated, and well-funded trafficking network that may have operated in Liberia for more than six years. Authorities later incinerated 4.2 metric tons of the drug, sending what Coleman called a message that Liberia was no longer “a place of comfort” for traffickers.

What has made the second bust politically explosive, however, is who it implicated. Coleman confirmed that Liberia’s chief of highway patrol and the head of the major crimes unit face charges, with a deputy police commander at the main airport also under suspicion — meaning the very institution now meant to lead enforcement, the Liberia National Police, has senior officers accused of facilitating the trafficking it is supposed to stop.

The credibility problem the U.S. visit runs into

That is precisely why Zadrozny’s meeting cannot be read purely as encouragement. Coleman himself has become a subject of serious, if unproven, allegations. In a July 15 letter to Zadrozny, CDC Secretary General Jefferson Koijee requested U.S. backing for an international investigation, alleging that Coleman took vehicles from a drug cartel and distributed them to President Boakai, Vice President Koung, and the presiding officers of the Legislature, and separately that the 2024 removal of former LDEA head Abraham Kromah was orchestrated by Coleman to protect a cartel he was allegedly connected to, and that Coleman later maneuvered Fitzgerald Biago — his own deputy at the police — into the LDEA’s top job. Koijee’s broader argument was structural: that repeatedly installing senior police officers atop the drug agency has blurred the LDEA’s independence and concentrated excessive influence within Liberia’s security apparatus.

Notably, Boakai’s own government has now partly validated that structural critique without validating the corruption allegation. Monday’s Executive Mansion release states that the Justice Ministry’s probe into Biago “did not establish any involvement… in illegal narcotics trafficking” but did identify unspecified “ethical concerns” — landing in a gray zone that neither clears the LDEA leadership pipeline of suspicion nor confirms the most serious claims against it. Biago’s own departure now repeats the very pattern Koijee flagged: a police-to-LDEA pipeline replaced, once again, by another appointee — this time a retired general rather than a police officer, which may itself be read as an attempt to break that cycle.

What the U.S. statement does — and doesn’t — say

Read against this backdrop, Zadrozny’s language is carefully calibrated. It reaffirms partnership and frames Liberian institution-building as serving “regional stability” and the “enduring friendship” between the two countries — standard diplomatic register. But it also pointedly addresses itself to “law and order” and “a just and accountable legal system,” phrasing that functions as quiet pressure on Coleman and Gaye specifically to see the investigations — including into their own ranks — through to a credible conclusion, rather than as an unqualified vote of confidence in current leadership.

The U.S. has skin in this game beyond diplomacy: earlier reporting has linked American law enforcement, including the Department of Justice, to the broader trafficking investigation tied to the record cocaine seizure, and West Africa’s role as a transit corridor — now carrying an estimated 30 percent of Europe-bound cocaine, according to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime — makes Liberia’s enforcement capacity a matter of direct interest to Washington and European partners alike, not just Monrovia.

The stakes for the investigation ahead

For Ziankahn’s incoming LDEA leadership, the practical effect of the U.S. engagement is likely to be twofold: continued technical and possibly intelligence-sharing support for dismantling the trafficking network behind the record bust, paired with implicit international scrutiny of whether Liberia’s own police leadership — the officials the U.S. just met with — can be trusted to police itself.

Whether Coleman and Gaye emerge from the ongoing probes as central figures in prosecuting this case, or as subjects of it, may do more than any embassy statement to determine whether Liberia’s “war on drugs” produces lasting institutional reform or simply another rotation of the same personnel through different chairs.

World.title: Guinea Border: Time for Government to Level with the Liberian People
World.content:
Since February, Liberia’s border with Guinea has seen repeated incursions, a flag removal, troop deployments, and the displacement of thousands of residents in Lofa County. President Boakai has pursued the right diplomatic path — tripartite summits, joint technical commissions, a special envoy — but the public has received only sporadic updates since. This editorial argues that quiet diplomacy without public transparency risks eroding trust at home and, given West Africa’s history, could let a manageable dispute harden into something far more dangerous. It calls on the government to communicate more regularly and plainly with affected communities, not just with counterparts in Conakry.

FOR NEARLY a year now, communities along Liberia’s border with Guinea have lived with a question their government has not fully answered: what exactly is happening on our land, and what is being done about it?

PICTURE A FAMILY in Sorlumba, in Foya District, going about an ordinary morning — tending a farm plot, walking to a river crossing they’ve used their whole lives — when armed soldiers from across the border appear and declare the ground beneath their feet belongs to someone else. That is not a hypothetical. It is close to what residents there say happened earlier this year, when Guinean soldiers reportedly crossed into Liberian territory, seized construction equipment from a Liberian road contractor, and — most provocatively — ordered the removal of the Liberian flag that had flown at the riverbank for decades, even through the years of civil war. ￼ For people who lived through that war, watching their flag come down was not an abstract diplomatic incident. It was personal.

THE BARE FACTS, as they have trickled out through news reports rather than official candor, are troubling enough on their own. Alleged incursions in February sent panic through border communities. Guinea responded to the rising tension not with reassurance but with troop deployments to the frontier, and Liberia’s own rights commission later found that the affair had displaced thousands of residents and exposed serious gaps in both border protection and regional diplomacy. Thousands of displaced people is not a statistic to file away — it is thousands of individual decisions to grab what could be carried and walk away from home, uncertain when, or whether, it would be safe to return.

TO ITS CREDIT, the Boakai administration did not let the crisis spiral into confrontation. President Boakai joined his Guinean and Sierra Leonean counterparts in Conakry in March for a tripartite summit that produced commitments to dialogue, joint technical commissions on border delimitation, and a pledge to convene a full Mano River Union summit within a month to “revitalize” the organization. In June, Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah reaffirmed that Liberia remained committed to resolving the dispute through diplomacy, and that a special presidential envoy had been dispatched to follow up on the Conakry commitments.

THESE ARE THE RIGHT instincts. Nobody serious wants Liberia and Guinea shooting at each other over a riverbank in Foya.

BUT GOOD INSTINCTS are not the same as good governance, and here is where the government’s approach has fallen short: the Liberian public still does not know, in any real detail, where things stand. The promised MRU summit, floated for July, has come and gone without a clear public accounting of whether it happened, what it produced, or why it may have slipped. The joint technical commissions on border delimitation — the actual mechanism that would settle, once and for all, whose land is whose — have operated largely out of public view. The people of Lofa County did not get to choose whether their homes sat on contested ground. The least they are owed is honesty about what their government is doing to protect them.

THIS MATTERS for reasons beyond transparency as a good-governance principle. West Africa has spent the better part of four decades relearning, at enormous human cost, how quickly a border dispute can metastasize into something far worse. Liberia’s own seven-year civil war and Sierra Leone’s decade of conflict were not born in a vacuum — porous, poorly governed borders and cross-border grievances were accelerants for both. Analysts tracking the current tensions have noted that all four Mano River Union countries have emerged from civil conflict, yet peace remains fragile due to weak border governance, contested territorial claims, and shifting political transitions ￼ — a diagnosis that should concentrate minds in Monrovia as much as in Conakry.

THERE IS ALSO a very human political risk in silence. When government communication goes quiet, the space fills with rumor, opposition point-scoring, and — as nearly happened in Foya, where young residents reportedly moved to confront Guinean soldiers directly rather than wait for diplomacy to work — with ordinary citizens deciding to defend their own communities because no one has told them help is coming. A government that explains its strategy clearly gives frightened people a reason to trust the process instead of taking matters into their own hands.

WE ARE NOT calling for saber-rattling, nor for the kind of “inflammatory rhetoric” the government has rightly said it wants to avoid. We are calling for the opposite: more information, delivered more often, in language ordinary Liberians in Foya and Vahun can understand and act on — not just diplomatic communiqués aimed at regional bodies and foreign audiences.

PRESIDENT BOAKAI has said, correctly, that this is “not a matter for confrontation, but for calm, facts and sustained engagement.” We agree entirely — provided that “facts” reach the farmers, traders, and families living along that border, and not only the diplomats in closed-door rooms in Conakry. Liberia has been here before. The region does not need reminding of what happens when land disputes are left to fester unexplained. Let this government show, through consistent and honest public communication, that it has learned that lesson.

World.title: Liberians Trapped in Cambodian Detention Plead for a Way Home
World.content:
A group of Liberian nationals, writing through spokesperson Emmanuel Johnson, say they’ve been held at a Cambodian immigration detention center in Phnom Penh since May 25, 2026 — not for any crime, but because they can’t afford flight tickets home. They say they were trafficked to Cambodia under false job promises, had their passports and phones confiscated, and were eventually rescued by Cambodian police. Their overstay violations were later resolved through Liberia’s Embassy in China. Still, with no funds for airfare, they remain detained — now facing the threat of transfer to Cambodia’s main prison if tickets aren’t secured soon.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia- Emmanuel Johnson, writing on behalf of the group, says they have been held at the Cambodian Immigration Detention Center since May 25, 2026. Their offense, in the eyes of Cambodian authorities, is not one of intent — it is one of poverty. Officials have told them the only thing standing between them and freedom is a plane ticket home. They cannot afford one.

A Promise That Became a Trap

The group’s story follows a pattern that has become disturbingly familiar across Southeast Asia in recent years. Johnson says the Liberians did not travel to Cambodia seeking trouble — they went believing they had secured legitimate jobs. The recruiters who arranged their visas and flights delivered them instead into a scheme with no real employment waiting on the other end. Their passports and phones were confiscated on arrival, and they were held until Cambodian police intervened and rescued them.

It is a story that echoes what international human rights investigators have been documenting for more than a year. Amnesty International, which interviewed 73 survivors of Cambodia’s scamming compounds — including nationals of Liberia, Ghana, Kenya, Ethiopia, and more than a dozen other countries — between July 2025 and April 2026, has found that victims recruited under false employment promises are routinely trafficked into compounds where they are confined and coerced. What makes the aftermath particularly cruel, according to that research, is what happens after rescue: not one of the 73 survivors Amnesty interviewed was recognized by Cambodian authorities as a victim of human trafficking, despite meeting the internationally agreed legal definition — instead, many were detained in overcrowded immigration centers, charged for visa overstays, and in some cases threatened with return to the very compounds they had escaped.

That is precisely the limbo in which Johnson and his compatriots now find themselves — rescued from exploitation, only to be imprisoned for the crime of having nowhere to go and no means to get there.

Government Channels, Dead Ends

According to Johnson’s account, the group has not sat passively. They say they approached Liberia’s Embassy in China, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Liberia Refugee Repatriation and Resettlement Commission (LRRRC), and were told that officials would work with the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in Cambodia to arrange their return. That effort, they say, stalled: IOM reportedly informed them it lacked the resources to provide flight tickets.

The Liberian Embassy in China did intervene on one front — securing a resolution of the group’s immigration overstay violations with Cambodian authorities. But that diplomatic success solved only part of the problem. Without tickets home, the men and women remain detained, their overstay technically resolved but their freedom still contingent on money none of them have.

A Race Against Time

The appeal carries new urgency because of what Johnson describes as an explicit threat: if flight tickets are not secured soon, the group will be moved from the immigration detention center into Cambodia’s main prison system — a transfer that would mark a sharp escalation for people who, as Johnson puts it, “have committed no crime.”

Their situation is not unique in scale, even if it is deeply personal in its telling. Regional reporting has described escapees from Cambodia’s trafficking and scam-compound networks as frequently left without documents, shelter, or access to social services after their rescue, with some detained for immigration violations even as enforcement against the criminal networks themselves gradually increases. Investigators covering the broader crisis have also noted that Cambodian authorities have in some cases threatened trafficking survivors with return to the compounds they fled, while journalists attempting to report on the crisis have themselves faced arrest and intimidation.

“We Are Not Asking for Special Treatment”

What Johnson’s letter makes clear is that the group is not seeking exceptional intervention — only the ordinary mercy of a way home. “We are simply pleading for an opportunity to return home to our families and rebuild our lives,” he writes, adding that every additional day in detention worsens their physical and emotional condition.

For now, their fate rests on whether Liberian authorities, humanitarian organizations, or public pressure generated by their appeal can produce what months of formal channels have not: the price of a plane ticket, and a door out of detention before it becomes a cell.

World.title: Growth Without Development: Again, Liberia’s Self-Inflicted Development Crisis
World.content:
In the early 1960s, a Northwestern-led team of economists arrived to study what was then one of the fastest-growing economies on earth. Liberia was booming. Iron ore was moving through new ports, rubber was flowing, and foreign capital was arriving faster than almost anywhere in the world. They spent years examining this miracle, and in 1966 they published their conclusion under a title that should have haunted us forever: Growth Without Development: An Economic Survey of Liberia.

By Sei Philip Pleiwon, contributing writer

Their verdict was simple and devastating. Liberia had enormous economic activity and almost no economic transformation. The concessions operated beside the country, not inside it. Money moved through Liberia without becoming Liberia.

Sixty years have passed. We have lived through the boom, the coup, the war, the recovery, and five national development strategies. Billions of dollars in aid, investment, and public spending have entered this country. And the central diagnosis of that book remains uncomfortably current.

We have just marked 179 years of independence. Here is the plainest way I can put our condition:

Liberia is trying to develop without building an economy.

Before anyone reaches for their political feelings, understand what this essay is not. A problem that has survived military rule, civil conflict, transitional governments, and successive elected administrations cannot be reduced to the failure of any president, past or present. It is an operating logic, diagnosed repeatedly in our own plans and never operationally corrected. Corruption is real, and it is a crime against this country. But in Liberia it is also partly a function of that same incoherence: where nothing is organized toward a defined national outcome, resources are easier to divert and far harder to miss.

Development is what accumulates

We have mistaken the ingredients of development for development itself. Foreign investment, roads, schools, agriculture, digital skills: these can improve lives directly, and that matters. But they are inputs, and the question is what the country does with them.

Here is the distinction six decades keep teaching and we keep refusing to learn. Investment, aid, public expenditure, exports, construction, and training are flows: things entering, moving through, or occurring within the country. Development is the accumulation of stocks: capable people, productive firms, domestic capital, functioning institutions, technical knowledge, and state capacity.

An economy compounds when today’s production becomes tomorrow’s productive capacity. Production creates wages, profits, and taxes; part of those flows must become savings, stronger firms, knowledge, infrastructure, and new investment.

Liberia’s cycle runs differently. Foreign capital finances production, but much of the equipment, expertise, contracting, and finance is imported. Commodities and a substantial share of the value leave. Wages and revenue enter an import-dependent economy and a recurrent budget. Too little becomes locally owned productive capital. The activity is real; the accumulation is weak. A new concession can therefore begin twenty years after the last one and meet the same shortage of Liberian engineers, suppliers, finance, and technical institutions that existed before.

That is the development gap: the failure to convert economic flows into accumulating national capability.

The evidence is not subtle. A child born in Liberia can expect to achieve roughly 32 percent of the productivity she would attain with full health and education, according to the World Bank’s Human Capital Index. Real income per person remains below its pre-war peak. After sixty years of flows, we are behind where we started.

Everything ends at its first output

Watch how development actually works here, and you will notice a pattern so common it has become invisible.

The road ends at the road. The training ends at the certificate. The project ends at the report. The study ends at the study. The concession ends at extraction and revenue. The education ends at the degree. The identity card ends at the card.

We complete the first output, hold the ceremony, and move on. But development lives in what the output enables. So does every government’s account of itself: kilometers paved, budgets grown, buildings dedicated, graduates counted, jobs announced. We have reduced development to new hospitals, new schools, new light posts. It is why the country feels the way it does, undirected and confused, a place where things are thrown at the wall to see what sticks.

The question we never ask

There is one question Liberia has never put at the center of its development, and everything else follows from its absence: what should our people become capable of doing?

Ask it of education first. In China, between 2021 and 2025, universities eliminated or suspended more than 12,000 undergraduate degree programs, over 30 percent of all offerings, and created 10,000 new ones, realigning higher education with where the economy is going. Set aside every debate about China’s model and notice only what the act reveals: a state that has decided what its people must become capable of doing, and treats education as the instrument for producing it.

Now ask it here. Not how many are enrolled, or how many graduated, but what can a Liberian high school graduate actually do on the day she finishes, and what should she be capable of doing? No government has produced and enforced an answer specific enough to govern what programs are authorized, what public money funds, or who receives a scholarship. Universities open programs based on what they can staff and what students will enroll in. Students choose qualifications in a labor market the country does not measure, and they carry all the risk of guessing wrong. We are expanding an academic model inherited from the 1960s without deciding what the expansion is for. And this in a country of five and a half million people, small enough to know its own labor market. We graduate her into a void and call the ceremony an outcome. Education without an answer to what our people should be able to do is not education. It is attendance.

Now ask it of mining, where the answer has had sixty years to arrive. Visit any major concession and watch who does what. The machines are imported, and so, overwhelmingly, are the people who operate at the top of them: the engineers, the technicians, the laboratory and logistics contractors. Liberians are present, and mostly at the bottom of the ladder, in a country that has been mining iron ore since before their grandfathers were born. So what mining capability does Liberia now possess? How many mining engineers, geologists, and certified technicians has this country deliberately produced? Which categories of mining procurement can Liberian firms reliably supply?

The answers embarrass us, and the blame is not where we usually put it. Mining companies cannot be expected to design Liberia’s national capability system; that responsibility belongs to the state. In the absence of credible Liberian pipelines, a company will import engineers and contractors because it must operate. Government presses episodically, scholarships this year, employment numbers next, and companies comply with the demand of the moment. The demands change. Nothing connects. Extraction continues, accompanied by activities. When the ore runs out, and ore always runs out, we will convene conferences on diversification and discover what sixty years of extraction left behind.

Employers complain constantly about workforce quality, and the answer is always more training. But a workforce employers can rely on is built deliberately, occupation by occupation, against real demand. It is not a social program. It is a foundation of production.

The same missing answer explains why agriculture, our announced salvation in every plan since independence, still does not feed us. And it explains the hollowness of our newest prescription. Entrepreneurship at scale is not a trait to be trained into a population; it is an outcome of an economy, of paying customers, working capital, and reachable markets. Where those are absent, we rebrand survival self-employment and ask young people to absorb the risk of a missing economy while calling it empowerment.

A country of projects without a national project

Someone will object that Liberia has a plan. Liberia has always had a plan. That is the evidence, not the defense.

We have produced five major strategies since the war, from the interim poverty-reduction strategy through the Agenda for Transformation to the Pro-Poor Agenda and now the ARREST Agenda. Each diagnosed us honestly. The PAPD said it plainly in 2018, in the government’s own words: Liberia is rich in human and natural resources but deprived of development because its people lack the capability to transform those resources into wealth. That is this essay’s argument, published by the state itself, eight years ago. It described the country. It did not govern the country. On the present trajectory we will not meet Vision 2030 either, and nothing in our planning culture guarantees the public autopsy such a failure should require. We do not learn from our plans. We replace them.

The ARREST Agenda deserves a fair reading, because its own arithmetic is the X-ray. It requires US$8.38 billion over five years. Government expects to finance roughly 30 percent; the rest is expected from private investment, development partners, and diaspora remittances. That does not make the plan unserious; most national strategies depend partly on capital beyond the budget. But it makes alignment the decisive test. Seventy percent of the plan depends on actors government cannot command. Unless their investments are connected to a governing national architecture, the plan remains a destination whose vehicle belongs to someone else.

Beneath every plan sits the same structural silence. Education manages education. Mines manages mining. Public Works builds roads. Partners fund projects. Every actor owns a component and can defend it. But who is accountable for whether the components add up to a different country? Who ensures a thirty-year concession changes what our technical colleges teach? Who decides that scarce capital will complete one system before starting five others? No one. Everyone is accountable for activity. No one is accountable for accumulation.

Our development partners are trapped inside this same gap, and they should hear this as a plea, not an accusation. In the absence of a national architecture, each partner rationally builds a project-level one: its own unit, database, consultants, and indicators. Local rationality, national irrationality. When implementation skills cannot be found locally, partners procure international firms, because the project window leaves no time to build local capacity to do the work. The work gets done. The capability leaves on the same flight as the consultants. The next project reassembles everything from zero. Knowledge behaves the same way: two decades of assessments, baseline surveys, and value-chain studies, one set per project, often covering the same sectors and the same farmers. Liberia may be among the most studied and least known countries on earth, because the studies function as project products rather than national assets. Knowledge, too, is a flow here. We have never let it become a stock.

So the question must be asked directly, with respect: if project cycles cannot absorb the time and risk required to build local delivery capacity, then who will? The projects are not more important than the levers required to deliver them.

Direction, conversion, accumulation

The answer is not another plan. God spare us another plan. It is three disciplines, applied without mercy.

Direction. A short list of concrete national capabilities we are deliberately building, so short that it forces exclusion. Everything is a priority in Liberia, which is how the budget gets spread until nothing we fund is ever finished, foundational, and usable. We have to stop trying to do everything and nothing.

Conversion. Design the connections, not just the components. Every road answers: what production does it unlock? Every concession answers: which occupations and suppliers, on what schedule? Every degree program answers: what demand? Every donor program answers: which national system does it strengthen?

Accumulation. Measure what remains, not what moved. Firms that survived. Occupations localized. Systems still operating. Value retained and reinvested. One question before every major intervention is approved, and again after it closes: what will Liberia permanently be able to do because this existed?

The question of 2040

Countries do not purchase direction. They choose it, and then organize institutions, capital, and public authority around the choice. Decisions of that kind are not imported. They are made.

So let us be honest about time. 2030 is around the corner, and the dream attached to it will not be met. The more important question is the one nobody is asking: what are we doing today that should make anyone believe 2040 will be substantially different? By 2040 we will certainly have more roads, more graduates, more agencies, more completed projects. More flows. The question is which stocks. What will Liberia be able to do in 2040 that it cannot do now, and can anyone name the mechanism currently building that capability? If the answer is silence, then 2040 is already written, and it looks like 2026, which looked like 1966.

I ended The Death of Potential with the warning that the greatest danger was not what Liberia lacked but what we had learned to accept. We have learned to accept activity as achievement. We have learned to celebrate what enters and never audit what remains. Sixty years ago, economists looked at booming Liberia and named our condition: growth without development. Their book should have been our warning. We made it our biography.

But a biography is not a destiny. We are 179 years old, small enough to know ourselves, young enough to redirect ourselves, and rich enough, in ore, in land, and in the ferocious untapped intelligence of our children, to build an economy that compounds within a generation. It begins the day this country answers, operationally and out loud, the question it has avoided since 1847:

What are we deliberately trying to become able to do?

Everything we build before answering that question is furniture.

Everything we build after it is a nation.

World.title: Govt. dismisses abduction allegations
World.content:
Government has dismissed allegations circulating on various media platforms suggesting that it has abducted individuals connected to some political parties.

Ministry of Home Affairs and Internal Security Permanent Secretary Dickson Matembo has clarified that several suspects, among them, three former senior government officials have been apprehended over an alleged plot to interfere with the 2026 general elections.

Speaking during a joint media briefing, Mr Matembo clarified that no abductions have taken place, stressing that all actions undertaken by the state are within the confines of the law.

Mr Matembo emphasised that contrary to speculation, individuals such as former Ambassador Martha Lungu and journalist Hannah Katontoka were not abducted, but lawfully apprehended to assist with investigations and have since been released.

And government has commended members of the public for their cooperation in providing information that aided law enforcement and urged citizens to remain vigilant, reporting any activities that may threaten national security, public safety, or peace.

“The government’s position is clear. The security of the Republic of Zambia is a responsibility of the state and must be protected through lawful, accountable and constitutionally established institutions,” he emphasised.

Mr Matembo also confirmed the arrest of businessman Valden Findlay in connection with investigations into alleged military-related training undertaken by Zambian nationals abroad.

The arrest follows the earlier interception of three Zambian nationals at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport on August 1st, 2026 who have since been arrested and charged with unlawful drilling, unauthorised use of uniform and prohibition of terrorism.

He explained that a joint intelligence-led operation involving defense and security agencies culminated in the apprehension of several suspects linked to attempts to interfere with the electoral process.

He added that the three former senior government officials are currently in lawful custody for allegedly providing technical services aimed at undermining the electoral system.

The Permanent Secretary revealed that Investigators have also extended invitations to Japhen Mwakalombe, Mwila Kakana and Sessho Banda to assist with ongoing inquiries after they were found in possession of over K7.3 million.

He explained that the source and intended purpose of the funds remains unclear, noting that the trio, however, have communicated through their lawyers that they will only be available after August 14th, 2026.

Mr Matembo further disclosed that sensitive military intelligence information was discovered on electronic devices seized from the suspects, raising concerns about unauthorised access to protected data.

In a related development, Mr Matembo also disclosed that a Kenyan national, Michael Juka, aged 56, has been apprehended for allegedly being contracted to carry out cybercrimes targeting the State.

And Ministry of Information and Media Permanent Secretary Thabo Kawana warned that anyone attempting to disrupt elections, peace, or national security will face the wrath of the law.

He noted that some political leaders had admitted to sending people abroad for training and later declared readiness to kill or be killed during elections, warning that such actions would not be tolerated.

Mr Kawana added that foreigners linked to treasonous activities were among those arrested, while others fled.

He reiterated that the government would not allow desperate individuals to endanger peace and security in pursuit of political power.

“We are aware of some individuals that also have finished their so-called training and would want to get back into the country to implement that which they want to come and do on the soil of this country. We want to say we welcome them. The law enforcement agencies are ready”, the Permanent Secretary warned.

World.title: ECZ deploys Poll staff in Chilubi
World.content:
The deployment of poll staff by the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) in Chilubi District ahead of the August 13 General Election has reached an advanced stage.

The exercise, which began yesterday, is scheduled to be completed today.

Chilubi District Electoral Officer Kenneth Kafumbwe says poll staff that have been deployed to swamp areas are being airlifted using a Zambia Air Force (ZAF) chopper, while those assigned to the mainland are being transported by boats, before continuing their journey on vehicles and motorbikes.

Speaking in an interview with the media today in Chilubi today, Mr Kafumbwe expressed optimism that the deployment exercise will be completed before the close of business today.

Meanwhile, stakeholders observing the electoral process have welcomed the timely deployment of poll staff noting that the Electoral Commission of Zambia has taken into account Chilubi’s unique geographical challenges.

New Buyantanshi Village Headman, David Mwaba said the Commission’s proactive approach has ensured that staff reach their destinations on time.

Mr Mwaba further expressed happiness for the peaceful atmosphere that has characterised the electoral process in the area.

World.title: Zambians urged to be peaceful- Haamaundu
World.content:
Government has called on members of the public to uphold peace during elections, stating that continued peace in the country acts as an asset in promoting investor confidence and economic development.

Ministry of Defence Permanent Secretary, Maambo Haamaundu, says that his ministry is committed to ensuring continued peace that can be exported to other countries in leadership and peace keeping missions.

Mr Haamundu added that despite crowd management falling under the Ministry of Home Affairs and Internal Security, the Ministry of Defence has its services on standby, should they be called upon due to a situation that demands their attention.

“We must continue to maintain the peace of our country, because like I said, it is the foundation for economic and social development,” he said.

Mr Haamaundu has since appealed to members of the public to refrain from the temptation of wanting to cause violence, as they remain as key stakeholders of championing peace in the country.

He said that the government will work with a government approach that will involve key collaborations with stakeholders such as correctional services and immigration, in order to maximize peace.

Mr Haamaundu expressed that he is hopeful of a peaceful environment as the people go about casting their votes and that individuals who want to cause unnecessary trouble will be dealt with accordingly.

World.title: ECZ commissions 2026 National Election Results Centre in Lusaka
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has officially opened the 2026 National Election Results Centre in Lusaka situated at the Mulungushi International Conference Centre.

Speaking during the commissioning of the Centre today, ECZ Chairperson, Mwangala Zaloumis, called for transparency, professionalism and respect for the democratic process during the results management period.

Ms Zaloumis said the media has a critical role to play in promoting transparency and providing accurate information to the public during the electoral process.

She implored journalists to report objectively, independently and in accordance with their accreditation, while ensuring that information is verified before publication or broadcast.

Ms Zaloumis said the media should rely on official results issued by the Commission and avoid amplifying speculation and unverified claims.

She said inaccurate figures and misleading information can spread rapidly, particularly through social media and other digital platforms.

Ms Zaloumis also urged the citizens to exercise caution over information circulating online, noting that photographs, documents, figures and other claims may be genuine, incomplete, taken out of context or entirely false.

The Chairperson encouraged the public to rely on official information from the ECZ and remain patient as the established results management processes are completed.

Ms Zaloumis, who was flanked by her Vice Vincent Mukanda, three Commissioners and Chief Electoral Officer, Brown Kasaro, further appealed to political parties, candidates and their supporters to avoid using unofficial or unverified information in ways that could create unnecessary tension, confusion and mistrust.

She said the launch of the National Election Results Centre is more than the opening of a physical facility, as it demonstrates the Commission’s commitment to making the presidential election results announcement process accessible to stakeholders and conducting it with the seriousness it deserves.

Ms Zaloumis said all stakeholders operating from the Centre should comply with established procedures and cooperate with officials responsible for its operations.

Meanwhile, ECZ Director of Information and Communication Technology (ICT), Victor Kachaka, said the Commission has put in place systems to facilitate the management and display of election results from the voting stage through to the announcement of results.

Dr Kachaka said internet connectivity will also be provided to facilitate access to the electoral results system.

He explained that the results display portal will enable users to access results and analyse trends at different levels, including provinces and constituencies.

Dr Kachaka said the portal will initially display presidential candidates in alphabetical order, but the figures will be updated as results are officially announced by the Commission.

He said the system will enable stakeholders to follow the results as they are progressively received and displayed by the Commission.

World.title: TIZ urges Zambians to adhere to the provisions of the law
World.content:
Transparency International Zambia (TIZ) Executive Director, Maurice Nyambe, has called on all stakeholders participating in this year’s General Elections to adhere to the provisions of the law.

Mr Nyambe says stakeholders should comply with the Electoral Process Act, electoral guidelines and the Electoral Code of Conduct to ensure a credible and peaceful election.

He also urged citizens to turn up in large numbers and exercise their constitutional right to vote in tomorrow’s General Elections.

Mr Nyambe noted that voting is an important civic duty through which citizens contribute and strengthen democracy and maintain the integrity of the electoral process.

The TIZ Chief said this in an interview with the media in Lusaka today ahead of tomorrow’s General Elections.

Mr Nyambe has further called on all stakeholders to allow the electoral and results management processes to take their full course.

He revealed that TIZ has deployed long-term monitors across the country since March this year to monitor the electoral process and report issues observed on the ground.

And Mr Nyambe has appealed to candidates who will lose the elections to genuinely accept the outcome.

Mr Nyambe said there can only be one winner in an election, and urged all candidates and their supporters to respect the outcome and use the legal channels provided should they wish to challenge the results.

He noted that even in the event of electoral disputes, all parties should allow the prescribed appeal processes to take their full course.

Mr Nyambe said TIZ wants to see Zambia maintain the peace it has enjoyed over the years by ensuring that all electoral disputes are handled within the confines of the law.

World.title: Maternal mortality rate has drastically dropped-Dr Lishimpi
World.content:
Ministry of Health Permanent Secretary for Technical Services, Kennedy Lishimpi, says maternal mortality rate has drastically dropped in the last five years of the United Party for National Development (UPND) administration.

Dr Lishimpi explained that in 2021 maternal mortality rate stood at 252 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births adding that in December 2025 the number has since dropped to 103 deaths per 100,000 live births.

He pointed out that the drop in maternal mortality rate is a direct response to President Hakainde Hichilema’s directive to reduce the maternal mortality ratio to fewer than 100 deaths per 100,000 live births by the end of 2026.

The Permanent Secretary said this when he featured on Zambia today programme on ZANIS TV.

Dr Lishimpi also attributed the drop in maternal mortality ratio to the newly constructed maternity annexes by the government across the country.

He disclosed that in the last four years over 324 maternity annexes have been constructed and commissioned.

Dr Lishimpi further revealed the recruitment of additional midwives at lower levels of healthcare facilities.

And commenting on blood collection, Dr Lishimpi says the Ministry of Health has strengthened the collection of blood nationwide.

Dr Lishimpi explained that each province has its own provincial blood bank centre.

He recalled that in 2021, about 81 thousand units of blood per year was collected adding that presently over 285 thousand units of blood is being collected in a single year.

World.title: Chipolopolo’s Musonda joins Zesco Utd
World.content:
Chipolopolo striker Kennedy Musonda has returned to the Zambia Super League, signing for Super Division side Zesco United after a three-year stint abroad.

Zesco officially announced Musonda’s acquisition on 12 August 2026 as part of its signings ahead of the 2026 Transitional League.

“ZESCO United Football Club is delighted to announce the acquisition of new players ahead of the Transition League. Kennedy Musonda returns to the Zambia Super League. At Young Africans he scored 32 goals and won 3 Tanzanian Premier League titles, 3 Cups, 2 Community Shields, and reached the CAF Confederation Cup Final,” the club stated.

Musonda spent two and a half years at Tanzanian giants Young Africans after leaving Power Dynamos.

During his final season with Power in 2022/2023, he helped the Kitwe side win the Super Division title with 11 goals.

After his contract with Yanga expired, the striker moved to Israel a year ago, joining second-tier side Hapoel Ramat Gan Givatayim.

He was linked with a return to Power Dynamos before opting for Zesco.

On the international stage, Musonda scored 4 goals for Chipolopolo during the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers.

Musonda is not the only new arrival at the Ndola club as Zesco have also bolstered its squad with more additions.

The club has also bolstered its squad with goalkeeper Patrick Chooma from Leopards FC, Chadian midfielder Yves Allarabaye from Foullah Edifice, Gilbert Tetani from Mufulira Wanderers, and John Mulenga who joins from Green Buffaloes having featured for Young Green Buffaloes.

The signing of Musonda is expected to add firepower as Zesco prepare for both domestic and continental assignments in the Transitional League.

Brice Sindjo – Cameroonian forward from Colombe Sportive

Happy Nsiku – Defender from Red Arrows

Patrick Chooma – Goalkeeper from Leopards FC

Yves Allarabaye – Chadian midfielder from Foullah Edifice

Gilbert Tetani – From Mufulira Wanderers

World.title: Police officers directed to be professional -Musamba
World.content:
Inspector General of Police, Graphel Musamba, has directed all police officers to discharge their duties with professionalism, integrity, neutrality and respect for the constitution, ahead of the August polls.

In a statement issued to the media, Mr Musamba, says the Police have enhanced crime detection operations and Rapid Response Teams across all provinces, in a bid to ensure that every eligible citizen can vote freely and peacefully, without intimidation.

Mr Musamba further directed the police officers to exercise respect for human rights while dealing with criminal conduct, protect every citizen equally and arrest all individuals who commit crime, regardless of political affiliation.

He said that the Police and Electoral Commission of Zambia have coordinated measures to safeguard electoral materials, polling stations, election officials and integrity of the electoral process.

“Every voter, every candidate and every election official will be protected without fear, favour or political consideration,” said Mr Musamba.

Mr Musamba said that the Zambia police service has progressively implemented its 2026 electoral security plan with additional police officers deployed across the country to strengthen police visibility, improve response times and reassure communities.

Mr Musamba also urged members of the public to play a part in safeguarding peace by returning home, to work or continue with lawful activities after casting their votes and avoid loitering around polling stations, unless as accredited by the ECZ.

He also urged members of the public to obtain election results only from official and authorised sources and to avoid circulating or relying on unverified information, rumours and speculative announcements on social media.

Mr Musamba further urged the public to expect increased police presence and snap security checkpoints on selected roads, as a preventive measure that is intended to enhance public safety.
