World.title: Farm linked to cyclosporaisis outbreak went years without FDA inspection
World.content:
The Food and Drug Administration conducted just under 1,000 foreign food safety inspections in 2025, and the farm in Mexico believed to be at the center of the ongoing cyclosporiasis outbreak in the U.S. was not one of them.

A federal law enacted to prevent diseased and dirty food from reaching Americans' plates requires the FDA to carry out nearly 20 times that many foreign inspections each year. But the FDA hasn't come close to meeting the congressional mandate — or even 10% of it — in the 10 years it has been in place, spanning administrations led by both political parties.

FDA officials have described the requirement as unrealistic, but have never asked Congress to revise it. A lower foreign inspection target the agency deemed necessary to safeguard foreign imports is still nearly five times higher than the number of inspections conducted last year.

Congress, meanwhile, has not increased the agency's food safety budget to outpace or keep up with inflation, and widespread layoffs during the first year of President Trump's second term squeezed resources further.

The rate of inspections has gotten markedly worse amid those reductions, with foreign food safety inspections falling by 29% from 2024. Outside of the COVID-19 pandemic, last year's inspection count was the lowest since 2011. Early numbers for 2026 show that the agency is on track to inspect a similar number this year.

"FDA inspections really are the first line of defense for mitigating outbreaks. If FDA isn't routinely going out to food facilities, it's just completely blind," said Meridith Seife, the lead author on a Health and Human Services Inspector General report on FDA inspections of U.S. facilities. "It's unable to ensure that those facilities are complying with the laws, with regulations, and that the food that they handle is safe."

About a third of FDA inspections of foreign firms for foodborne hazards over the last decade found violations, inspection data show. Inspectors have previously found toilet paper and human feces in growing fields in Mexico and observed air conditioning units dripping onto crawfish in China. Around 2% of the time inspectors visited firms over the last 10 years, they found violations significant enough to prompt enforcement action.

Before the cyclosporiasis outbreak, the FDA last inspected its potential source, Taylor Farms de Mexico, seven years ago, records show. The FDA's last visit before that was six years prior — to respond to another cyclosporiasis outbreak in 2013. The 2019 inspection found no violations, while the 2013 post-outbreak review found the facility was recycling wash water for salad mix, but couldn't conclusively pinpoint the source of the outbreak.

The FDA is "actively working to expand staffing at foreign posts," according to Emily Hilliard, senior press secretary for HHS. Public health experts say the inspection count is only one input in the whole system, and that food companies bear primary responsibility for day-to-day safety. But they also said the count still matters as an outside check regulators alone can provide.

"Suggesting that FDA's ability to protect the food supply can be measured by a single inspection statistic ignores the agency's comprehensive oversight system, which prioritizes resources based on risk and deploys personnel where they have the greatest public health impact," Hilliard wrote in a statement to CBS News.

The FDA inspects producers of fruits and vegetables, dairy, processed foods and most seafood, while the U.S. Department of Agriculture is responsible for inspections of meat and poultry producers.

About 47,000 foreign manufacturers accounted for 90% of non-meat food shipments into the U.S. last year, a CBS News analysis of import data found. The FDA has inspected 4.5% of them since 2023.

The FDA employs a risk-based model to determine where to send inspectors, based on how much and how often a company sends food into the U.S. and its prior inspection and import refusal record. In addition to inspections, the FDA also uses an algorithm to assign scores to imports for screening at ports of entry, and can block any imports without examining them if they deem a shipper problematic. Federal law also puts the burden on U.S. companies importing food to ensure their suppliers follow safety standards.

An "unrealistic" target

Since 2011, federal inspectors have visited an average of about 1,300 foreign factories and farms annually (in non-pandemic years) to check for hazards that could lead to foodborne illness, federal data shows.

The FDA, state and local agencies conducted more than 10,000 inspections annually inside the U.S. in recent years, according to the HHS Inspector General.

The Food Safety Modernization Act, or FSMA, set a rising annual target for foreign inspections, capping it at 19,200 in 2016. The FDA told a federal watchdog as early as 2015 that the number was unworkable, so it directed the FDA to propose an adjusted target to Congress. The agency later conducted an internal analysis pegging the needed number of inspections at 4,700, about three to five times what the FDA has managed in recent years. But the agency never brought the number to Congress.

After the Government Accountability Office urged the FDA to revisit the target again last January, the agency created a workgroup to redo the analysis.

"The GAO was right in its January report when it said that the agency is handicapped by underfunding and understaffing. It's even more so now," said Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat of Connecticut, who requested the more recent watchdog inquiry. "There's clearly a need for more resources, better management, more commitment. Some of it can be legislated, but it also has to come from the administration."

At an average of $38,700 per foreign inspection, according to the FDA's estimates, meeting the existing Congressional mandate would cost about $743 million a year — more than 10% of the FDA's entire budget.

In its budget request for the upcoming year, the FDA asked for an additional $9 million to increase foreign inspector capacity. The agency also proposed requiring foreign food firms to pay a fee to register to import to the U.S., which would add an estimated $71 million in funds.

Staffing challenges

The FDA had 432 inspectors in 2024, and its hiring rate has not outpaced losses, according to the GAO report. Congress directed the hiring of 5,000 inspectors under FSMA, but the agency says it has never had the budget to increase staffing that much.

"Retaining inspectors has been a challenge at the FDA for more than a decade due to the difficulty of the job," wrote Sen. John Hoeven, a Republican of North Dakota, chair of the Senate appropriations subcommittee that drafts funding legislation for the FDA, in a written statement.

Last year's mass government layoffs spared inspectors but slashed support staff, leaving front-line inspectors to book their own flights and translators.

With just a fraction of its inspectors — 20 in 2024 — dedicated to foreign providers, the agency often pulls from domestic inspector ranks. It sends inspectors overseas for weeks to combine multiple stops in one trip. The FDA has also worked out agreements with Canada, New Zealand and Australia to accept their food systems and inspection results as equivalent to the U.S.

The required 19,200 inspections "was an impossible number for them to meet," said Stephen Ostroff, former FDA deputy commissioner for foods and veterinary medicine. "They have worked very hard to try to come up with alternatives to doing those foreign inspections."

Beyond inspections

With inspections happening infrequently, "the day-to-day operations and management of food safety is really on the company rather than on the regulatory agency," said Dr. Don Schaffner, chair of Rutgers University's Department of Food Science.

Economic incentives reinforce that self-monitoring: sales of prepackaged lettuce dropped nearly 20% in July amid the cyclosporiasis outbreak, Reuters reported. Taylor Farms says it invests $200 million annually in food safety protocols and independent audits, including regular monitoring of water quality and worker hygiene.

"The food industry is very good in terms of food safety overall if you think of how much food we eat," said Dr. Kali Kniel, chair of microbial food safety at the University of Delaware.

Still, inspections remain "a critical food safety and consumer protection activity," said Sandra Eskin, CEO of the nonprofit Stop Foodborne Illness.

"We're not in the field. We're not in the processing plant. So, we can't see what goes on," she said. "We bring a food item into our house, we can't tell if it's contaminated."

About the data

CBS News analyzed inspections and import data from FDA's Data Dashboard. The analysis was limited to inspections of firms outside of the U.S. that were inspected under the "Foodborne Biological Hazards" program. To determine how many foreign manufacturers imported 90% of food into the U.S. last year, CBS News counted foreign-based manufacturers who delivered the most shipments of human food into the U.S., grouping together deliveries of multiple products on the same day by the same company as a single shipment. Meat and poultry were excluded, as they are under the purview of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, not the FDA.

World.title: Zhu Rongji, who drove China's 1990s economic reforms, has died at 97
World.content:
Zhu Rongji, who drove China's 1990s economic reforms, has died at 97

Enlarge this image toggle caption K.Y. Cheng/South China Morning Post via Getty Images K.Y. Cheng/South China Morning Post via Getty Images

Zhu Rongji, former premier of China, has died at age 97. The cause of death was given as illness, according to state media.

Zhu, an acerbic technocrat and a trained engineer, was renowned for far-reaching economic reforms throughout the 1990s that sought to transition China from the chaos of its post-Maoist years to a more global market-oriented financial system, without completely ceding the Communist Party's control over the economy.

Despite staying almost completely out of the public eye after retiring from the premiership in 2003, he remains both loved and reviled in the country indelibly shaped by him. His reform legacy remains contested in China; in freeing up the country's enormous labor and financial resources, he helped to create vast amounts of wealth over the next three decades while also seeding institutions with future vulnerabilities.

Sponsor Message

"From the point of view of a policymaker, [he] embraced the notion of a China whose economic system was more compatible with that of the West. And by compatible, I mean vastly reformed, more open, less state-dominated, very limited state intervention," said Charlene Barshefsky, a lawyer and former U.S. trade representative who sat across the negotiating table from Zhu over years-long talks to let China enter the World Trade Organization (WTO).

In order to join the WTO, China first needed to get preferential trading status with the United States — which in turn demanded hard concessions and that it open up its closed economy to American companies. Zhu was under huge pressure to find compromise, and he let his views be known.

Enlarge this image toggle caption Joyce Naltchayan/AFP via Getty Images Joyce Naltchayan/AFP via Getty Images

In 2000, the U.S. Senate voted to give China that preferential trading status, and the following year, China joined the WTO. The agreement was a windfall for the nascent Chinese economy. The country became an export powerhouse, and foreign businesses rushed to China to establish a foothold.

The 6 1/2-year process let Zhu show off his flinty personality, though he struck U.S. officials as inquisitive and flexible. "This was not talking points. It was a lot of give and take," said Kenneth Lieberthal, a China expert who was a national security adviser for then-President Bill Clinton. He met Zhu multiple times during the negotiations.

Sponsor Message

Zhu was born in 1928 in the city of Changsha, in China's Hunan province. He graduated from Beijing's Tsinghua University, where he was also chosen as president of the student union, with a degree in electrical engineering, the winter before the Communist Party won control over China. In October 1949, when the new Communist-led republic was founded, Zhu officially joined the Chinese Communist Party.

His blunt, say-it-like-it-is style got him in trouble

Zhu's father died before he was born, and his mother died when he was 9 years old. Being an orphan, the need to survive helped shape his strong personality: thick-skinned and extremely direct.

"My defining characteristic is independent thought," he told bureaucrats in 1987, right before becoming mayor of Shanghai. "I say what I think."

When Chinese troops fatally fired on pro-democracy protesters in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989, Zhu did not issue the standard propaganda line denying the tragedy. "The event that occurred recently in Beijing is a historical fact, and historical facts cannot be covered up by anybody. The truth will always come out," he wrote in an essay published in a Shanghai newspaper.

His blunt, say-it-like-it-is style got him in serious trouble. In 1958, he was labeled an ideological "rightist" and briefly expelled from the party for criticizing Chairman Mao Zedong's economic policies, but managed to hold on to a job in state planning. In 1970, he was purged again during the Cultural Revolution and sent to do five years of manual labor at a party reeducation school.

Zhu was rehabilitated after Mao died in 1976 and Deng Xiaoping came to power as China's leader. Zhu then worked his way back up the bureaucratic ladder with the same pragmatism he had learned as an engineer.

"Regardless of what country your company is from, when you arrive in China, you should receive fair and equal treatment. I just want you to pay taxes," he joked in 1999 to an audience of American businessmen, explaining that China was open for foreign investment.

Sponsor Message

A career state planner, Zhu nevertheless quickly adjusted to the economic chaos of the 1990s, as China careened between capitalism and state-led socialism. As central bank governor, Zhu successfully tamed runaway inflation. While vice premier, he also led a dramatic centralization of the tax system that incentivized land sales and huge wealth creation, along with hugely unsustainable levels of debt.

After being appointed premier in 1998, he entered office with a bold promise: He would reform the indebted state banks within two years and inefficient state enterprises within three. That earned him both instant enemies and fans.

"No matter whether what lies ahead is a minefield or a bottomless abyss, I will carry out my duties until the last breath in my body," he vowed.

Zhu's most controversial legacy by far remains restructuring China's bloated state-owned enterprises. He axed smaller, inefficient companies, leaving an estimated 30 million state workers suddenly jobless.

Worker protests erupted all over China. Zhu had the willpower — or callousness, as his critics would say — to ignore them.

"The central government decided that the laid-off worker problem could just be ignored and forgotten," said Dorothy Solinger, a professor emeritus of political science at the University of California, Irvine, who studies migrant labor in China.

Zhu tried to offset the layoffs' impacts. He created a basic social welfare system that exists to this day and made steps to boost basic health care, which had crumbled in rural areas. But pockets of China, especially in the northeast region of the country, where workers were reliant on state employment in heavy industry sectors, never fully recovered economically.

"I think their children also have a problem because they miss out on the things that the better-off part of the population could do, such as hiring tutors or going on extracurricular activities, going to the better schools," said Solinger. "It's a growing underclass."

Sponsor Message

Zhu took the criticism in stride. Unlike most Communist leaders, who read off staid and carefully prepared scripts, he loved engaging with and ad-libbing to the press.

"He loved answering all the questions, no matter how tough or sensitive," remembered Rose Luqiu, a former journalist for Hong Kong outlet Phoenix News who spent 10 years covering Zhu during his international state visits. "The only way he refused to answer was using a quite humorous way to dodge the questions."

His gallows humor allowed him to weather intense periods of criticism from senior ideologues within the Communist Party, once quipping during an anti-corruption campaign: "I have prepared 100 coffins: 99 for the corrupt officials and one for myself."

Other reforms of his did not materialize, in part because an austere Zhu never managed to cultivate the political patronage networks that would have allowed him to overcome fierce opposition within party ranks to his proposals. His efforts to reduce bad debt at China's state banks and reform the pension system floundered.

Enlarge this image toggle caption Greg Baker/AFP via Getty Images Greg Baker/AFP via Getty Images

Zhu "represented really a different time, a different era for China"

Zhu is now invoked with pleasant nostalgia. Under China's current leader, Xi Jinping, the country became more nationalistic, more beholden to the state and more closed off to the outside world.

"I think that Zhu Rongji represented really a different time, a different era for China: the time when China wanted to find its way in what, due to that time, was the best possible way, which was to move towards Western-style economics, to move toward Western-style rules," said Barshefsky, the former U.S. trade negotiator.

Zhu Rongji spent the last years of his life at his Beijing home in the western hills of the Chinese capital. He loved Peking Opera and spent much of his days listening to music — and quietly advising some of the newest generation of technocrats running China, though not all appear to have listened to him.

World.title: White House had an 'ethical requirement' to tell reporters about plane swap, former CIA director says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump secretly swapped planes by hiding in a catering truck when leaving the NATO summit in Turkey last month, according to U.S. media reports. The move was allegedly due to security concerns after threats from Iran.

The covert movements that saw U.S. President Donald Trump depart a plane carrying reporters and some White House staff in Turkey last month have few, if any, precedents in modern history, and have left lingering questions.

Following a NATO summit in Ankara, Trump was secretly transferred from Air Force One to a military ​plane via a catering truck in an extraordinary deception prompted by an ​Iranian assassination threat, U.S. media reported.

The White House did not disclose the change — even though reporters and some White House staff remained on Air Force One — and it remained a secret until the Washington Post first reported it on Monday.

Trump, who said Tuesday he was only acting at the direction of the U.S. Secret Service, was accompanied by several close aides to the smaller military aircraft.

Former CIA director John Brennan — a vocal Trump critic whom the president perceives as an enemy worthy of prosecution — said Tuesday the White House had an "ethical requirement" to let the press pool know.

"None of the presidents I worked for would have allowed the White House staff and a planeload of journalists to go if the threat was not mitigated sufficiently for the president," Brennan told MS Now.

'For old time's sake'

Trump had taken a newly renovated, Qatari-donated jet ​to the summit ⁠but said while there that he'd take the older Air Force One — for "old time's sake" — upon departing for the U.K. The statement piqued the curiosity of the press, given that Trump has often expressed his displeasure over the two Air Force One planes that have been in use from 1990 until this year.

The trip to Ankara was also the first time the new plane took Trump overseas, after speedy upgrades triggered questions over its cost and security.

New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman has since said "there could have been an off-the-record conversation" with the press about the arrangements, and which kept them off Air Force One.

"The press would then report it later but [officials] would not have potentially jeopardized anyone," she said on the newspaper's podcast The Daily, on Wednesday.

That actually happened in 2000. And apparently, a reporter kept the confidence for 25 years, only discussing it in the wake of this week's revelations.

U.S. President Donald Trump waves as he switches planes at RAF Mildenhall in England on July 8, as he headed back to Washington. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

Susan Page of USA Today told the Post this week about the time in 2000 when President Bill Clinton used an unmarked executive jet to fly into Pakistan, while sending Air Force One as decoy.

"They told me about the extraordinary security procedures being taken because of the dangers in flying there, including use of the decoy plane," she said. "Of course, the dangers threatened the journalists covering the trip as well as President Clinton."

It's not clear if that approach was ever considered by the Trump White House, which has an antagonistic relationship with several media outlets. In fact, the administration sought to subpoena some of Haberman's colleagues at the Times when they reported about security concerns regarding the Qatari jet — backing off after a hearing in which a federal judge assailed the government over the threats to reporters.

Haberman said it was "unsettling" to learn about the switch, but it's not clear if the reporters were in any real danger.

The legacy Air Force One is checked before boarding and is equipped with a range of advanced defensive systems including flares, electronic jammers and infrared detection systems that protect against missile strikes, though it is impossible to know how effective those systems would be.

Trump suggested to reporters late Tuesday that the decoy plane was likely safer than the U.S. air force C-32A he travelled on to England. It's not clear if the plane the press travelled on received any kind of military escort.

Democrats want answers

There is no law that the president's whereabouts must be known at all times, but the press generally has a sense of the day's schedule.

A notable exception was the day of the 9/11 attacks on U.S. soil, when it was several hours before the press and the public learned of President George W. Bush's travels from a Florida school to, eventually, an air force base in Nebraska. But on that occasion there was no misdirection, just a delay in the face of extraordinary and uncertain circumstances.

A threat was also present this time, the Wall Street Journal emphasized in an editorial published late Tuesday.

"The press corps, which had been left on the decoy Presidential plane, understandably is up in arms. But the real story is the seriousness of Iran’s efforts to kill the President," the paper said.

White House spokesperson Steven Cheung said in a statement that "there are many enemies of America … and we use every tool at our disposal to address" threats against the president.

Trump has faced a number of assassination threats domestically, including the attempt on his life in Pennsylvania in 2024 which led to the resignation of the Secret Service director at the time.

Iranian-linked entities have been monitored since a U.S. drone strike in early 2020 assassinated Iranian military commander Qasem Soleimani. U.S. law enforcement and intelligence agencies have since described plots to kill Trump, high-profile members of his first administration John Bolton and Mike Pompeo and, in an alleged plot involving Canadian residents, unspecified individuals who lived near D.C.

Trump has said he's "No. 1 on the kill list for Iran," a claim likely exacerbated by this year's killings of of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other Iranian military, political and religious leaders.

Democrats are, not surprisingly, full of questions about the plane swaps.

"Trump has put America's sons and daughters in harm's way by getting into an unnecessary and reckless war, and this administration has repeatedly refused to provide Congress and the public with the transparency they deserve," Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Democratic minority leader, wrote in a statement.

Schumer, according to the Post, was demanding that the White House brief congressional leaders about what happened.

World.title: Montreal police never fired on civilian during deadly daytime shooting: Radio-Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Contrary to what was spread on social media in the aftermath of a deadly shooting in Montreal on June 22, an SPVM police officer did not fire on civilian Michel Mizrahi, who died in the operation, according to Radio-Canada sources.

The information was first reported by La Presse Wednesday morning.

According to the autopsy results, Mizrahi was shot multiple times that day and fatally struck in the head.

Radio-Canada sources say the impact of the fatal shot suggests a left-to-right trajectory and not one from underneath him, which is where a police officer was crouching, taking cover from the active shooter.

This allowed forensic pathologists to rule out the theory that the shot came from the police officer.

More to come.

World.title: B.C. officials 'can't even think about' lifting Summerland evacuation orders until wildfire under control
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The latest:

Regional officials said they "can't even think about" lifting evacuation orders for Summerland until the Bald Range fire is better controlled.

Temporary access permits to Summerland are being triaged, with utility crews getting priority to ensure services are running.

People are asked to stay clear of the Bonanza Creek wildfire, which is burning in a popular recreational area surrounded by numerous provincial parks.

of the Bonanza Creek wildfire, which is burning in a popular recreational area surrounded by numerous provincial parks. Yellow and orange air quality warnings are in place for regions across southern B.C.

are in place for regions across southern B.C. The Ainslie Creek wildfire saw growth towards Highway 8. The highway remains open as crews maintain 24-hour operations.

as crews maintain 24-hour operations. The B.C. Wildfire Service says "new ignitions occurring during periods of hot and dry weather can establish and spread quickly."

Bald Range wildfire still burning out of control

During a Tuesday livestream from the Regional District of Okanagan-Similkameen, Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes said they cannot consider lifting evacuation orders or alerts until the Bald Range wildfire is under control.

A B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS) update on Tuesday said overnight recoveries were poor due to clear skies and fuels remain "exceptionally dry and highly receptive to fire."

Officials say the volatile nature of the wildfire challenges their ability to plan ahead, as they are still responding to the fire as it progresses.

Ground crews are pictured battling the Bald Range fire overnight on Aug. 7, 2026. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

"We have to make sure it's safe," said Holmes.

Until then, temporary access permits are being granted in some circumstances.

Permits are "basically triaged," according to Deborah Jones-Middleton, the protective services manager with the district. She said utilities professionals, for example, will be permitted into the area as long, as it's safe to do so, to ensure utilities are adequately running to sustain a community.

There were 100 firefighters from Mexico battling the Bald Range fire on Tuesday, bringing the total number of ground personnel to 193. Heavy equipment, aviation personnel continue to construct control lines, while structure protection is in place around the community.

Brunswick Complex nears another highway

As of Tuesday afternoon, the Ainslie Creek wildfire had scorched roughly 614 square kilometres of land, and its northeastern edge was only about three kilometres west of Highway 8, which runs through Merritt.

The northeast edge of the wildfire is roughly 20 kilometres northwest of Merritt. The BCWS noted the Ainslie Creek fire hasn't crossed control lines or entered the community.

As a result of the growing fire, the Lower Nicola Indian Band expanded its evacuation alert to cover all properties in the Nicola Mameet Indian Reserve No. 1. It also issued an evacuation order for a property on its Speous Indian Reserve No. 8.

The BCWS said in its Tuesday update that the fire remains active along the northeast and southeast flanks, growing eastward throughout Monday. It added that as of Tuesday morning , the fire stopped about two kilometres short of control lines, and had not impacted Highway 8.

The Ainslie Creek wildfire has a pattern of showing aggressive behaviour and major growth, according to the service, when any two factors of elevated winds, low humidity and clear skies combine.

The Ainslie Creek fire burns along the Fraser River on July 27, 2026. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

The Brunswick Complex consists of the Brunswick Creek wildfire, burning on the east bank of the Fraser River above Boston Bar, and the Ainslie Creek wildfire, burning on its west bank. Highway 1 is directly affected by the wildfires and remains closed.

There were 236 firefighters, 20 helicopters, 59 pieces of heavy equipment and 85 structure protection personnel fighting the Brunswick Complex as of Tuesday.

Road closures

According to DriveBC , most of the major highway closures from previous days remain the same.

Due to the Bald Range wildfire, Highway 97 is closed between Peachland and the Pyramid Picnic Area in Kickininee Provincial Park. Traffic is being redirected to Highway 33.

Westside Road also remains closed due to the Bradley Creek Complex, burning on the west bank of Okanagan Lake, north of Penticton.

Other closures to Highway 1 north of Hope and Highway 97 north of Cache Creek remain in place.

World.title: Top adviser to Iran's IRGC says U.S. military is 'weaker than what we perceived' in rare interview
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A top adviser to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says Iranian officials have seen "how the American military is weaker than what we perceived" since the United States and Israel first launched their attack on Iran in February of this year, as talks to end the fighting continue to stall.

In a rare IRGC interview with Western media, Brig.-Gen. Mohammad Reza Naqdi told PBS News Hour in an interview aired Tuesday that Iran has not reached their "final objective" when asked if they have won the war.

"Up until now, we are victorious. In the future, we will continue to be victorious," said Naqdi, who is supreme adviser to IRGC's commander-in-chief.

An interim deal between Washington and Tehran aimed at ending the fighting had been reached in mid-June and is set to expire Monday.

Naqdi's comments come weeks after the ceasefire collapsed and the U.S. and Iran exchanged strikes for more than two weeks before pausing.

"The longer this war lasts, the more experience we gain. We had never seen a real war to gain real experience to learn how to fight with America," Naqdi told PBS. "In these five months, we have learned how."

"We have also seen how the American military is weaker than what we perceived."

WATCH | Trump responds to reports of U.S. military running low on munitions: Trump says U.S. brimming with weapons, vows to 'hunt down' leakers | Duration 2:08 U.S. President Donald dismissed reports of America's military running low on munitions due to the war with Iran, and said whoever leaked the information to U.S. media outlets will be 'hunted down' and given 'long term jail sentences.'

On Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump reiterated that the U.S. is in "total ​control" of ​the Strait of Hormuz.

"I THINK WE WILL ⁠KEEP IT! Our Naval Blockade ‌is being called, by everyone, 'A WALL OF STEEL,' ​and there ⁠is nothing Iran ⁠can do about ⁠it," ⁠Trump ​wrote in a post on his Truth ​Social ⁠platform.

Since the war in the Persian Gulf began when the U.S. and Israel launched a massive co-ordinated military campaign against Iran on Feb. 28, Trump has alternated between threats of escalation and claims that a peace deal is imminent.

Pakistan continues efforts to resume negotiations

Meanwhile, Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar met Iranian Ambassador Reza Amiri Moghadam in Islamabad on Wednesday, attempting to resume peace negotiations between Iran and the U.S.

Their meeting came a day after Pakistan sent Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi to Tehran for talks with Iran's top leaders.

Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesperson Tahir Andrabi told reporters Wednesday the June deal remains valid and the deadline could be extended.

"We are not closing the chapter," Andrabi said.

Pakistan's Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, left, meets with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Tehran on Tuesday. (Iranian Foreign Ministry/WANA (West Asia News Agency)/Reuters)

Talks have bogged down over Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil supplies passed before the war.

The U.S. accuses Iran of failing to honour an agreement under the deal to reopen the vital Strait of Hormuz shipping route. Tehran says Washington has reneged on its commitments, including lifting a blockade of Iranian ports and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

Thousands of people have been killed in the conflict, mainly in Iran and Lebanon.

Iran has struck U.S. assets and infrastructure in countries including Oman, Jordan, Kuwait, Israel, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.

The June interim ceasefire agreement set a 60-day period, extendable by mutual consent, within which Iran and the U.S. were expected to reach a final deal limiting Tehran's nuclear program and lifting U.S. sanctions.

Both Iran and the U.S. have stepped up rhetoric in the past two days.

Iran's top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, said on Tuesday the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed unless the U.S. accepted Iran's conditions to end the war.

That followed a new demand from Trump on Monday that Iran should pay compensation for people killed in 50 years of wars, attacks and protests.

World.title: Bear encounters in Canada: What's been happening and how can you reduce the risks?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It may feel like Canadians are crossing paths with bears more often than before.

In recent months, several encounters have been reported in B.C., Alberta and Saskatchewan — and some of them have turned deadly, though experts say fatal attacks remain extremely rare.

Lana Ciarniello, an independent conservation scientist and expert on human-bear conflict, said multiple factors — including wider media coverage — are contributing to the perception that bear encounters are rising.

"You’re definitely hearing about things more," she told CBC News. "But with that said … we do believe there is an increase, as well."

She explained that, in the case of black bears, the number of encounters can fluctuate from year to year based on food availability and the natural environment: When less food is available or when a bear's habitat is disrupted, that can drive encounters with people.

"It’s kind of seeming like it's [the case] this year," Ciarniello said. "The berries, some of them are dried out in some places, and we’re having the wildfires…. That's going to drive conflicts."

She said communities should put more "bear-smart" measures in place, such as locking up their garbage, to avoid a dangerous run-in with a black bear.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: Have you had a close encounter with wildlife? What’s your story? Leave your comment here and our team may get in touch or read your comment on air.

Separately, when it comes to encounters with grizzly bears in backcountry areas, Ciarniello explained that other environmental and behavioural factors come into play.

Right now, for example, it's berry season and trees are full of leaves, which can obstruct a hiker's ability to spot a bear early along a trail.

"We try to prevent [those encounters] first from happening by making noise … letting the bear know that you're there before you even see the bear," she said, adding that hiking in groups and carrying bear spray will also reduce the chances of a negative encounter.

Here's a look at some of the most recent cases of bear encounters in Canada.

WATCH | How to avoid a dangerous bear encounter: How to avoid a dangerous bear encounter, according to an expert | Duration 6:39 After several serious bear encounters in B.C., including an attack that sent a three-year-old girl to hospital, bear safety expert Kim Titchener explains what attracts bears to residential areas, how people can reduce the risk of an encounter and what to know if they do come across one.

Grizzly seriously injures 72-year-old hiker in B.C.

A 72-year-old woman was attacked by a grizzly bear in a remote hiking area about 70 kilometres north of Pemberton, in southwestern B.C., in early August.

The woman was airlifted to hospital with a neck fracture and l acerations to her face, arms and neck, a local search-and-rescue official said.

The provincial Ministry of Environment said it believed after an initial investigation the attack was defensive, involving a female grizzly with at least one cub.

Man survives grizzly attack near Pemberton, B.C.

A man escaped serious injury after a grizzly bear attack on Aug. 9 in a backcountry area, also near Pemberton, about 30 kilometres north of Whistler in southwestern B.C.

The B.C. Conservation Officer Service said its investigation determined "the attack was defensive in nature and resulted from a close-range surprise encounter."

The man suffered non-life-threatening injuries and was able to seek medical attention, the service said.

WATCH | Facial recognition software offers rare glimpses of grizzlies: Tracking individual grizzly bears with facial recognition software | Duration 0:21 Camera traps and facial recognition software are providing a rare glimpse into individual grizzly bear behaviour in the southern B.C.'s Great Bear Rainforest. Credit: BearID Project/Nanwakolas Councilil

3-year-old B.C. girl injured playing in backyard

Earlier that same day, around 11:30 a.m. on Aug. 9, a three-year-old girl was attacked by an adult black bear while playing on her family's backyard deck, the B.C. Conservation Officer Service reported.

"A parent who was nearby was able to intervene and chase the bear away," it said. The service said the girl was treated in hospital for non-life-threatening injuries.

The agency said on Aug. 10 a bear that was killed in response to the incident was determined after a necropsy "to not be the offending black bear responsible" for attacking the girl.

"Efforts to locate and capture the bear responsible are continuing," it said.

Couple killed in remote area of Saskatchewan

A couple from Regina was killed in July in a black bear attack at McTavish Lake, a fly-in lake about 90 kilometres north of La Ronge, Sask. Family members later identified them as Jay and Deb MacDonald.

The province's Ministry of Community Safety confirmed on July 17 a bear was involved in the fatal incident but did not provide further details on what happened.

"After careful investigation, conservation officers have located and euthanized the bear suspected to be involved in the incident," the department said, adding the case remained under investigation.

WATCH | Jay and Deb MacDonald found near cabin at McTavish Lake: Regina couple killed in black bear attack | Duration 1:55 Wildlife officials have euthanized a black bear suspected in the deadly attack on a Regina couple in remote northern Saskatchewan on Wednesday. The bodies of Jay and Deb MacDonald were found near their cabin at McTavish Lake.

Attack in northern Saskatchewan kills 27-year-old

A man working at a uranium exploration project site in northeastern Saskatchewan's Athabasca Basin was killed in a black bear attack in May.

The man was later identified as Hrishikesh Koloth, a 27-year-old from India.

World.title: Manitoba mother whose 'little angel' died in CFS care says she was trying to get kids back
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A grieving mother says someone needs to be held accountable after her four-year-old daughter died in the care of Child and Family Services and her two other children were taken to a Winnipeg hospital with serious injuries.

Manitoba First Nations Police Service officers were called to a home in Long Plain First Nation on Sunday morning after the four-year-old was found by first responders with injuries and in medical distress, RCMP said in a news release Tuesday.

The girl was pronounced dead and her two sisters, a one-year-old and two-year-old, were taken to the hospital — one of them in critical condition.

Her mother said her four-year-old daughter was starting kindergarten in September and was about to celebrate her fifth birthday later this month.

"She was just a little angel. She loved her little siblings." the mom told CBC Tuesday. "She loved to sing, she loved to dance."

CBC is not identifying the mother to protect the identity of the two children who remain in the care of Child and Family Services.

RCMP Major Crimes Services said they took over the investigation from First Nations police due to the nature of the girl's death and the injuries to the siblings. No charges have been laid.

Children under care of CFS

The children were under the care of Waywayseecapo CFS, a western Manitoba agency based in Waywayseecapo First Nation, according to emails viewed by CBC.

A representative from Waywayseecapo CFS agency — which is under the umbrella of the Southern First Nations Network of Care authority — said the agency is not commenting on the death at this time.

The mom spent the last two days visiting her children at Health Sciences Centre's children's hospital.

"They're just babies and they're just sweethearts," said the girls' mother, who spoke to CBC Tuesday outside of the hospital.

The mother said her kids had been in care since October and the last time she saw them was in February.

At that time, she says they looked skinny and she could see bruising on one child's eyes — a concern she raised with her CFS worker.

"I had a gut feeling something was happening and nobody listened to me," she said.

Families minister to do internal investigation

Manitoba's Families Minister Nahanni Fontaine said her department will be doing its own internal investigation and they have reported the death to the Manitoba Advocate for Children and Youth to also investigate.

In an emailed statement, Fontaine said she is "deeply saddened by the tragic death of this young child."

She cannot comment further on the circumstances of the case due to the active RCMP investigation, she said.

Families Minister Nahanni Fontaine said the province will conduct its own internal investigation into the death. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

Her government remains committed to "working with the Southern Network of Care and all authorities to strengthen supports and ensure children and families receive the care and services they need," she said in the statement.

A spokesperson for the Southern Chiefs' Organization, which represents 33 First Nations in southern Manitoba including Waywayseecappo First Nation, sent condolences to the family.

"Given the ongoing investigations into the circumstances surrounding the child’s death and the injuries sustained by the other children, SCO will not comment further or speculate at this time," the spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

'Time to take my baby back in a casket'

After her kids were apprehended in October, the mom says she went into a four-week treatment program in December, took parenting classes and was hoping to get her kids back this summer.

"I did everything, I went to treatment, I did the programs, I stayed sober. I cleaned my house," she said.

"Then just nothing was done about it. And now look, time to take my baby back in a casket and my other girls are just so broken."

She is speaking about what happened to her daughter because she doesn't want to see another death in care and she wants answers as to how this happened.

"I just want her voice to be heard and make sure it doesn't happen to any other kids. Some things need to be done about this," she said.

"All I wanted was them to be home with me where they were safe. And nobody listened."

World.title: From last place to the post-season? Here's how the 2026 Blue Jays could pull it off
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. It's been a frustrating season for the Toronto Blue Jays after the team made it all the way to Game 7 of the World Series last year, but a winning surge in the past two weeks has kept their playoff hopes alive. The CBC's Greg Ross has more on the Jays' turnaround and their chances of making it to the post-season. Prime Minister Mark Carney says "you've got to believe" the Toronto Blue Jays can still make the playoffs. But can they, really? The Jays have played some scrappy baseball lately, as the team finds itself on the fringes of playoff contention with a quarter of the season to go and it's still possible they might find a way to the post-season in the anemic American League. Toronto beat the Boston Red Sox tonight, in a 5-3 victory that improved their season record to 58-63 and kept the team in the hunt for a potential playoff spot. Thanks for the sweater, Karla.

My message to Jays Nation: you've got to believe. pic.twitter.com/oP6IQ9dHmJ —MarkJCarney "At this point, you just kind of throw everything other than winning out the window and show up every day and try to win," Jays infielder and all-star Ernie Clement told CBC News, earlier Tuesday. There are a half-dozen teams, including Toronto, that are within four games of the last wild-card spot in the wider American League — and the Blue Jays would have to leap past all of them to secure a return to the post-season. Here's a look at why the Jays are where they are with just over 40 games to go, and what they have to do to get back to the post-season. From the World Series to last place? That's the reality: Toronto has gone from a team that competed for a World Series title last fall to a team curently sitting in last place in the American Leage East. They can't win the division at this point, so that means they'll have to claim a wild-card spot to reach the post-season. WATCH | The end of an era for some Toronto fan favourites: Blue Jays lose fan favourites in big trades | Duration 2:09 Less than a year after competing for the MLB championship, the Toronto Blue Jays made some big trades ahead of the deadline, including fan favourites Daulton Varsho and pitcher Kevin Gausman. The win over Boston Tuesday night improved Toronto's season record to 58-63 — 12 fewer wins than they had at the same point last year. At present, the Tampa Bay Rays lead the AL East, followed by the New York Yankees in second place, and the resurgent Boston Red Sox — who put together lengthy win streaks in July and August — in third. The Baltimore Orioles (with a 58-62 record) and the Jays sit in fourth and fifth place. Just 2 teams have done it According to Elias Sports Bureau, the official statistician of Major League Baseball (MLB), there are just two teams that have stood at 58-63 through 121 games — the same record the Jays have right now — that went on to make the playoffs in the wild-card era: The 2024 Detroit Tigers and the 2009 Minnesota Twins. Randy Robles of Elias Sports Bureau believes "there's some hope" for the Jays, noting that if there ever was a year for a struggling team to still have a chance, it would be this one, when so many American League teams have been playing so poorly. Blue Jays rookie Charles McAdoo runs the bases at Toronto's Rogers Centre after hitting a solo home run in Monday's game against the Boston Red Sox. (Getty Images) What it will take Toronto has begun to claw its way to a better record, claiming series wins against the Washington Nationals, the St. Louis Cardinals, the Houston Astros and the Philadelphia Phillies in the past couple of weeks. That winning trend has to continue for the team to have a shot at the post-season: "They gotta get to .500," Robles told CBC News, referring to the point when a team has won as many games as it has lost. The Texas Rangers, the team currently sitting in the third wild-card spot the Jays are vying for, was only one game above the .500 mark prior to Tuesday's matchups. All the teams seeking to take the Rangers' spot — Toronto included — currently have losing records. Summing up the challenge the Blue Jays face in climbing the standings, Toronto Star baseball columnist Mike Wilner saw a certain parity in the teams involved in the wild-card fight. "Every team in front of the Blue Jays kind of stinks," Wilner told CBC News. "The problem is, the Blue Jays kind of stink, too." Dylan Cease is the ace of the Blue Jays' starting pitching staff and in the hunt for a Cy Young Award this season. (Paul Beaty/The Associated Press) Cease leads the rotation The Jays are thin on starting pitching right now, but the rotation includes pitching ace Dylan Cease, the newly acquired José Soriano, Shane Bieber, as well as veteran Max Scherzer. Cease is on the hunt for a Cy Young Award, and has been in the midst of a sizzling run this summer that included bid for a no-hitter in July that he carried into the ninth inning. He started Tuesday's game against Boston, going five innings and striking out seven. Soriano was solid in his recent Blue Jays debut. Bieber, who missed most of the first half of the season, has been battling for consistency since rejoining the team in June. Scherzer has had two decent starts for Toronto this month — and the team will be counting on him to deliver more if they have a shot at a wild card. "We have a job to do: Every time we come to the park, we've got to win," Scherzer told CBC News. In the bullpen, the Jays will continue to look to closer Louis Varland and workhorse reliever Tyler Rogers in high-leverage situations. Rookie pitcher Spencer Miles, as well as relievers Braydon Fisher and Mason Fluharty will also be key to any push for the post-season. Kazuma Okamoto rounds the bases after a July 28 home run at Nationals Park. The rookie is leading the Jays in home runs this year with 24. (Brad Mills/Imagn Images/Reuters) What about the bats? Hitting has been a real problem for the Blue Jays this year. The team sits near the bottom of the major leagues in terms of home runs, runs scored and on-base percentage. Only two Blue Jays have a double-digit home run total: Kazuma Okamoto (24) and Springer (12). Last year, Toronto had four players who swatted 20-plus homers. This year, they'll be fortunate to have two.

World.title: What to know about the trial of Lindsay Clancy, woman accused of killing her 3 children
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and attempted suicide.

The Lindsay Clancy murder trial is making headlines around the world as jurors hear harrowing details of the Massachusetts mother who killed her three young children.

Clancy's legal team does not deny that she killed her children, but is arguing she shouldn't be held criminally responsible because she was mentally ill — in the grip of bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis, a rare condition that the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health says occurs in approximately one to two cases per 1,000 births. Postpartum psychosis can cause extreme mood swings, delusions and confusion, according to the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada.

Prosecutors argue Clancy is guilty of three counts of first-degree murder, having plotted to get her husband out of the house so she could carry out the murders.

The trial, which is being held in Plymouth, Mass., is being livestreamed on CourtTV and major Boston TV stations, as well as YouTube. On Tuesday, the trial moved into day 11, and proceedings are expected to continue for several more weeks.

Here are some details about the case and what court has heard.

The killings

Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse, was struggling with her mental health and seeing multiple specialists in 2022. The court has heard she was prescribed 13 different psychiatric medications across different providers.

Her attorneys say Clancy did everything she could to seek help: She turned to multiple outpatient providers, tried various drugs they prescribed, called a suicide hotline, went to an emergency room and approached but wasn’t accepted into a hospital-based, full-day treatment program for women with postpregnancy mental health problems. Clancy also checked herself into a psychiatric hospital for several days.

Rather than improving her condition, her attorneys and family say the shifting cocktail of psychiatric medications made things worse.

Cellphone records show that on Jan. 24, 2023, she texted her husband Patrick late in the afternoon, asking him to pick up takeout and medicine.

During his absence from their Duxbury, Mass., home, prosecutors say Clancy used exercise bands to strangle their three children: five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson and eight-month-old Callan. She then cut her own wrists and throat and jumped out of a second-storey window in an apparent suicide attempt.

Clancy, who turned 36 on Tuesday, was paralyzed from the waist down and has been attending the court proceedings in a wheelchair.

Court hears diary entries

Opening statements began on July 27, after an 18-member jury was selected.

Patrick Clancy, Lindsay's now former husband, took the stand early, detailing her mental health struggles and his experience on the day of the killings. Jurors were shaken when his 911 call was played in court.

The court later heard from Duxbury first responders, crime scene analysts and the family's nanny, who said Lindsay was a "wonderful mom who loved her kids."

Clancy's diary entries were also read in court, including a section where she wrote that she was “completely overwhelmed” trying to take care of her children.

“I feel like I’m drowning every day,” she wrote.

She sobbed in court when details of the autopsy reports were read.

Testimony from medical experts

Recent days have focused on Clancy's mental state, including testimonies from her psychiatrists and mental health experts.

On Monday her lawyer probed Dr. Jennifer Tufts, who saw Clancy via video meetings from September 2022 until the day before the killings.

Defence lawyer Kevin Reddington questioned Tufts' expertise, prescribing decisions and overall treatment, spotlighting her use of 25-minute video appointments and the series of recommended pharmaceuticals.

Defence attorney Kevin Reddington, left, questions psychiatrist Dr. Jennifer Tufts about her hand written notes on Monday. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

"I do not believe that I've been negligent," Tufts testified.

Clancy is suing Tufts and other practitioners in civil court.

On Tuesday, Rebecca Jollotta, a psychiatric nurse practitioner who treated Clancy, testified about a concerning mid-December call with the couple during which she heard Clancy had her "worst day" and was "having persistent, intrusive thoughts of suicide."

Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham has urged jurors not to view the trial as "a public debate about women's mental health and how the medical system treats women," but rather to focus on the specific actions Clancy took and the intent behind them.

If convicted of murder, Clancy faces life in prison without parole.

If found not guilty due to a lack of criminal responsibility, she would be committed to a state mental health facility.

Legal expert Margaret McLean told Parade that Clancy's case would then shift to a "civil commitment process" overseen by the court and mental health experts.

Clancy could eventually be released under strict conditions, or, if her illness is deemed "chronic and dangerous," she could remain institutionalized for the rest of her life.
