World.title: Irakli Kobakhidze: “‘Deep state’ is trying to artificially fuel Russophobia in Georgia”
World.content:
“Radical anti-Russian sentiment in the country is being artificially fuelled and is part of a new campaign against Georgia,” Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said at a briefing. He said attempts to intensify Russophobia in Georgia were part of a plan carried out by agents of the “deep state”.

Kobakhidze recalled that the Georgian government had repeatedly said that, after Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022, the so-called “global war party” had tried to draw Georgia into the conflict and open a “second front” in the country.

The prime minister said this “window of opportunity” created an “existential threat” to Georgia and its population. He said calls for Georgia to join international sanctions against Russia soon followed. According to the government, complying with those demands would have had serious consequences for the country’s economy.

“Because the Georgian government refused to comply with these demands, pursued a sovereign policy and acted in the interests of the state, our country became a target for the European bureaucracy and Western leaders working in tandem with informal oligarchic forces,” Kobakhidze said.

He also addressed the sanctions imposed by Western countries on the Georgian government. According to Kobakhidze, pressure mechanisms, including sanctions, were already being used when the previous US administration under Joe Biden was in power.

Kobakhidze said the sanctions had targeted senior Georgian government officials, ruling party honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili, judges, senior police officers and others.

He said the West had also used Georgia’s EU membership prospects as a tool to pressure the government.

“They failed to break the ruling party, which enjoys the support of the Georgian people, so now they are trying to use their agents to drag Georgia into a new provocation,” he added.

Kobakhidze said a “new stage of the attack” on Georgia, its people and its sovereignty had begun:

“This is a qualitatively new stage of the attack on Georgia, the Georgian people and the country’s sovereignty, unfolding simultaneously on several fronts.”

Background

Several days before the anniversary of the August 2008 war, Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy letter addressing the issue of “Russophobia”.

In the letter, Kobakhidze discussed the links between Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgia’s domestic political situation and the opposition’s position. He said the “global war party” benefited from the ongoing conflict in Ukraine because it wanted to “fuel Russophobia at the highest level among its agents around the world, including in Georgia”.

Kobakhidze accused the opposition and civil society of changing their attitude towards Russia. He described their current tough stance towards Moscow as “Russophobia”.

The letter reignited political disputes over the events of the 2008 war. This time, however, the debate focused not only on the circumstances that led to the war and Russia’s responsibility. The prime minister shifted the focus from Russia’s actions to the position of his Georgian opponents.

Georgian PM on “Russophobia”

World.title: Ilham Aliyev’s AzTV interview during Nakhchivan visit: industrial park, energy projects and Zangezur Corridor
World.content:
Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Nakhchivan

On 11 August, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva visited the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. It was Aliyev’s 17th visit to Nakhchivan since he became president.

During the visit, officials held foundation-laying ceremonies and opened several facilities. Aliyev also visited historical sites and presented battle flags to military units.

The visit ended with an interview with Azerbaijan Television (AzTV), in which Aliyev outlined his plans for Nakhchivan’s development.

The interview focused on the autonomous republic’s economic and social development, energy security and transport infrastructure. Aliyev also discussed Nakhchivan’s place in Azerbaijan’s broader strategy, particularly its future development in conjunction with Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur, territories that came under Baku’s control after the Second Karabakh War.

Key events during the visit

During the visit to Nakhchivan, President Ilham Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva inspected work at the Shams-1 and Garbi Ufug solar power plants, which have a combined capacity of 50 MW.

One of the key events was the laying of the foundation stone for the Nakhchivan Industrial Park. It will be Azerbaijan’s second-largest industrial park by area, after the Sumgayit Industrial Park. A 300 MW thermal power plant is also planned for the site.

Nakhchivan’s total generating capacity currently stands at around 200 MW. Once the new plant comes online, this will increase by roughly half.

The visit programme also included:

the opening of the Nakhchivan Regional DOST Centre;

the presentation of new electric buses and an inspection of railway infrastructure reconstruction works;

the laying of the foundation stone for the Nakhchivan hotel complex, which is expected to be completed by around 2028;

the laying of the foundation stone for a social housing complex;

an inspection of restoration work at the Momine Khatun Mausoleum and the unveiling of a monument to architect Ajami Nakhchivani;

the presentation of Nakhchivan’s General Development Plan through 2044, which envisages expanding the city and increasing its population;

the presentation of battle flags to new commando units of the Separate Combined Arms Army.

Key points from the AzTV interview

Aliyev described his visit to Nakhchivan as a “sign of the autonomous republic’s comprehensive development”. He said every visit should produce concrete results. He highlighted strengthening defence capabilities, energy security, job creation, preserving historical and cultural heritage, and developing transport links as key priorities.

Defence and governance

Aliyev said Nakhchivan’s geographical position – particularly its lack of a direct land connection with mainland Azerbaijan – requires special attention to the region’s defence. He highlighted the creation of the Separate Combined Arms Army and new commando units as key steps.

According to the president, “Azerbaijan’s Armed Forces carry weight in the region”. He also said Nakhchivan had introduced a system of special presidential representatives, similar to the model used in Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur. Aliyev said the benefits of this system of governance were already becoming apparent.

Energy

Nakhchivan has been fully supplied with gas for around 15 years, Aliyev said, thanks to a gas swap agreement with Iran.

The president also placed particular emphasis on the region’s solar energy potential. He said Nakhchivan was Azerbaijan’s most favourable region for solar power generation. More than 600 hectares of land have already been allocated for the development of this sector. The potential is estimated at at least 500 MW and could reach 1 GW in the future.

Aliyev also highlighted the growing role of the private sector. Projects to build solar power plants with a combined capacity of 50 MW are already under way.

The president described electricity exports as a strategic priority. Iran and Turkey are currently the main destinations, but Azerbaijan ultimately hopes to export electricity from Nakhchivan to the European market as well.

Zangezur Corridor – TRIPP

Aliyev said that “the creation of the Zangezur Corridor was our initiative”, recalling that connecting mainland Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan, an integral part of the country, had remained one of Baku’s strategic goals for many years.

He said he had insisted that a provision on the corridor be included in the trilateral statement signed by Azerbaijan, Russia and Armenia on 10 November 2020. Aliyev claims the Armenian side did not want to agree to this, but had no other alternative because continuing the war was not in its interests.

Noting that there had been no practical progress on the issue for five years, Aliyev said a solution emerged after the Washington summit on 8 August 2025, when the TRIPP project (Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity) was launched.

Speaking about the current state of the work, the president said the Horadiz-Aghband highway was almost complete, with only minor technical issues remaining. He said construction of the railway was also progressing rapidly.

Aliyev added that a project for power transmission lines linking mainland Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenia had already been prepared, and locations for the pylons had been identified.

Aliyev predicted that these projects would eventually turn Nakhchivan into one of the region’s key transport and energy hubs.

A unified development concept

The president stressed that Nakhchivan, Eastern Zangezur and Karabakh should develop under a unified concept. He said the geographical proximity of the three regions requires a common approach to their development.

Aliyev noted that master plans for cities in the territories that came under Azerbaijan’s control after the Second Karabakh War had already been approved. He also said he had ordered the preparation of a similar document for Nakhchivan. The “Nakhchivan City Development Master Plan through 2044” was presented to the president during the current visit.

Speaking about the region’s tourism potential, Aliyev said Nakhchivan had significant opportunities thanks to its rich historical heritage, scenic landscapes and clean air. At the same time, he acknowledged that the hotel infrastructure remained underdeveloped and that the existing hotels were generally of a low standard, hindering the growth of tourism.

He said that to address the problem, construction had begun on a new five-star hotel complex in the city centre. The project is expected to be completed around 2028.

Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Nakhchivan

World.content:
New road safety rules in Georgia

Georgia plans to tighten road safety rules under the National Road Safety Strategy for 2026–2030, approved by the government on 5 August 2026. The strategy includes changes in several areas.

At this stage, the measures remain proposals, and some will require further legislative amendments before they can take effect.

What is changing:

Child seats will become mandatory for pre-school children. This means that when transporting a child of the relevant age, it will no longer be enough simply to seat them in the car or secure them with a standard seat belt.

Georgia plans to establish a standard for alcohol-based ignition interlock systems. Under the strategy, authorities intend to take alcohol interlock technology into account when setting requirements for vehicles entering the Georgian market. The government strategy says seat-belt use is one of the key ways to reduce deaths and serious injuries in road accidents. It pays particular attention to rear-seat seat belts because unrestrained passengers in the back can endanger not only themselves but also people sitting in the front of the vehicle.

World.title: Lasha Bugadze becomes first modern Georgian writer whose book was barred from being sent to prison
World.content:
Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

The administration of Rustavi Prison refused to allow Lasha Bugadze’s new novel, The Observer, to be delivered to the prison. The book was intended for Nana Sander, who was convicted over her participation in a protest on 4 October 2025.

Notably, the penitentiary code contains no provision explicitly banning fiction from being brought into prisons.

The book’s synopsis describes a fictional political reality involving the long rule of a “despot”, the “division of the country into zones” and a “cult of the leader”. It also mentions the scheduling of elections and a decision by the country’s population on whether they should take place.

According to Bugadze, a prison official refused to allow the book in, saying the novel contained “political content”.

The writer says it is unclear to him who determined that the book contained political content and what criteria they used. He suspects the decision may have been prompted by words and phrases in the novel, such as “despot” and “cult of the leader”.

“The employee told me directly that the book could not be delivered because it was political in nature. I don’t think he sat down and read the book. I doubt he even read the synopsis,” Bugadze said.

In his view, someone appears to have judged the work to be political without giving any clear reason.

“Who put this label on the text? [Who decided] whether it was political or not? What does that even mean? And, excuse me, even if the content is political, why should a citizen – whether a prisoner or anyone else – not have the right to read such a book?” the writer said.

Bugadze sees the incident as a potential precedent for censoring literary works:

“It can be described as the first significant example of literary censorship in modern Georgian history. This is an extremely dangerous precedent, and under no circumstances should it be considered normal. The situation requires a response. No one has the right to stop someone from reading.”

The head of the human rights organisation Sapari, Baia Pataraia, announced that legal proceedings would begin over the incident:

“We are taking legal steps. <…> First, we will demand a written and reasoned refusal.”

The organisation PEN Georgia also responded to the case. It described the incident as an alarming precedent for censorship of a literary work, linked not only to the novel’s content but also to the author’s political and civic stance. The organisation stressed that censoring fiction and restricting freedom of expression are unacceptable in a democratic society.

Lasha Bugadze’s The Observer

Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

World.title: Armenia seeks alternatives amid concerns over possible Russian gas price hike
World.content:
Russian gas pressure on Armenia

If the issue of raising gas tariffs arises, the Armenian authorities will discuss it with their Russian counterparts in a friendly atmosphere, Sargis Khandanyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, told journalists.

Khandanyan added that he had no information about any negotiations with Russia over gas tariffs. However, he expressed confidence that, if necessary, Armenia would be able to find alternatives to Russian gas. These could include supplies from Iran, although this is not the only option.

Yerevan and Tehran have already discussed the issue. Following talks held with Iranian partners by Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure, Davit Khudatyan, it emerged that the volume of Iranian gas supplies could potentially be doubled.

“This decision has nothing to do with any other country, Russia in particular. It is a profitable economic activity that both countries are interested in expanding,” the Armenian minister said.

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan notes that there has recently been increasingly frequent talk of a possible revision of Russian gas prices. He views the issue in the context of the levers of pressure being used against Armenia. In his view, Moscow has already exhausted much of its arsenal and is now resorting to economic leverage, including in the energy sector.

“Political, cultural and terrorist levers, as well as the influence of the criminal subculture, are no longer working for various reasons. And Russia, in order to prevent Armenia from strengthening its independence, has decided to make full use of its last remaining lever,” Ghevondyan said.

‘This scenario cannot be ruled out’: On gas imports from Azerbaijan

Journalists asked MP Sargis Khandanyan how likely it was that the tariff on gas imports from Russia could change by the end of the year.

“I am not aware of when this issue was last discussed with Russia. Nor am I aware of any information that would give grounds to believe that the gas tariff could change,” he replied.

At the same time, the MP noted that the government attaches great importance to diversifying supplies. He recalled the agreements reached during the visit of Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure to Iran. According to him, the “Trump Route” could also be considered as one such opportunity:

“As part of the transit route that will connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenian territory, a gas pipeline will be built. This could provide another opportunity. We could consider this pipeline as an additional source. Of course, this is a very theoretical idea, but it would not be difficult to implement.”

Asked about the possibility of importing gas from Azerbaijan, Khandanyan said that Yerevan and Baku were discussing a broad range of issues:

“I do not know how far we have progressed on the issue of gas supplies, but this scenario cannot be ruled out.”

In late October 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev announced that all restrictions on transit to Armenia would be lifted. Since then, Armenia has been receiving petroleum products from the neighbouring country by rail. According to official figures, Azerbaijan has already supplied Armenia with 20,000 tonnes of petroleum products.

Yerevan and Tehran agree to increase gas supplies. Can Moscow stand in the way?

Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan paid a three-day visit to Iran. Upon returning from Tehran, he said that the volume of Iranian gas supplied under the “Gas for Electricity” programme could be at least doubled. He explained that the pipeline’s capacity exceeds the volume of gas currently being supplied.

Under the programme, Armenia has been receiving gas from Iran since 2009, converting it into electricity which is then supplied back to Iran.

To increase gas imports and export a corresponding volume of electricity to Iran, construction of the Iran-Armenia high-voltage power transmission line needs to be completed. The Armenian government hopes that the long-delayed project will be completed by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline carrying gas from Iran has been controlled by Russian company Gazprom.

As a result, some experts doubt whether Iranian gas supplies can be increased without Moscow’s consent. The Armenian government, however, has assured that there will be no obstacles to expanding supplies under the “Gas for Electricity” programme.

Expert commentaty

Political commentator Artem Yerkanyan says:

“Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexei Shevtsov threatened that unless Armenia revises its foreign policy course, it will have to pay $800 for Russian gas instead of the current $177. Compensating for that difference would cost at least $1bn. That is more than the €50m the European Union has promised Armenia as compensation for the impact of strained relations with Russia.

It is worth explaining what the figures of $177 and $800 actually mean. Russia’s Gazprom sells gas for $177 to Gazprom Armenia, which is owned by Gazprom itself. In other words, it also earns revenue from the distribution of the gas, and that revenue also goes to Gazprom. Therefore, I think it would be incorrect to say that Armenia buys gas for $177.

It is also unclear where the figure of $800 comes from, considering the following:

China buys Russian gas for $258;

Turkey for $280;

Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia for $400;

Spain, France and Belgium for $450.

Moreover, according to a forecast by Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development, by the end of this year the average price at which Russia will sell gas to countries outside the EAEU [an economic bloc led by Russia] will be $290.

If the average price is $290, why are they planning to sell it to Armenia for $800? That is unclear.”

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan argues:

“Following the elections, the Armenian authorities have continued to pursue a multi-vector foreign policy. Dependence on Russia is steadily declining, with the economic dimension playing an increasingly important role in this process.

While Russia is trying to exert economic pressure, Armenia is opening up new markets that Armenian businesses previously ‘failed to notice’ because of their excessive focus on the Russian market. Although problems remain with some goods, economic diversification is advancing rapidly.

In the energy sector, Armenia has alternatives when it comes to building a new nuclear reactor, which in itself is a headache for Russia.

It is no coincidence that, alongside economic blackmail, Rosatom executives periodically make Armenia ‘attractive’ offers to build a new Russian nuclear reactor. However, the Armenian authorities are likely to opt for a different proposal.

A rise in gas prices could initially cause problems. But Armenia has alternatives here as well: Iranian, Turkmen and now Azerbaijani gas.

Consequently, in the near future, Russian gas may find itself merely competing on the market. This would limit the Kremlin’s ability to use gas prices to blackmail Armenia.

In conclusion, it should be noted that increased pressure from Russia is having the opposite effect. Armenia is steadily ‘freeing itself’ from excessive Russian influence and diversifying its economy. The Kremlin does not appear to recognise this yet, but that is its problem.”

World.title: Kobakhidze: Georgia does not publicly declare Russia an enemy because this would require follow-up steps
World.content:
Georgian prime minister on Russia

Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that the Georgian government does not publicly call Russia an “enemy” because such a political statement would require corresponding action.

A journalist asked Kobakhidze whether the Georgian government considers Russia an enemy. The prime minister replied:

“Your questions are shameful, you look ridiculous. Let me explain in simple terms why this question is shameful: you want to get a sensational headline, even in the Russian media, saying that I have declared the Russian Federation an enemy. This is a specific political statement that would have to be followed by specific steps – roughly the same, or exactly the same, as those your party” (referring to the United National Movement – JAMnews) “took in 2008 and before.”

The journalist asked whether this was precisely why the government was reluctant to openly call Russia an enemy.

“Of course. What, should I repeat it again?!” Kobakhidze replied.

Kobakhidze also addressed Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and reiterated that the Russian Federation occupies 20% of Georgia’s territory.

“Of course, the Russian Federation is the only state and party that has occupied Georgian territories. This is an absolutely clear fact. Numerous statements have been made about this, and there is no doubt about it,” Kobakhidze stressed.

He said Russia’s occupation of Georgian territory was a “crime against the Georgian state and the Georgian people”:

“This is an egregious crime: first the occupation, and then the so-called recognition.”

Georgian prime minister on Russia

World.title: Are We OK? Jebediah doco is both nostalgic triumph and cautionary tale
World.content:
Early in Jebediah: Are We OK?, a career-spanning documentary on the beloved Perth alt-rock band, frontman Kevin Mitchell offers:

"The success or failure of the band has never been the glue that held the band together. It was that mateship that existed before the band started."

It's essentially the thesis statement of a film that examines the deep, enduring bonds tying four friends together for more than 30 years. But also, a surprisingly emotive second half where that proverbial glue risks disintegrating.

Each member — Mitchell, his drumming brother Brett Mitchell, bassist Vanessa Thornton and guitarist Chris Daymond — gets equal footing in a doco that will entertain and enlighten viewers who might only be familiar with Leaving Home or She's Like A Comet.

Dedicated fans will appreciate the revealing insights of a doco that's both a joyful celebration and a serious look at the sobering realities of rock stardom.

Loading Instagram content

"Seeing it all together was like, 'Wow, we actually did some really cool stuff,'" bassist Vanessa 'Ness' Thornton tells Double J.

After meeting director Arlo Dean Cook while shooting a music video, she later asked him to capture Jebediah's 20th anniversary tour, back in 2015.

Cook ended up becoming part of the inner circle, chronicling the band both on- and off-stage.

"It was pretty obvious they had something special," says Cook, drawn to Jebediah not just as a fan but to their mateship and "pure" motivations.

"It wasn't about ego or money or fame or anything like that. Their integrity was so strong and the bond they had together was such a joy to watch."

The halcyon days

Are We OK? kicks off revelling in a vivid period of Australian music history: The '90s alt-rock boom.

An era where a healthy musical patriotism was cultivated via touring festival Big Day Out, ABC TV's Recovery and triple j. Jebediah was championed by all three.

Hailing from Perth, a city historically isolated from the East Coast's music industry hubbub, was to Jebediah's benefit.

Only a year after forming, to play their year 12 ball, the high school mates had "every major label in the country wanting to sign us", remembers Mitchell.

Jebediah's Vanessa Thornton, Kevin Mitchell, Chris Daymond and Brett Mitchell in the early days. (Supplied: Arlo Dean Cook)

Under the management of Heath Bradby, they inked a deal with Murmur, an imprint of major label Sony. The rave reception to Jebediah's 1997 debut album Slightly Odway, was "almost instantaneous," remarks triple j royalty Richard Kingsmill.

They became the first Perth band to reach the top 10 in triple j's Hottest 100 (with Harpoon in 1997), paving the way for WA acts — everyone from Eskimo Joe and John Butler Trio to Tame Impala — to populate the annual countdown's pointy end.

This vibrant period is showcased through exhaustive archival footage, much of it framed through the kind of rumpus room TV set guaranteed to give gen X viewers flashbacks.

Jebediah has a "young fan base these days", says Cook. "People that weren't born [in the '90s]. So we kind of introduce this world to them in a way." (Supplied: Arlo Dean Cook)

From humble beginnings to hardship

Securing more than 1,300 legal approvals for various press shots, street press articles, and footage was "quite the undertaking. [It] took months and months", says Cook.

But it proved essential to showcasing this "beautiful, youthful band".

"The theme of the film ended up being growing up. We really needed to drop the audience back there; soak that up and relive it."

Filmmaker Arlo Dean Cook spent 11 years with Jebediah working on the documentary. (Supplied: Jessica Wyld)

The doco remains engaging as it enters a new decade, one where "pop used to be a dirty word", but came back in vogue right as audiences looked to internationally prompted garage and indie rock revivals for new sounds.

So did Sony, who folded Murmur back into the corporate fold and by 2004, following the lukewarm reception to their fourth album Braxton Hicks, Jebediah took a sabbatical where 'real life' overtakes the band.

Unlike your typical rockumentary, humble scenes of day jobs and domesticity are featured, underscoring larger patterns of renewal following fallow periods.

Loading Instagram content

The quartet's commitment to each other endures, be it through the "difficult second album", managing their independent label Redline Records, or re-fastening frayed relations after Kevin Mitchell's ARIA winning solo sojourn as Bob Evans.

Helping pull back the curtain on the not-so-glamorous elements are members from contemporaries like Spiderbait, You Am I, Grinspoon, Magic Dirt and more.

Providing a textured commentary that authenticates Jebediah's harder challenges, they offer praise but also echo the temptations and surrealism of the touring lifestyle.

"Everything you'd possibly ever need to become an alcoholic is provided," confesses Mitchell.

Early on, he describes Jebediah as a "functional band surrounded by dysfunction". In a bit of foreshadowing, he adds: "I honestly thought we were immune … but we're not."

Addiction and the bigger picture

Eleven years in the making, Cook was halfway into the project when "some drama" surfaced.

Without spoiling the impact of a key reveal, Are We OK? wades into heavy territory concerning a band mate dealing with alcohol and substance abuse issues.

We witness, in sometimes uncomfortable detail, the band at their most fraught. During a co-headline tour with You Am I, they stage an intervention, urging one of their own to seek professional help.

"We just kept the camera rolling," says Cook. "There were a few years there where we didn't know what was going to happen …

"The edit was years and years long because we initially thought it was going to have to be this dual narrative."

Thornton was "shell-shocked" watching the first cut with Cook. "It put me right back there to that intense time. I started to feel nauseous watching."

Jebediah told Arlo Dean Cook, "you do what you need to do to tell the story", says bassist Vanessa Thornton. (Supplied: Arlo Dean Cook)

For his part, Cook developed a deep trust with everyone involved but also an anxious physical tic from the stress.

"I made it clear it was never going to be a puff piece," he says. Similarly, he wasn't interested in a cliched "drugs and alcohol in rock" story. "I didn't really have any interest in that."

Instead, Are We OK? is concerned with, and animated by, the relationship between four people who are friends first, musicians second.

"That's what I cared about most. This band is so funny, so full of life, that when it got heavy it really did change the film's dynamic."

30 and thriving

The slow recovery and repair of Jebediah's connection leads to a hard-won denouement. The effect is like watching a wound heal in real time, alongside candid reflections on the scars left behind.

Even the way Cook juxtaposes imagery of the young, rakish members with the modern-day paints a thousand words about the tolls paid on their mind and bodies.

The story of Jebediah How a bunch of Perth kids playing Ratcat covers became beloved Australian favourites.

Lesser documentaries would sensationalise, or even sanitise, such tough truths. But here, "it still supported this same notion of why we started making the film", says Cook.

"Let's celebrate this bond these guys have together. And when one of them fell down, they just did what they always did and rallied behind them and supported them. It only heightened this beautiful story about a family we were trying to tell."

The darker, candid revelations don't overshadow the good times, they augment them. The 2024 comeback album OIKS resulted in the "busiest year we've had since the '90s", Thornton notes.

Are We OK? expertly navigates a tricky tightrope, sincerely conveying both the thrills and cautionary perils of success.

The takeaway is that meaningful friendship, like a rewarding career or sobriety, takes perseverance. Something you work on, even in the good times.

With a film to promote and gigs filling the calendar, Thornton is most looking forward to reconnecting with her lifelong buddies.

"We haven't played a show since December. Seeing everyone: that's what I'm most excited about because once we're all in a van together, it's always going to be fun."

Jebediah: Are We OK? premiers at Melbourne International Film Festival on Thursday August 13, with additional screenings throughout August.

It opens in cinemas nationwide Thursday October 8.

World.title: Drag moves to the silver screen in Stop! That! Train!
World.content:
May the light of RuPaul shine upon me. I was gagging when a sweet moment of sincerity spiralled into a hilarious smackdown between RuPaul's Drag Race superstars Ginger Minj (AKA Joshua Allen Eads) and Jujubee (AKA Airline Inthyrath).

Fast facts about Stop! That! Train! What: RuPaul's Drag Race board a ridiculously queer read on Flying High! Directed by: Adam Shankman Starring: Ginger Minj, Jujubee, Brooke Lyn Hytes, RuPaul, Sarah Michelle Gellar When: In cinemas now Likely to make you feel: Like it's time to PANIC in a fabulous outfit

We've hopped online, tragically too early for cocktail hour at my end, to chat about their top billing in comical disaster movie, Stop! That! Train!

Think Leslie Nielsen in Flying High! but much queerer.

It all started so innocently.

"Juju and I have been very close friends for 11 years now," Ginger says.

"We practically live together on tour. We know each other's nuances, when we should be there, and when we should back off. We've definitely grown through our pain together."

And then the 'bye, girl,' moment erupts, as Jujubee pulls a theatrically affronted face thunderous with shade.

"I never knew we had any pain," Jujubee intones faux-imperiously.

"I'm just discovering this in this interview. Thank you so much, Stephen A Russell, for allowing me to hear the truth come out of Ginger Minj. What are you saying? What kind of pain?"

Ginger blinks: "Are you saying I told the truth?"

To which Jujubee responds: "Finally. Put it all over the internet. That needs to be the headline."

Ginger Minj (left) and Jujubee make a dynamic duo in Stop! That! Train! (Supplied: Maslow Entertainment)

Chemical reaction

Watching Ginger Minj and Jujubee spar playfully is a hoot, as is Stop! That! Train!

They play Tess and DeeDee, two employees of the unglamorous Stank Rail who smuggle their way into a better gig aboard the Glamazonian Express.

Facing the wrath of snooty first-class attendant Amber, played by fellow Drag Race queen Brooke Lyn Hytes, is only half the battle. There's also the small matter of the once-in-a-generation 'stormaganza' that's bearing down on the train, in the face of which even RuPaul's President Gagwell is powerless.

Director Adam Shankman tasked Ginger and Jujubee with playing Tess and DeeDee (relatively) straight, anchoring the movie’s outrageous misfortune.

"The rest of the cast is in Airplane! but the two of us are in Thelma and Louise," Ginger says. "That was so great, because with Drag Race, the acting challenges are about being as big as possible. Being a scene-stealer.

"But this was an opportunity to be the antithesis of that, and it was such a challenge, but so much fun."

Jujubee concurs. "There's a beauty in how grounded their comedy plays."

Shankman directed The Wedding Planner. He also officiated Stop! That! Train! co-star and Buffy alum Sarah Michelle Gellar's union with Freddie Prinze Jr and is a Bob Fosse Award-winning choreographer.

"That's why the shots are so beautiful," Jujubee says. "He's always thinking about the movement behind the scenes."

The film features a sweet and saucy romance for DeeDee in the compact shape of M3GAN actor Brian Jordan Alvarez's hunky train conductor, Cal.

Much of the action happens on the luxurious Glamazonian Express train line. (Supplied: Maslow Entertainment)

"I'm three times bigger than him and begged to be put in the background," Jujubee laughs. "Can I just hold his hand from back here, so I look a little smaller? If we were floating in the ocean and there was a door, I'd let him on."

But the real love story is the friendship between Tess and DeeDee.

"There's no faking chemistry," Jujubee says. "You can't act it. You either have it or you don't. It's science. I don't know what chemical we make, but it's explosive."

Ginger grins. "It's probably a chemical imbalance."

Canadian club

Canadian Drag Race host Brooke Lyn Hytes (aka Brock Hayhoe) relished embracing Amber's queen bee energy as the antagonist to Tess and DeeDee.

"I feel like I was typecast," she cackles. "I have that face."

RuPaul said drag would never go mainstream. 24 Emmys later, his show is a global phenomenon From its humble campy beginnings, RuPaul's Drag Race has grown into a juggernaut of reality television and a springboard for performers the world over.

The hardest part of getting into character was letting go of control over costume, hair and makeup, allowing Salvador Pérez Jr, Jeri Baker and Kerry Herta do their thing.

"Drag queens are so used to driving the bus when it comes to their career and what they look like," Hytes says. "We're self-made creatures, so to give that over to somebody else's vision takes a lot of trust. But it turned out so well."

As did Stop! That! Train!'s ritzy dance numbers, choreographed by Jamal Sims.

"He's amazing," Hytes says. "I'm a bit of a backseat everything, giving suggestions, and have a hard time not stating my opinion. But it was a very collaborative environment."

Hytes knows her moves, having been a ballet dancer as a kid.

"I was in the boys' class, doing the male steps, and I realised pretty quickly they weren't for me," she says. "I wanted to be the swan, not the prince. And if I'm not interested in something, I'm putting zero effort in."

Instead, Hytes headed to the drag troupe Les Ballets Trockadero de Monte Carlo and on to Drag Race, now hosting the Canadian edition. It's an opportunity she does not take for granted.

"Drag Race has changed all of our lives," Hytes says. "It's changed popular culture. There aren't enough words to describe how grateful I am for everything it's given me. None of us would be here doing anything without RuPaul and World of Wonder. So please don't fire me."

Days Of Our Lives icon Lisa Rinna is just the tip of the cameo iceberg in Stop! That! Train! (Supplied: Maslow Entertainment)

Movie stars

Ginger Minj is equally effusive about the power of her president. “I grew up in a little Southern Baptist town where all the good Christians knew each other,” she recalls.

"When The Brady Bunch Movie (1995) came out, my mom took me to see it. The cinema was full of people I would see at church on Sunday, and I remember holding my breath when RuPaul came on the screen."

She needn't have worried.

"Everybody laughed. They bought into it. And in my head, when my mom looked at me and smiled, I was like, 'Oh, I can do that. I can be that. It gave me hope."

That young queer kids can look up to her and Jujubee as movie stars alongside Gellar brings them both such joy.

"All I ever dreamed, as a kid, was to be a movie star," Jujubee says. "So sharing this queer joy with the masses is really cool. The film's full of people who have always been othered. Who felt like the odd one out.

"And now they get to be a fabulous star in this equally fabulous disaster movie that explodes like a confetti cannon with particles that go everywhere for all eternity."

Stop! That! Train! is in cinemas now.

World.title: Box office quiz: Zendaya vs Tom Holland vs Robert Pattinson
World.content:

World.title: Trump sued over scheme to sell instant access to Truth Social posts
World.content:
Two US media groups are suing US President Donald Trump over his move to charge for early access to his often market-moving Truth Social posts.

The lawsuit, filed in New York by The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation, states that the scheme is "extraordinary, corrupt and unconstitutional".

Subscribers to the paid service are supposed to get almost instantaneous access to Mr Trump's messages on Truth Social, crucial seconds ahead of the general public.

The billionaire US leader often uses the platform to announce huge news, ranging from developments in the Iran war to trade tariffs, all of which can instantly send market values tumbling or soaring.

Truth Social is one of the chief ways Donald Trump communicates with the public. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

Early access to the service can cost up to $US100,000 ($141,000) per month, according to the lawsuit, which was filed on Wednesday, local time.

At least five trading companies signed up shortly after the launch, according to The Wall Street Journal.

"This scheme is profoundly corrupt," the court filing said.

Why selling Truth Social access is causing controversy For up to $US100,000 per month, subscribers can receive the US president's Truth Social posts milliseconds before everyone else. But experts say the bigger question is whether some traders are already getting information much earlier.

"The President stands to gain financially by giving 'market-moving' government information to those who are willing and able to pay his personal company."

Trump Media and Technology Group, the company operating the platform, has dismissed concerns over the product, which is called Truth API and was first unveiled in mid-July.

The scheme has further highlighted how Mr Trump and many of his close relatives have allegedly made billions of dollars in his second White House term through cryptocurrency ventures, property deals, stock trades and payouts from lawsuits.

Prominent members of the Democratic Party have accused the president's latest venture of being corrupt.

Democratic Senator Mark Warner announced last Tuesday on X that he has introduced a bill to the US Senate that would "crack down on this corruption and ensure all Americans have free and equal access to public announcements from government officials."

AFP

World.title: Aluminium smelter bailout to cost taxpayers $2.5b over 10 years
World.content:
A bailout of the country's largest aluminium smelter will cost taxpayers $2.5 billion dollars, with the New South Wales and federal governments expected to split the bill down the middle.

Late last year mining giant Rio Tinto warned the Tomago Aluminium plant could be forced to close when its energy supply contract ran out in 2028, due to the rising cost of renewable and coal-fired power.

Tomago is currently Australia's largest electricity user, using about 10 per cent of the state's total electricity supply annually.

A joint statement from the NSW and federal governments said the funding package would "secure the future of aluminium smelting in the region."

Anthony Albanese announced a deal would soon be reached on a visit to the site in December. (ABC Newcastle: Ben Clifford)

"The joint investment will deliver a long-term renewable energy solution for the Tomago Aluminium smelter that supports commercially sustainable operations beyond 2028 and accelerates decarbonisation of more than 10 per cent of NSW's electricity grid," a spokesperson said in a statement.

The spokesperson noted the contribution from the NSW government "is capped at $1.225 billion over 10 years from 2029".

The smelter's owner, Rio Tinto, will invest a minimum of $1.1 billion on top of the taxpayer funding, to reduce its energy usage and gear it toward renewables.

"This includes $100 million to drive further decarbonisation activities at the smelter and undertake an innovative demand-response program to support the NSW grid," the spokesperson said.

"This demand-response program aims to position the Tomago smelter as the international leader in electricity demand response and flexibility services."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and NSW Premier Chris Minns will visit the smelter on Thursday to tout the deal.

During a previous visit to the Hunter site, the prime minister told Tomago workers he suspected a deal could be reached quickly.

However, plans stalled when a clear-cut funding agreement could not be reached with NSW.

It is understood the federal government wanted an even 50:50 funding split, similar to a deal inked with the Queensland government for the Boyne Aluminium Smelter near Gladstone.

At the time, Mr Minns pushed back on the even-funding proposal, saying the deal was being led by the federal government and any contribution from the state must work in the interests of NSW taxpayers.

The full details of the bailout are expected to be announced tomorrow. (ABC Newcastle: Nakita Jager)

Flow-on effects

The smelter employs about 1,000 workers and has been operational 24 hours a day since 1983.

The long operating hours and heavy production processes make the smelter the largest single electricity user in NSW.

The rescue package follows a string of similar bailouts offered by the Albanese government to struggling heavy industries, including Glencore's Mount Isa Copper smelter and the struggling Nyrstar smelters in Tasmania and South Australia.

The Electrical Trades Union said workers had been on edge for months as they eagerly waited for an announcement about their future.

Union organiser Brad McDougall said a deal could not come fast enough.

"It's been very difficult for all employees on the site," he said.

"We get comments made like, 'I wake up every day not knowing if today is going to be the day', positive or negative ... so this news will be fantastic."

Rio Tinto's latest annual report showed it had recorded a $10 billion profit after tax across 2025, attributable to its owners.

Its total aluminium and lithium projects were valued at $4.6 billion, up from $3.6 billion in 2024.

World.title: Ex-Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji, architect of growth, dies at 97
World.content:
Former Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji has died at the age of 97, according to state media.

Known as a reformer, he helped ignite China's explosive economic boom by forcing wrenching change on state industry in the 1990s and leading the country into the World Trade Organization.

The official Xinhua news agency reported that Zhu died of illness in Beijing on Wednesday morning, local time.

Once sent into rural exile to do manual labour for praising reforms in other communist countries, Zhu pushed through a dizzying array of changes as premier, China's top economic post, from 1998 to 2003.

Zhu clashed with Communist Party conservatives and state industry bosses as he pushed state-owned companies to become efficient and profitable.

That cost millions of layoffs, but helped propel China to overtake Japan as the second-largest economy behind the United States in 2010.

Building on former leader Deng Xiaoping's 1979 reforms, Zhu is credited with supplying the resourcefulness and tenacity to push through history-making changes such as China's WTO membership, which helped to transform China into the world's biggest exporter.

Those changes helped to keep economic growth above 8 per cent a year from 2000-2010, peaking at 14.2 per cent in 2007.

Zhu launched China’s home ownership boom in 1998 with an initiative to sell apartments owned by state companies. Families rushed to buy, and within a decade the majority of urban housing was privately owned.

In 1992, on a visit to Sydney when Vice Premier, Zhu spoke of a "strengthening" relationship between China and Australia that, he said, could contribute to the stability of the Asia-Pacific region.

According to the state news agency, an obituary jointly issued by China's top political bodies said he lived "a life of revolution, a life of struggle, a life of glory".

"It was a life dedicated wholeheartedly to serving the people, one given to the communist cause. His passing is a major loss for the Party and the country."

AP/AFP

World.title: Dozens dead after Zimbabwe ferry capsize, major retrieval mission launched
World.content:
Survivors are describing frantic passengers pleading with the captain of an overloaded ferry to turn back from strong waves shortly before it capsized and killed at least 44 people on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe.

The number of people on board the vessel when it sank on Tuesday, local time, was unclear as estimates reached as high as 153 people on a government agency-operated ferry whose capacity, authorities said, was just 90.

"Some of us survived by standing on top of the capsized hull," one of the two crew members who survived, Anyway Chambati, told state broadcaster ZBC News.

"Before it went down, passengers were screaming at us that the boat was flooding, water was pouring into the engine room and goods were spilling out."

Multiple witnesses told ZBC that passengers urged the captain to turn back as waves grew perilous, only to be dismissed.

When water surged into the vessel, chaos erupted as frantic travelers scrambled for life jackets beneath their seats.

Investigations suggested the boat was overloaded when it went over during heavy winds on Lake Kariba, officers said on Wednesday.

The Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation earlier cited a local official as saying that 114 tickets had been issued for the ferry's journey, suggesting more people were on board.

Zimbabwe’s Civil Protection Unit said in a statement it could only confirm there were 114 adult passengers onboard, along with five crew members.

There could have been an unknown number of children below ticketing age who were onboard and not accounted for, the unit said.

Zimbabwe's The Herald newspaper then first reported that 15 bodies had been recovered and 27 people, including children, were still missing.

Within hours the news outlet reported more bodies had been pulled from the water and the death toll had risen to 37.

Zimbabwe's the national disaster management agency also said 77 people had been rescued and made it to a small island on the lake, with boats dispatched to bring the survivors back.

Police only confirmed 67 rescues of people who had been taken to a primary school for medical attention.

Zimbabwean state broadcaster ZBC published video of speedboats making their way to what appeared to be an overturned boat on the lake as a helicopter hovered overhead.

An underwater team for search and rescue operations was deployed on the huge lake.

Mutsa Murombedzi, a local member of parliament, posted a video of what she said were people on shore waving off what appeared to be the aging ferry at the start of its journey.

She said rural communities use the boat to travel along the lake to the town of Kariba, a journey that usually takes about five hours.

Some people standing on the shore were also concerned about whether the ferry would survive strong waves on the lake, according to the video.

Kariba is the largest man-made lake in the world by volume and was created in the late 1950s and early 1960s by building a dam wall to block the Zambezi River.

Its construction resulted in a valley slowly filling with water to form a huge lake that is now more than 200 kilometres long and up to 40 kilometres wide in places.

Wires

World.title: Neo-Nazi vandal attack at SA workers club is 'modern-day fascism'
World.content:
A century-old Adelaide workers club has condemned the neo-Nazi vandalism of its premises as an act of "modern-day fascism".

Semaphore Workers Club staff said the venue had been broken into sometime earlier this week by intruders who daubed Nazi symbols on two of its pool tables.

Dave Kirner, from the club's administration committee, told 891 ABC Adelaide the attack had "appalled" and "disgusted" staff.

"A group of people broke into the building and smashed the heritage bay window and then ended up spraying swastikas onto the heritage 120-year-old billiard tables," he said.

"We got calls about it today after tradies saw the broken windows. Representatives of the club came in and just saw and [were] just absolutely horrified."

A window was smashed during the break-in. (Supplied: Dave Kirner)

Mr Kirner said he suspected whoever was responsible was opposed to the club — which has strong ties to the trade union movement — and its support for a "lot of progressive issues".

"All it's done is it's mobilised a whole lot of people in opposition to what basically appears to be modern-day fascism in South Australia," he said.

"There's been a lot of activities by these types of groups right throughout Australia and it normally involves aggressive violent approaches.

"We're strongly opposed to that and strongly opposed to the sort of messages they put out which are disgraceful [and] racist."

The club says the pool tables are of great heritage value. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

SA Police confirmed it was investigating a break-in "at a premises at Esplanade, Semaphore" which occurred between 4:30pm on Monday and 3pm on Tuesday.

"It is believed entry was gained after a window was smashed," police said in a statement.

"Damage was caused within the premises and items including alcohol were stolen."

The incident comes amid a federal royal commission into antisemitism in Australia, and follows the vandalism of an Adelaide property with antisemitic messages and symbols last month.

The club earlier said it would ensure police were notified of the incident, and Mr Kirner estimated the cost of repairs at more than $15,000.

Workers club president Sally Mitchell said the site was a popular live music venue and that it had previously been targeted for political reasons.

"We've had stickers put on the fence and that type of thing," she said.

"This invasion, coming into the premises causing the damage, is outrageous and unacceptable.

"They've tried entry at the rear of the premises without success … [and] then have caused quite significant damage coming through a window."

The club says whoever was responsible smashed their way in. (Supplied: Dave Kirner)

She said the club had insurance, but had no footage — and would be "upgrading our security, of course".

"We're just in the process of upgrading cameras … [but] not soon enough, basically," she said.

"The premises will retain its character and its political nature — that doesn't change. We don't shy away from fascists."

Police said investigations were continuing and urged anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: Chiropractor who sparked outrage for cracking newborn baby’s spine now convicted sex offender
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Sarah Rose was a young aspiring ballerina, chiropractor Dr Ian Rossborough had a reputation among Melbourne’s elite dance world as a “Mr Fix-It” for injuries. She first met Rossborough for a torn hamstring when she was just 10 years old, following an injury that occurred as a result of a gruelling dance training regimen and trying to perfect her turnout. Sarah Rose, was sexually assaulted by chiropractor Dr Ian Rossborough when she was a teenager. Steven Siewert Rose says that Rossborough, who shot to prominence a decade ago when he was accused of dangerously cracking the spine of a four-day-old baby, told her he admired her discipline and maturity and said he wanted to help her achieve her dream of being a professional ballet dancer. He recommended she see him every four to six weeks for ongoing treatments and chiropractic manipulations. Rose, who gave permission for her name to be published, was one of several young Melbourne dancers who were treated by Rossborough over many years. She is also one of at least two women who have accused him of grooming and sexual abuse when they were children.



Sarah Rose was groomed and sexually assaulted by chiropractor Dr Ian Rossborough as a teenager. “He had this belief that he was very much the best and the most important in the world at what he does and we as dancers were lucky to have him in our corner and supporting us,” Rose, who is now 25, says. Last September, the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court found Rossborough guilty of four counts of sexual assault and grooming of a child aged 16 to 17 for an assault on Rose. Related Article Healthcare Call for age limit after chiropractor breaks baby's neck He was given a two-year Community Correction Order and is now a convicted sex offender. Rossborough was suspended from working as a chiropractor by the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) last year and has surrendered his registration. This masthead can reveal that another alleged victim, who was also a young dancer treated by the chiropractor, has contacted police and alleges she was groomed and sexually abused by Rossborough over a period of almost three years when she was a teenager. The woman says she was referred to Rossborough by her dance school.



Following the criminal case last year, the alleged victim, who is now in her 30s and spoke to this masthead on the condition of anonymity, submitted a 13-page statement of allegations against Rossborough to AHPRA. The national healthcare watchdog is conducting its own investigation into Rossborough. The woman hopes the matter will be referred to a civil tribunal, which examines the most severe complaints against Australian health practitioners, and will allow her to have her allegations heard. “The injustice of it really weighs on me,” she says. “I strongly believe he’s still a threat to the community, which is what prompted me to follow through with this.” Ian Rossborough was found guilty of sexual assault and grooming last year. In the statement, seen by this masthead, the woman alleges that Rossborough told her after the sexual abuse began: “You have the power to destroy me, if you ever tell anyone”. “I now feel deep discomfort and distress when I reflect on what occurred,” she wrote in her statement. “It is confronting to recognise that Ian took advantage of my youth, vulnerability, and impressionable nature.



“I was a young and emotionally vulnerable girl when I met him, and he exploited the imbalance of power.” When Sarah Rose turned 14, Rossborough gave her his personal phone number, telling her she could bypass his long waiting list whenever she needed to see him. He started texting her regularly and confided in her about his personal life and divorce. He called her his “good buddy”, and invited her to do yoga classes with him. Rose says her appointments with Rossborough were only meant to be 15 minutes, but he would often stretch them out to an hour without charging her. “All my focus was on my career. Dance was my entire identity,” Rose says.



“Dance gave me a chance to process all my emotions of the world, but it is really hard to look back now and realise how much I was ignoring and shoving down just to cope.” On the night she was assaulted, Rose was 17 and about to fly overseas for a life-changing summer program at the Washington Ballet. Sarah Rose Steven Siewert Rossborough promised to help get her body into the best physical shape before she left and, under the guise of helping her lose weight, instructed her to use the sauna in a yoga studio next to his clinic and strip completely naked before entering. About 45 minutes later, Rossborough came into the sauna took off his clothes and sexually assaulted Rose. “I just froze when it happened,” Rose says. “He was my lift home that night, so I knew no one was coming to get me, and no one was there to help. I remember thinking, ‘You have no other way home ... Just act normal. Don’t let him know you’re freaking out’.” After a video of him manipulating the spine of a newborn went viral across the world in 2016, Rossborough was temporarily banned from treating children while he was investigated by the nation’s medical watchdog.

World.title: Labor backs down on late change to get news scheme across the line
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Labor backs down on late change to get news scheme across the line Paul Sakkal August 12, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has reversed a late change to a scheme forcing tech giants to pay for news, clinching a deal with Opposition Leader Angus Taylor that media firms hope will lead to hundreds of millions of dollars in new revenue. Powerful news bosses from this masthead’s owner Nine and News Corp revolted last week after Labor reduced the cut that any one media outlet would receive from a tech firm’s payout from 25 per cent to 17 per cent of the total levy each social media platform is charged. This was a reduction the government made without consultation. That reduction has now been scrapped. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Communications Minister Anika Wells. Alex Ellinghausen The change to the News Bargaining Incentive was aimed at spreading the wealth and benefiting smaller publishers, but large outlets argued it undervalued businesses that hire most journalists. Albanese has been talking to top news executives. He worked with Taylor to strike a deal that rekindled bipartisan support for the world-first scheme. Initially struck by the Morrison government, Labor’s revamped model pushes digital giants to compensate news businesses for articles on social platforms.



Communications Minister Anika Wells said the government was “delivering for journalists”, while Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino recognised “the significant benefits strong journalism brings to communities across the nation”. Labor made another change that it did not previously disclose: guaranteeing that Australian Associated Press, a newswire owned by a not-for-profit, will gain 5 per cent of any payments made by tech outfits. Sources in the news sector said such a high payment for a small publisher was questionable, though they did not expect news bosses to complain, given Albanese had stepped in to reverse the substantive change. The incentive works by levying a 2.5 per cent charge on tech firms’ local ad revenue. To encourage firms to strike voluntary deals with media businesses, the government offers digital platforms an offset to the charge. The aim is to deliver up to $250 million to media companies whose business models have been smashed by advertising money flowing to tech giants. The digital platforms argue there is no justification for the policy because news outlets actually benefit from distributing their work on social media.



The Trump administration considers the tax a form of “foreign extortion”. The tech sector in the US has called on Australia to face higher tariffs as a penalty. On Tuesday, Trade Minister Don Farrell lobbied the US over Donald Trump’s decision to impose a 12.5 per cent tariff on Australian exports. Related Article Publishing ‘Deeply misled’: Nine says news bargaining plan could cost jobs Separately, the government made a tweak to the accounting method for the NBI that will increase the base of tech firms’ revenue subject to the charge. The number of deals each firm will be forced to do has also increased from six to eight. Legislation will be introduced to parliament on Thursday and will most likely pass the Senate next week, putting pressure on Meta in particular to come to the table. Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, last year threatened to block news articles on its platforms rather than pay any charge. Google was already keen to do deals. World.title: Australia’s biggest aluminium smelter saved in $2.5 billion rescue deal
World.content:
NationalManufacturing Australia’s biggest aluminium smelter saved in $2.5 billion rescue deal Nick Toscano and Michael McGowan August 12, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s biggest aluminium smelter will receive a $2.5 billion government bailout package to stay open, ending months of crisis negotiations with federal and NSW officials over ways to keep the plant viable and safeguard more than 1000 jobs. Tomago Aluminium, majority-owned by resources giant Rio Tinto, has been consulting the smelter’s workforce and their union officials since late last year about the risk of the site closing when its existing power contract expires in 2028, and electricity costs are set to double. Tomago’s owners and government officials have been in crisis talks over assistance to keep the smelter viable beyond 2028. Under the agreement, expected to be announced at the site on Thursday, Tomago Aluminium will invest $1.1 billion into the future of the smelter, including $100 million in driving lower-carbon manufacturing processes and making the electricity-hungry plant more flexible so it can power down and reduce its consumption to support the grid at critical times. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Energy Minister Chris Bowen, Industry Minister Tim Ayres and NSW Premier Chris Minns will travel to the smelter near Newcastle to announce the multi-year deal, according to sources briefed on the agreement but not yet authorised to discuss it publicly.



While many details remain unknown, the joint package would deliver a “long-term renewable energy solution” to Tomago Aluminium that would support the site’s commercially sustainable operations beyond 2028 and accelerate its decarbonisation, a joint statement from the federal and state governments said. Albanese said Tomago was not only important for the Hunter region, but was a “critical asset for the country and our manufacturing future”. “In December last year I stood in the rain at Tomago and told the workers ‘we have your back’,” Albanese said. “Today, alongside the NSW government, we deliver on that promise.” The Tomago deal is the latest in a series of taxpayer-funded rescue packages to prop up struggling metals processors over the past two years. The Albanese government has contributed to bailouts worth $2 billion for Rio Tinto’s Boyne smelter in Queensland, $2.4 billion for the collapsed Whyalla steelworks in South Australia, and $600 million for Glencore’s copper smelter and refinery in Mt Isa.



The support for Tomago comes despite Rio Tinto last month reporting a $US6.7 billion ($9.5 billion) half-year profit, up 47 per cent from the same time a year earlier. Tomago Aluminium has indicated that electricity accounts for 40 per cent of the plant’s costs, but prices were set to double from 2028 once its contract with AGL expires. The cost of coal-fired generation had increased significantly, the company said, and it was uncertain when enough renewable projects, plus back-up firming capacity, would be available at the scale it required. Related Article Updated

Manufacturing Nation’s manufacturing at ‘dangerous crossroads’ with more big bailouts to come Government and industry sources have previously indicated that a deal for Tomago may include a power purchasing agreement with discounted energy supplied to the smelter via a Commonwealth-owned entity like Snowy Hydro. Minns said the agreement secured more than 1000 jobs at Tomago and thousands more that rely on the smelter, giving the region “certainty about its future”.



“This is a good day for the Hunter,” he said. “I want to thank the prime minister and the Commonwealth government – we’ve worked closely together to get to this point and deliver an agreement that to find a way through and secure the future of Tomago.” Aluminium smelters, which need huge amounts of electricity, have been under mounting financial pressure across the nation as their owners face the dual challenges of intensifying competition from cheaper Chinese producers of the metal and the elevated cost of energy. The Tomago smelter is the single largest user of electricity in NSW. It consumes more than 10 per cent of the state’s power supply. Tomago Aluminium, Australia’s largest aluminium smelter, produces up to 590,000 tonnes of the metal a year, which is widely used to manufacture construction materials, cars, drink cans, foil packaging and electrical products. Aluminium is also increasingly in demand in the construction of solar panels and wind turbines. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Redacting the dress code
World.content:
“Graham Russell’s friend was turned back at the Cuesta border in 1971 as his hair was too long (C8),” notes Mia David of Wollongong. “My friend was married in 1968, and, while on her honeymoon, she (dressed in a very fetching pants suit) and her husband went to a club for lunch. She was denied entry, as ladies in pants were not allowed. Not a worry. She removed the trousers, and they accepted her attire of a very short miniskirt. Apparently, she had to be extra careful as she sat down for lunch.”

“My own experience in early 1970 in Singapore was similar, but different,” says Rhod Jeffrey of Surry Hills. “I was marooned there for six weeks awaiting a money transfer. I had to renew my visa weekly where there was a sign stating: ‘Persons with long hair will be served last so as to cause them the maximum of inconvenience’. I had fairly long hair but encountered no animosity or inconvenience because of it.”

“Working as a commercial artist in Jakarta 1973, (pre-Photoshop), my job was retouching poster artwork for rock stars touring Singapore,” says Peter Barker of One Mile. “I think I’m the only person with the honour of giving Mick Jagger a short-back-and-sides for The Rolling Stones’ Pacific Tour in 1973. So horrific was my retouching, the band never made it to Singapore because the doctored publicity material made them unrecognisable!”

It’s a long way from Rhoda and Gus’ surprise Joburg snowfall of ’81 (C8), but Pauline McGinley of Drummoyne is well versed when it comes to the white stuff: “Growing up in Scotland, I spent my childhood in the snow. Fingers and toes stuffed into woollen gloves and socks. Snow days off school. When you would wake up in the morning after a nightfall of snow, you knew immediately, before even looking out the window. Quiet, hushed and an intense stillness. The joy!”

“I had a similar opera experience to Nola Tucker (C8),” recalls Elizabeth Savage of Hughes (ACT). “Berlin Opera House, L’italiana in Algeri, sung in Italian with German surtitles. No idea what the story was, but the music was pleasant, and the ballet interludes were impressive.”

World.title: ‘There was no precedent’: The moment that had Alone producers terrified
World.content:
CultureTV & radioReality TV ‘There was no precedent’: The moment that had Alone producers terrified Karl Quinn August 12, 2026 — 8:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For producers and contestants alike, making Alone is all about anticipating risks and being prepared to meet them. But as viewers of the latest season of the Australian iteration will know, this year the survival competition broke the sort of new ground nobody wanted: a contestant went missing. “It was a world first, which is why the panic levels were so high,” says executive producer Riima Daher. “There was no precedent, nothing to fall back on in this scenario.” Former refugee Arash ascribes his behaviour to going into “survival mode”. SBS When Afghanistan-born wrecking-yard worker and taekwondo champion Arash went AWOL after 26 days, Daher says, “honestly, the first thought was ‘Is he dead?’ I was absolutely terrified. You worry that something really bad has happened, the sorts of things you don’t want to think about, but the sorts of things that can happen in the woods sometimes. And you start to check the water to make sure he hasn’t fallen in there.” The Sapmi region of northern Finland, where this season was filmed, is home to bears, wolves and reindeer, all of which posed potential threats to the 10 contestants from the other end of the Earth. But Arash’s disappearance – leaving behind the GPS tracker and emergency phone he was supposed to carry at all times, as well as his camera equipment – was not down to any of those things. It was, rather, the result of some sort of brain snap.



Though he declined to answer questions from this masthead, Arash does offer some insight into what happened in the episode that aired on Wednesday night. In a voiceover as he is being extracted by boat, Arash attempts to explain what was going through his mind when he ditched everything and wandered away from his camp. “I grew up in a war zone. I crossed seven countries with no documents. I’ve been lost in the sea, slept in the jungle, and I think this experience activated a survival mode that I know the best,” he said. “And when I get in that mode, the rules do not matter. I only rely on myself. All I was thinking was just to survive.”



He labelled his behaviour a “blunder” that had cost him a “very beautiful great opportunity” to change his life by winning the $250,000 prize for whichever contestant stays the longest. “I made a mistake, and I take full responsibility for it,” he said. “That will stay with me for the rest of my life.” It will stay with Daher and her team, too. Riima Daher and team search frantically for Arash. SBS At the height of the panic, there were “about 15 or 20 people” on the ground searching for Arash. “We called on people who weren’t even part of our rescue team to help,” Daher says. The six or seven hours it took to find him was, she says, “the most scared I’ve ever been personally or professionally. You question your career choices. I’m like, ‘Why am I not just working on Love Island? Everyone’s in the villa. What am I thinking?’ And you do start to fear the worst. You start to spiral, you start to see headlines.”



Did you see yourself in the dock in a courtroom? Related Article Reality TV Alone Australia’s new season is ‘the polar opposite’ of what we’ve seen before “One hundred per cent I did, I can’t lie. And then you retrace your steps. You go, ‘Did I do everything I’m supposed to do? Where are the holes in my responsibility?’” And when you finally did locate him? “We could have killed him.” Despite the anxiety he had caused, the producers didn’t immediately want to pull Arash from the contest. “You always want to give the participants as much rope as possible,” Daher says.



The problem was, he couldn’t articulate why he had done what he had, and that cast serious questions over his mental state. “It was a serious breach,” Daher says. “I mean, it placed him in real danger, it placed all of us in danger to have to go and look for him. Had he been able to explain it in a way that made sense, perhaps we could have left him in there, but he couldn’t. “From a duty-of-care point of view – as well as a rule-break point of view – we just couldn’t put him back in.” Alone Australia is on SBS, Wednesdays from 7.30pm
