World.title: Chiropractor who sparked outrage for cracking newborn baby’s spine now convicted sex offender
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Sarah Rose was a young aspiring ballerina, chiropractor Dr Ian Rossborough had a reputation among Melbourne’s elite dance world as a “Mr Fix-It” for injuries. She first met Rossborough for a torn hamstring when she was just 10 years old, following an injury that occurred as a result of a gruelling dance training regimen and trying to perfect her turnout. Sarah Rose, was sexually assaulted by chiropractor Dr Ian Rossborough when she was a teenager. Steven Siewert Rose says that Rossborough, who shot to prominence a decade ago when he was accused of dangerously cracking the spine of a four-day-old baby, told her he admired her discipline and maturity and said he wanted to help her achieve her dream of being a professional ballet dancer. He recommended she see him every four to six weeks for ongoing treatments and chiropractic manipulations. Rose, who gave permission for her name to be published, was one of several young Melbourne dancers who were treated by Rossborough over many years. She is also one of at least two women who have accused him of grooming and sexual abuse when they were children.



Sarah Rose was groomed and sexually assaulted by chiropractor Dr Ian Rossborough as a teenager. “He had this belief that he was very much the best and the most important in the world at what he does and we as dancers were lucky to have him in our corner and supporting us,” Rose, who is now 25, says. Last September, the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court found Rossborough guilty of four counts of sexual assault and grooming of a child aged 16 to 17 for an assault on Rose. Related Article Healthcare Call for age limit after chiropractor breaks baby's neck He was given a two-year Community Correction Order and is now a convicted sex offender. Rossborough was suspended from working as a chiropractor by the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) last year and has surrendered his registration. This masthead can reveal that another alleged victim, who was also a young dancer treated by the chiropractor, has contacted police and alleges she was groomed and sexually abused by Rossborough over a period of almost three years when she was a teenager. The woman says she was referred to Rossborough by her dance school.



Following the criminal case last year, the alleged victim, who is now in her 30s and spoke to this masthead on the condition of anonymity, submitted a 13-page statement of allegations against Rossborough to AHPRA. The national healthcare watchdog is conducting its own investigation into Rossborough. The woman hopes the matter will be referred to a civil tribunal, which examines the most severe complaints against Australian health practitioners, and will allow her to have her allegations heard. “The injustice of it really weighs on me,” she says. “I strongly believe he’s still a threat to the community, which is what prompted me to follow through with this.” Ian Rossborough was found guilty of sexual assault and grooming last year. In the statement, seen by this masthead, the woman alleges that Rossborough told her after the sexual abuse began: “You have the power to destroy me, if you ever tell anyone”. “I now feel deep discomfort and distress when I reflect on what occurred,” she wrote in her statement. “It is confronting to recognise that Ian took advantage of my youth, vulnerability, and impressionable nature.



“I was a young and emotionally vulnerable girl when I met him, and he exploited the imbalance of power.” When Sarah Rose turned 14, Rossborough gave her his personal phone number, telling her she could bypass his long waiting list whenever she needed to see him. He started texting her regularly and confided in her about his personal life and divorce. He called her his “good buddy”, and invited her to do yoga classes with him. Rose says her appointments with Rossborough were only meant to be 15 minutes, but he would often stretch them out to an hour without charging her. “All my focus was on my career. Dance was my entire identity,” Rose says.



“Dance gave me a chance to process all my emotions of the world, but it is really hard to look back now and realise how much I was ignoring and shoving down just to cope.” On the night she was assaulted, Rose was 17 and about to fly overseas for a life-changing summer program at the Washington Ballet. Sarah Rose Steven Siewert Rossborough promised to help get her body into the best physical shape before she left and, under the guise of helping her lose weight, instructed her to use the sauna in a yoga studio next to his clinic and strip completely naked before entering. About 45 minutes later, Rossborough came into the sauna took off his clothes and sexually assaulted Rose. “I just froze when it happened,” Rose says. “He was my lift home that night, so I knew no one was coming to get me, and no one was there to help. I remember thinking, ‘You have no other way home ... Just act normal. Don’t let him know you’re freaking out’.” After a video of him manipulating the spine of a newborn went viral across the world in 2016, Rossborough was temporarily banned from treating children while he was investigated by the nation’s medical watchdog.

World.title: Labor backs down on late change to get news scheme across the line
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Labor backs down on late change to get news scheme across the line Paul Sakkal August 12, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has reversed a late change to a scheme forcing tech giants to pay for news, clinching a deal with Opposition Leader Angus Taylor that media firms hope will lead to hundreds of millions of dollars in new revenue. Powerful news bosses from this masthead’s owner Nine and News Corp revolted last week after Labor reduced the cut that any one media outlet would receive from a tech firm’s payout from 25 per cent to 17 per cent of the total levy each social media platform is charged. This was a reduction the government made without consultation. That reduction has now been scrapped. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Communications Minister Anika Wells. Alex Ellinghausen The change to the News Bargaining Incentive was aimed at spreading the wealth and benefiting smaller publishers, but large outlets argued it undervalued businesses that hire most journalists. Albanese has been talking to top news executives. He worked with Taylor to strike a deal that rekindled bipartisan support for the world-first scheme. Initially struck by the Morrison government, Labor’s revamped model pushes digital giants to compensate news businesses for articles on social platforms.



Communications Minister Anika Wells said the government was “delivering for journalists”, while Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino recognised “the significant benefits strong journalism brings to communities across the nation”. Labor made another change that it did not previously disclose: guaranteeing that Australian Associated Press, a newswire owned by a not-for-profit, will gain 5 per cent of any payments made by tech outfits. Sources in the news sector said such a high payment for a small publisher was questionable, though they did not expect news bosses to complain, given Albanese had stepped in to reverse the substantive change. The incentive works by levying a 2.5 per cent charge on tech firms’ local ad revenue. To encourage firms to strike voluntary deals with media businesses, the government offers digital platforms an offset to the charge. The aim is to deliver up to $250 million to media companies whose business models have been smashed by advertising money flowing to tech giants. The digital platforms argue there is no justification for the policy because news outlets actually benefit from distributing their work on social media.



The Trump administration considers the tax a form of “foreign extortion”. The tech sector in the US has called on Australia to face higher tariffs as a penalty. On Tuesday, Trade Minister Don Farrell lobbied the US over Donald Trump’s decision to impose a 12.5 per cent tariff on Australian exports. Related Article Publishing ‘Deeply misled’: Nine says news bargaining plan could cost jobs Separately, the government made a tweak to the accounting method for the NBI that will increase the base of tech firms’ revenue subject to the charge. The number of deals each firm will be forced to do has also increased from six to eight. Legislation will be introduced to parliament on Thursday and will most likely pass the Senate next week, putting pressure on Meta in particular to come to the table. Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, last year threatened to block news articles on its platforms rather than pay any charge. Google was already keen to do deals. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Australia’s biggest aluminium smelter saved in $2.5 billion rescue deal
World.content:
NationalManufacturing Australia’s biggest aluminium smelter saved in $2.5 billion rescue deal Nick Toscano and Michael McGowan August 12, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s biggest aluminium smelter will receive a $2.5 billion government bailout package to stay open, ending months of crisis negotiations with federal and NSW officials over ways to keep the plant viable and safeguard more than 1000 jobs. Tomago Aluminium, majority-owned by resources giant Rio Tinto, has been consulting the smelter’s workforce and their union officials since late last year about the risk of the site closing when its existing power contract expires in 2028, and electricity costs are set to double. Tomago’s owners and government officials have been in crisis talks over assistance to keep the smelter viable beyond 2028. Under the agreement, expected to be announced at the site on Thursday, Tomago Aluminium will invest $1.1 billion into the future of the smelter, including $100 million in driving lower-carbon manufacturing processes and making the electricity-hungry plant more flexible so it can power down and reduce its consumption to support the grid at critical times. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Energy Minister Chris Bowen, Industry Minister Tim Ayres and NSW Premier Chris Minns will travel to the smelter near Newcastle to announce the multi-year deal, according to sources briefed on the agreement but not yet authorised to discuss it publicly.



While many details remain unknown, the joint package would deliver a “long-term renewable energy solution” to Tomago Aluminium that would support the site’s commercially sustainable operations beyond 2028 and accelerate its decarbonisation, a joint statement from the federal and state governments said. Albanese said Tomago was not only important for the Hunter region, but was a “critical asset for the country and our manufacturing future”. “In December last year I stood in the rain at Tomago and told the workers ‘we have your back’,” Albanese said. “Today, alongside the NSW government, we deliver on that promise.” The Tomago deal is the latest in a series of taxpayer-funded rescue packages to prop up struggling metals processors over the past two years. The Albanese government has contributed to bailouts worth $2 billion for Rio Tinto’s Boyne smelter in Queensland, $2.4 billion for the collapsed Whyalla steelworks in South Australia, and $600 million for Glencore’s copper smelter and refinery in Mt Isa.



The support for Tomago comes despite Rio Tinto last month reporting a $US6.7 billion ($9.5 billion) half-year profit, up 47 per cent from the same time a year earlier. Tomago Aluminium has indicated that electricity accounts for 40 per cent of the plant’s costs, but prices were set to double from 2028 once its contract with AGL expires. The cost of coal-fired generation had increased significantly, the company said, and it was uncertain when enough renewable projects, plus back-up firming capacity, would be available at the scale it required. Related Article Updated

Manufacturing Nation’s manufacturing at ‘dangerous crossroads’ with more big bailouts to come Government and industry sources have previously indicated that a deal for Tomago may include a power purchasing agreement with discounted energy supplied to the smelter via a Commonwealth-owned entity like Snowy Hydro. Minns said the agreement secured more than 1000 jobs at Tomago and thousands more that rely on the smelter, giving the region “certainty about its future”.



“This is a good day for the Hunter,” he said. “I want to thank the prime minister and the Commonwealth government – we’ve worked closely together to get to this point and deliver an agreement that to find a way through and secure the future of Tomago.” Aluminium smelters, which need huge amounts of electricity, have been under mounting financial pressure across the nation as their owners face the dual challenges of intensifying competition from cheaper Chinese producers of the metal and the elevated cost of energy. The Tomago smelter is the single largest user of electricity in NSW. It consumes more than 10 per cent of the state’s power supply. Tomago Aluminium, Australia’s largest aluminium smelter, produces up to 590,000 tonnes of the metal a year, which is widely used to manufacture construction materials, cars, drink cans, foil packaging and electrical products. Aluminium is also increasingly in demand in the construction of solar panels and wind turbines. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Redacting the dress code
World.content:
“Graham Russell’s friend was turned back at the Cuesta border in 1971 as his hair was too long (C8),” notes Mia David of Wollongong. “My friend was married in 1968, and, while on her honeymoon, she (dressed in a very fetching pants suit) and her husband went to a club for lunch. She was denied entry, as ladies in pants were not allowed. Not a worry. She removed the trousers, and they accepted her attire of a very short miniskirt. Apparently, she had to be extra careful as she sat down for lunch.”

“My own experience in early 1970 in Singapore was similar, but different,” says Rhod Jeffrey of Surry Hills. “I was marooned there for six weeks awaiting a money transfer. I had to renew my visa weekly where there was a sign stating: ‘Persons with long hair will be served last so as to cause them the maximum of inconvenience’. I had fairly long hair but encountered no animosity or inconvenience because of it.”

“Working as a commercial artist in Jakarta 1973, (pre-Photoshop), my job was retouching poster artwork for rock stars touring Singapore,” says Peter Barker of One Mile. “I think I’m the only person with the honour of giving Mick Jagger a short-back-and-sides for The Rolling Stones’ Pacific Tour in 1973. So horrific was my retouching, the band never made it to Singapore because the doctored publicity material made them unrecognisable!”

It’s a long way from Rhoda and Gus’ surprise Joburg snowfall of ’81 (C8), but Pauline McGinley of Drummoyne is well versed when it comes to the white stuff: “Growing up in Scotland, I spent my childhood in the snow. Fingers and toes stuffed into woollen gloves and socks. Snow days off school. When you would wake up in the morning after a nightfall of snow, you knew immediately, before even looking out the window. Quiet, hushed and an intense stillness. The joy!”

“I had a similar opera experience to Nola Tucker (C8),” recalls Elizabeth Savage of Hughes (ACT). “Berlin Opera House, L’italiana in Algeri, sung in Italian with German surtitles. No idea what the story was, but the music was pleasant, and the ballet interludes were impressive.”

World.title: Polling booths open in Cook Islands
World.content:
Polling is opening in the Cook Islands where 110,000 registered voters will elect their leaders for the next four years.

Voting stations open at 9am on Wednesday morning, Cook Islands time (7am Thursday NZT) and will close at 6pm. TBC

There are 24 constituencies, 10 on the main island of Rarotonga, and the other 14 spread across the Pa Enua, or outer islands.

Thirteen seats are needed for a majority to form a government.

A total of 63 candidates were confirmed for the 2026 general election, down from the 71 who contested the 2022 election. This year's lineup includes 49 men and 14 women.

With independents making up 20 per cent of candidates, should no party claim the 13 seats needed for majority, the independents could hold the power over who forms government.

One seat has already been won this election, with Mangaia's Ivirua candidate Agnes Helen Armstrong running uncontested as an independent.

There's been a delay in the Northern Cooks, as bad weather meant electoral officers were unable to get ashore in Nassau.

Officials have announced the island's polling will be postponed to Thursday afternoon local time.

The issues for voters

The local newspaper, Cook Islands News, ran a poll which found a majority - 50.5 percent - of respondents across the Pa Enua and Rarotonga identified the cost of living and inflation - including fuel prices, water and power bills, housing, transportation and consumer goods - as their primary concern.

Editor Rashneel Kumar told Pacific Waves last week that global conflicts, contributing to resource restraints and costs, have a flow-on effect on local customers.

"With the Middle East conflict, obviously, we have seen a impact on small island nations, and Cook Islands is not spared as well," he said.

"We end up the supply chain, so we do absorb a lot of additional cost - and by the time the goods land here, the prices does have an impact as well as price of energy through the increase of petrol has affected the people.

"So cost of living obviously is number one issue."

World.title: Housing plan stokes fears for 'taonga species' at Christchurch's Willowbank
World.content:
Christchurch's Willowbank Wildlife Reserve is sounding the alarm over a planned housing development next door, saying it could threaten the park's future.

The Christchurch City Council is consulting on a private plan change that would allow about 230 houses to be built on Willowbank's southern boundary.

The wildlife park and nature reserve has operated on the site for 52 years and is home to native wildlife including kea, tuatara, kākā, takahē, and kiwi.

DOC staff vaccinate a takahē at Willowbank Wildlife Reserve in Christchurch. Supplied / DOC

Willowbank director Mark Willis said noise, vibration, light pollution, and increased human activity from the development could disturb animals.

"We have both short-term and long-term concerns and think there needs to be more examination on what those impacts might be. The question really is, is it worth the risk for a few houses to jeopardise the unique work that an organisation like Willowbank does?," he said.

"We're highly involved with a number of what's known as New Zealand's taonga species and their conservation, and we know that these species are very sensitive to disturbance."

Willowbank directors and siblings Mark and Kirsty Willis. Supplied

Willis said Willowbank's kiwi breeding centre was situated not far from the boundary.

"We know kiwi by nature being nocturnal are sensitive to light, they have poor eyesight and they compensate by having exceptionally good hearing. They, through their feeding methods, are exceptionally sensitive to vibration," he said.

"They offer quite a good example as to why activities that would be generated by a large residential development might impact upon their wellbeing, their stress levels and ultimately whether they are going to breed."

Willis was also concerned the reserve might end up having to restrict its operations if residents kicked up a fuss about noisy animals.

Supplied / Willowbank Wildlife Reserve

He said while it might sound fanciful to be a neighbour of a wildlife park, "the reality is our animals generate noise as loud as rock concerts - at any hour of the day or night. Animals and animal management also generate odours that residential neighbours may not enjoy."

"We are seriously concerned that complaints from new neighbours will lead to constraints on Willowbank's operations that limit our conservation efforts, animal wellbeing, and our ability to continue as a much-loved community experience as it is for so many today.

"Not only is our current boundary close to our existing activities but it is the obvious area should we need to expand those activities which would just bring them closer and closer to that residential activity and make the effect of it more and more pronounced."

Willis acknowledged some mitigation measures had been proposed in the plan change - including the requirement for housing next to Willowbank to have ventilation systems so people did not need to open windows -but he believed the reserve needed to be protected by a special purpose zoning.

The submission period for the plan change closes on 21 August.

World.title: Christopher Luxon's leadership victory: You come at the King, you best not miss
World.content:
Analysis: National MPs who tried and failed to take down Christopher Luxon on Wednesday should be embarrassed and ashamed.

After plotting, leaking, and destabilising the party enough to pressure the National Party leader into calling an emergency in-person caucus meeting, the agitators could not get the job done.

In the process they've left Luxon wounded and limping his way to the election with a caucus, which as far as the public is concerned, is more interested in itself and its own ambitions than the cost-of-living crisis much of the country is enduring.

Luxon has identified one of the detractors and made him the fall guy. After fleeing Parliament for Auckland, the prime minister sent out a statement saying Defence Minister Chris Penk was to blame for the destabilisation after launching a leadership challenge this week, resulting in the confidence vote.

"This makes his role untenable and as such I have removed his portfolios," Luxon said.

By 8pm Penk had given up any pretense he could stay on in the party and announced he wouldn't seek re-election in November in his safe seat of Kaipara ki Mahurangi - a seat once held by Sir John Key.

National MP Chris Penk arrives at Parliament ahead of urgent Caucus meeting on 12 August. RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

It's a bold call to punish his opponents, and a bit of a farce when he's only gone after one of what is clearly a group of disgruntled MPs.

But he could hardly demote senior MPs like Erica Stanford and Chris Bishop - two of his best operators - who were clearly being lined up as the true leadership contenders.

So for now Luxon has to leave it at one and hope that that has sent a strong enough message to the rest of the anti-Luxon brigade to keep their grievances to themselves until the election has run its course.

The instigators of a second round of confidence vote chaos have now had their chance and must accept the mess the party is now left with until the election.

Luxon looked like he had been through 12 rounds in the ring when he fronted the media after a three hour caucus meeting.

He spoke for a total of 75 seconds where he confirmed he had won a confidence vote, and had the full confidence of a caucus that was "united and determined to win this election".

In a complete repeat of his April confidence vote, he made his remarks following the meeting in the Banquet Hall - the least prime ministerial room in Parliament - and took no questions from the waiting reporters.

Unlike in April he didn't label the whole saga a "media soap opera" or blame reporters for the speculation and rumour. Instead he trotted out National's tired promise to "fix the basics and build the future".

Yet National has failed in the basics of what is a functioning caucus - being unified behind its leader. Likewise it hasn't looked like a party with any idea who might be its leader tomorrow, let alone in the future.

Within hours of the short and sombre press conference ending, the party was trying to return to some sense of normality with a media advisory from Bishop about an announcement on Thursday morning and an education press release from Stanford.

Meanwhile, Luxon was straight back to Auckland to prepare for the arrival of the Vietnamese president, who up until 1pm on Wednesday would have been wondering who he would be meeting the next day.

RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

Exactly what Luxon said in the caucus room to persuade enough MPs to back him will never truly be known. Any leaks to the media would have to be taken with a grain of salt.

More surprising than Luxon successfully rallying his MPs to swing in behind him was the failure by his detractors to make a more convincing argument for change.

While Luxon's stared down his challengers, he's now crawling his way to election night with a target on his back.

Chances of him surviving after the election are slim and the uphill battle to get the party's polling up in the next 86 days has been made all the more difficult.

The pressure on Luxon intensified after he won the first confidence vote - it just ramped up again after coming through a second round.

Every blunder, gaffe, miscommunication or misjudgement will be analysed, scrutinised and tucked away as ammunition for a later date.

If Luxon can blow things out of the water in the next three months and get the party in a position to form a strong National-led government, not controlled by its coalition partners, he will have proven his opponents wrong.

World.title: Concerns potential buyers of Kāinga Ora house not told of 'meth lab' history
World.content:
Neighbours who say they were terrorised by the former occupants of a Kāinga Ora house fear prospective buyers haven't been told about the home's history as a "meth lab".

The deadline sale for the two-bedroom Kāinga Ora property in the Lower Hutt suburb of Naenae closed on Tuesday, but Langford Street's residents say its chequered past hasn't been disclosed.

The 1940s home was billed as a "project you don't want to miss" and being offered for sale on an "as-is, where-is basis".

On Monday, a post-it note was plastered on the 'for sale' sign on the property's front lawn and across half a dozen of the home's windows and doors: "Warning. This house was previously a meth lab for years. Buyer beware."

Neighbours say crews arrived in "hazmat suits" a year ago to strip and clean the property, with Kāinga Ora confirming the home has undergone remediation for methamphetamine contamination.

Regional director for Greater Wellington Sarah Willson said the relevant reports were given to the listing agent, but a neighbour said they've received no toxicology reports despite multiple requests.

Bayleys residential sales manager Bhakti Mistry declined to comment.

'A terrifying time'

The Kāinga Ora house was the target of a drive-by shooting and multiple police raids, according to neighbours, before it was vacated about 18 months ago.

For a period of a couple of years, they said people would come and go from the home at all hours of the day and night and described drug deals, fights, and a rotating cast of gang members at the property.

Kāinga Ora said it couldn't comment on previous tenancies due to privacy considerations.

Barry - a resident on the street for 30 years - said it was a "terrible" and "frightening" time, with the occupants making no effort to hide what was going on.

"I see cars pull up. They'd ... tap on the window. People would pass out the drugs ... and they would drive off. This would happen continuously, a dozen times a day," he said.

"It's hard to describe just how bad it was. It was not just a simple drug-dealing house. It was a place where everyone hung out and parked on the berms ... just total chaos."

Police outside the property in July 2023. Supplied

The problematic behaviour culminated in a drive-by shooting one night, he said, describing the noise of the gun as "incredible," and showing RNZ what he claimed were multiple bullet holes in the Kāinga Ora home.

He said the spray of bullets also caught the house next-door.

Another neighbour, Benjamin said he remembered picking up casings in the aftermath and maintained it was luck no-one was hit.

"Honestly, it was a terrifying time. We didn't know what was going to happen next. We didn't know whether there was going to be an all out gun fight on the front lawn across the street and our kids would be collateral damage.

"We didn't know if the next drive-by they'd just shoot in our direction."

Damage following what residents describe as a drive-by shooting. Supplied

Three of the street's residents said crews in head-to-toe protective gear arrived to strip and clean the home once it was empty, with Benjamin saying they were at pains to protect themselves.

"They're putting on their hazmat suits and getting fully kitted-up."

Barry said the cleaners were at the property "on and off" for about two months, scrubbing walls and removing gib.

"I spoke to [one of the cleaners] and he said it's really bad, one of the worst he's seen.

"Whatever drugs they were cooking up ... [it's] penetrated throughout the whole house."

The property is to be sold 'as is, where is' after remediation for methamphetamine. RNZ

Meth remediation completed - Kāinga Ora

The neighbours told RNZ they were concerned that prospective buyers could be in the dark about the home's history.

Benjamin said it's been close to two weeks since he requested to see reports about methamphetamine contamination and remediation, but they have not been provided.

In a text exchange seen by RNZ, the agent said they did not have a toxicology report, but had requested it.

Bayleys declined to comment, directing RNZ to Kāinga Ora.

Willson said following the previous tenancy ending, the property was tested for methamphetamine contamination and specialist contractors completed remediation work.

"We advised the listing agent that the property had undergone methamphetamine remediation and have provided the relevant remediation reports to support the sale process."

Kāinga Ora declined to answer RNZ's follow-up question about when those reports were provided.

Langford Street RNZ

Director at law firm Pidgeon and Judd, Joanna Pidgeon said years ago there had been "massive issues" with methamphetamine contamination, with companies testing for meth also providing remediation service, giving them a "nice little income stream".

She said legislation fixed that issue and in 2018, former chief science advisor Sir Peter Gluckman established guidelines for acceptable levels of meth contamination in the home - below 15μg per 100cm2 where the drug had been smoked, and below 1.5μg per 100cm2 for manufacturing.

Pidgeon said if a meth-contaminated home had been remediated to below those levels, there was no obligation for the listing agent to disclose it to prospective buyers - unless specifically asked.

"Then they have to tell you the answer."

She said if the vendor had a report but didn't provide it, they would be implicated in the non-disclosure.

Pidgeon said information about contamination could affect whether someone was willing to buy the property and for what price, and said for one of her clients it was a deal-breaker.

"They just couldn't bear the thought of their baby...crawling around on floor that may or may not have some contamination. It wasn't something that they were prepared to deal with, but their agreement was conditional on it, so they were able to exit on that basis."

Pidgeon said if purchasers learned of contamination after signing an agreement, exiting it or negotiating the price was possible, but would depend on factors such as the level of contamination and context around whether it should have been disclosed.

Bad reputation

Langford Street in Naenae. RNZ

Benjamin stressed he had no idea how contaminated the house was or still is, but said that was the problem. Someone trying to do their due diligence could be just as clueless as him, he said.

"They may have done an excellent remediation job and it's completely removed all contamination - and that would be amazing. It's just that we don't have that information."

Barry said regardless of the contamination, he didn't think the home was fit-for-purpose and wanted to see it bowled.

"It's got that bad a reputation. I wouldn't want to see a family in it with people still wanting to turn up and thinking it's a viable drug house.

World.title: Bridges not up to scratch, roads to be returned to gravel - South Island counts cost of under investment
World.content:
Only one in $9 of government roading funds gets spent in the South Island, a new report obtained by RNZ reveals.

The south accounts for almost a quarter of the country's population, 22 percent of GDP, a third of export goods and 40 percent of international visitor spending, but receives only 11 percent of transport spending.

Local political and business leaders say the lack of investment is disappointing.

Southland mayor Rob Scott has told RNZ that trucks are unnecessarily driving an extra 3.5 million kilometres in his district every year because bridges are not up to scratch and the council will soon have to weigh up reverting sealed roads to gravel.

But South Island Minister James Meager says the government has made a huge investment in the South Island's roads and other infrastructure, as well as simplifying and speeding up consent processes and cutting red tape.

It was "simplistic" to suggest the government was not listening to the South Island's leaders and delivering on their priorities, Meager said.

The report, released on Thursday and commissioned by the South Island Regional Transport Committee Chairs Group, highlighted the disparity between the south's contribution to the economy and what was being delivered by the National Land Transport Fund.

If National Land Transport Fund expenditure matched the population in the South Island it would have resulted in an extra $1.2 billion in spending in the past year alone -about the cost of the currently unfunded Woodend Bypass or the Hope Bypass.

South Island Minister James Meager RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

"That's a fair point," Meager said.

"I guess my response would be is that it's a little more complex than just looking at the population makeup. It's actually part of my job, and part of my colleagues' jobs, to make sure that we raise these issues with decision makers, with cabinet, and making sure that we've got the investment in the right place.

"The key thing is we need to not necessarily look at writing checks based on what the population is here or there. What we need to do ... is to identify the infrastructure constraints that we have in the South Island that actually are holding back growth.

"And we have got a lot of stuff underway. We can't underestimate all the work that actually is happening. You've got Ashburton Bridge. The Woodend Bypass is proceeding - just got consenting, just got fast-track consent. In the budget there was $400 million for roading infrastructure resilience and $140 million of that went to the South Island. So there is a lot happening."

'It's keeping us awake at night'

RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Canterbury Regional Transport Committee chair Deon Swiggs said the report highlighted what many in the South Island had been feeling for some time.

"When I look at the numbers it's disappointing ... and resilience is the big piece that we are fighting for in the South Island," Swiggs said.

"We've got storm events that are happening, we've got ageing infrastructure. So, yes, the South Island is definitely punching above its weight from an economic activity point of view and the money generated here is going towards New Zealand at large, but the South Island needs this investment.

"We've been saying this for quite some time that the numbers do not stack up ... and investment in the South Island needs to improve. We do not want to see the degradation of our existing corridors. We all know that when you don't maintain what you've got, it costs a lot more to then fix it."

Rob Scott said Southland was at a tipping point.

"I've seen the great work that our staff have been doing and I'm seeing the stress coming through now and it's keeping us awake at night as a council, knowing that once we get over that tipping point we're not going to be able to recover as a Southland region and also as a country. It's going to be a lot more expensive to fix the roads up later on ... rather than just actually keeping on top and maintaining our network properly," he said.

"If you look at the length of road per capita that people are looking after, in Auckland a resident is looking after four metres worth of road. Wellington, 1.6 metres. And if we come to the South Island and we've got our fastest growing district in the country at the moment, Selwyn, someone's looking after 30 metres. What do you reckon Southland's number is? It's 151 metres.

"We are subsidising Auckland, which I don't mind, but it's actually coming at the expense of our roads. All of the road user charges that we generate on our roads, only half of that is coming back for that road maintenance."

Rob Scott. Matthew Rosenberg / LDR

It led him to write a letter to Transport Agency chair Simon Bridges calling for a new way of allocating road funding as Southland was tens of millions of dollars short of just maintaining the status quo.

Meanwhile central government was pushing ahead with further expressways and highways that would put even more pressure on maintenance spending, Scott said.

"If the heartbeat of New Zealand's export market loses the routes to get that produce to market, we're going to be in trouble as a country," he said.

"We're not actually asking for much. I scratch my head when I see all of this money - that $55 million going onto that Harbour Bridge Extension paperwork, the $250 million going on a [Queenstown] roundabout, the new 26 kilometres worth of expressway in the North Island - we just need a drop in the bucket from all of those projects just to be able to maintain our roads."

'We have two Cabinet ministers in the whole of the South Island'

Swiggs said politics was at play.

"What we're seeing here is that there is a weighting of North Island politicians and less South Island politicians and especially in Cabinet. I think we have two politicians in Cabinet from the South Island," Swiggs said.

"We need to have a better mix of proportionality around the politicians that are decision makers at Cabinet. But we also need a more transparent process about how the money has been apportioned and where these big projects are."

Local councils had to be far more transparent in how they decided to spend money compared to central government, Swiggs said.

Business Canterbury chief executive Leeann Watson agreed South Island representation was lacking among senior politicians.

"We are underrepresented, absolutely. We have two cabinet ministers in the whole of the South Island and I believe Auckland has 16. So that in itself speaks some volume," she said.

Despite that Business Canterbury had regular contact with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour and Finance Minister Nicola Willis, Watson said.

Willis claimed after this year's budget she had not "had a request for a major headline project in Canterbury".

Luxon offered a similar view last year and called for Canterbury's leaders to get their priorities straight.

Watson said the remarks were frustrating.

"There is no doubt that we have asked for some investment," she said.

Business Canterbury chief executive Leeann Watson. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Swiggs said there was "no shortage of projects that we could do tomorrow to make the South Island a better place".

"I'm going to pick on one, which is the long-touted mass rapid transit for Christchurch. Mass rapid transit is an end goal," he said.

"To get to the mass rapid transit system we need to do the investment in our existing public transport. We've put through business cases to NZTA. This council appropriated the money through our long-term plan. We went through consultation. We had it on our budgets and then the [Government Policy Statement] comes out and cut the funding.

"That has a flow-on effect to us not being able to deliver the improvements to our public transport that we wanted and then that has an impact on the mass rapid transit down the line. When the government puts a cap on what the region wants or the city wants it has flow-on effects.

"That was there and that could be delivered relatively quickly if there was a will from the government and ... they have that information. So that's just one example. They could invest in that with us, with the region, with the city, but they've chosen not to."

Meager said the government was committed to delivering the Woodend Bypass.

"We're not short on ambition. What we are short on is, quite frankly, the revenue needed to get these projects across the line," he said.

"Now part of that is to do with the growth we need to generate revenue, whether that's through fuel excise and road users which help fund the land transport fund or general growth.

"So we need more revenue coming in. We also need to make these projects a lot more affordable and a lot cheaper and so that's why we've done things like Fast-track and reforming the RMA system so that when these large scale projects are actually underway, we can make them more affordable."

There was a significant amount taking place in and around Canterbury, including the recently opened Te Kaha Stadium in Christchurch, flood protection improvement and spending in health, education and transport, Meager said.

'The South Island is outperforming the North Island'

The report laid bare what has been described as New Zealand's "two-speed" economy.

"The South Island is outperforming the North Island with GDP growing by 1.2 percent in the March 2026 year compared with 0.2 percent in the North Island," the report said.

South Island economic snapshot Supplied/Benje Patterson

"This outperformance has persisted, with South Island GDP growth averaging 0.6 percentage points above the North Island over the five years to 2025.

"South Island employment rose by 0.4 percent, while North Island employment fell by 1.2 percent. Southland, the West Coast, Canterbury and Otago recorded growth. The South Island's unemployment rate is 4.1 percent, below the North Island's 5.7 percent."

The South Island was making an outsized contribution to the country's economy but further investment was important to maintain it, the report said.

The roading network was vital to connect people and businesses with supply chains and markets and for tourism.

The South Island accounted for 43 percent of the country's roading network and 45 percent of the State Highway network.

"The South Island's share of roading expenditure appears disproportionately low relative to its contribution and level of road use. In 2025 the South Island received 11 percent of NLTF roading expenditure despite generating 27 percent of national vehicle kilometres travelled, 22 percent of GDP, one third of goods exports, and 40 percent of international visitor spending," the report said.

"This imbalance is evident across South Island regions, where shares of population, GDP, exports, visitor spending and road use generally exceed each region's share of NLTF roading investment. Ensuring that South Island transport infrastructure is adequately maintained and invested in is therefore important not only for the South Island but for New Zealand's overall economic performance."

The report also underscored the importance of the Cook Strait ferries to the South Island's economy.

"The Cook Strait ferries provide a 'sea bridge' connection between the South Island and the North Island. The transportation infrastructure provided by the ferries is a critically important economic enabler for the South Island economy and its broader contribution to New Zealand.

"An estimated 3.5 million tonnes of annual freight are carried on ferries."

More than $10 billion crossed the strait last year with 71 percent southbound and 29 percent northbound.

About $1.8 billion of South Island international spending came from visitors who took the ferry.

"This is equivalent to about 23 percent of the total international visitor spending that occurred in the South Island over the past year, which highlights the critical importance of the ferries as an enabler of international tourism earnings. Transport connectivity is fundamental to sustaining this contribution."

South Island road funding Supplied/Benje Patterson

Back the South Island for stronger productivity and higher incomes - business leaders

Watson said the government needed to be investing more in the South Island's infrastructure for the good of the country's economy.

"We can have the best innovation, we can have the best quality products, but if we haven't got the infrastructure to support the imported components coming in to make those manufactured goods or the right roads to get our exports to Lyttelton Port or to Christchurch Airport or not sufficient freight capacity then ... we can't actually realise the full potential of those exports to this country," she said.

"Infrastructure is vital, just like energy is. It underpins everything that we do from moving our people, moving our freight and just having connectivity across the South Island.

"Our message to political parties is really simple - if New Zealand wants stronger productivity and higher incomes and greater resilience then backing the South Island right now is exactly what they should be doing because we can provide all that with the right settings."

The government could not afford to not invest in the south, Watson said.

"We often talk about what the costs are of delivering projects but we don't talk about the cost of delaying and deferring," she said.

"First of all, I think we've got to do a better job of actually costing up the project. Secondly, I think we need to look at those alternative procurement and funding and financing models because we know if we continue to use the same funding and financing and the same procurement models that we've always used, we'll get what we've always got.

"Right now we've got a country that has definitely got some resilience issues in terms of some of its core infrastructure. We've got a whole lot of maintenance that we need to do and so we've got to make sure that we also look at those alternative ways of doing things."

Watson and Swiggs emphasised that funding infrastructure in the South Island was an investment.

Swiggs said money spent in the South Island benefited the whole country.

"This is definitely not a handout. We have shown where the money has been generated, we've shown the economic activity is happening here," Swiggs said.

Watson said Business Canterbury was working on a project called Canterbury Ambition that set out the region's vision for improving growth, innovation and quality of life.

She said that, alongside government investment, could unlock the private sector.

"In some cases it's actually about getting the government out of the way," she said.

"The piece of work around Canterbury Ambition is actually about not waiting for government to tell us what we should be as a region or what we should do. It's about us shaping our own future. So the private sector is in the driving seat of that and actually pushing ahead and what we've heard from this government is that they actually want to partner with business.

World.title: The dairy farmer behind latest grocery price comparison app
World.content:
A dairy farmer has launched a free app that lets shoppers check their online grocery list to see which local supermarket is the cheapest on the day.

CheckMyTrolley is the latest grocery comparison tool to hit the market as the cost of living continues to bite into household budgets.

Will Duff said people are surprised to learn he's behind a new food price-checking app when he tells them what he does for a day job.

"People get thrown back quite a bit when I say I'm a dairy farmer and I'm not an IT person but I am the person behind the idea."

He works at a dairy farm on the Taiere plain near Dunedin.

After returning from a decade working in Australia, he found grocery prices had become a pinch-point for most and tested his theory in a social media post that received more than 100,000 views.

People agreed supermarket shopping had become a part-time job if they wanted to check for the best prices.

"To me, that was pretty simple to go, right, this is a problem in New Zealand and I think building this app is going to actually make a huge difference for New Zealanders to save money."

Duff took his idea to a developer and CheckMyTrolley launched a few months ago on Apple devices with android coming soon. It allows shoppers to create an online list and check which supermarket is the cheapest.

"If I can help New Zealanders, I guess that's my drive, that's what I'm hoping to get is to be like, look, someone's created this app that helps New Zealanders, saves money, well, hopefully saves a little bit of money for you. And I guess that's a success for me."

He saved $148 using the app in one month.

"It's easier to compare over those prices and be like, right, I'm definitely not shopping there because that's too expensive. I guess everyone feels it in New Zealand."

CheckMyTrolley is the latest grocery comparison app to launch, joining Grocer and Grosave, each with different features.

Both have roughly 70,000 users.

Consumer NZ researchers recently analysed the online prices of a basket of 16 everyday grocery items, across eight weeks and four cities, to find New Zealand's cheapest supermarket. Pak n Save came out top.

Consumer's head of research and advocacy Gemma Rasmussen said people prefer to shop online to stick to their budgets.

"It means that they can really stick to a list and purchase just that, whereas sometimes when you go into the store you might deviate a little bit," she said.

"Being able to compare your whole shop online can lead to some pretty significant savings."

A recent Consumer NZ survey shows the cost of groceries is a top financial concern for households, a change from five years ago when it ranked below rent and power.

"We are seeing a massive swing towards buying the private label brands with shoppers they're just trying to make any way they can to purchase their food as cheaply as possible."

Grocer is still a hobby project, according to its developer Roc Wong, a software engineer.

Grocer developer Roc Wong SUPPLIED

He started the price comparison app five years ago.

"I started this as a side hockey project to collect the price data points from the supermarkets, website apps, and help myself do a bit of comparison."

And so far the data has been interesting, some pricing patterns have emerged.

"I have this observation also backed by the data I've collected so far, a lot of products' prices have a high-low pattern," he said with one week being high and the next low.

"This is very common for processed goods like ice cream, chocolate, whereas the fresh produce is more bound to the season."

Wong said the supermarkets have not expressed any concern about the app or data scraped for it.

Dunedin student Lara Bishell uses the CheckMyTrolley app to compare prices and said over the last month she has saved $100.

"I'm on the app just to save some money because I don't eat meat and plant based foods can be expensive," she said.

"It was interesting because I thought Pak'nSave was the cheapest but when I was looking it was telling me Woolworths or New World."

Bishell said a brand of tofu she buys is $3 cheaper at one supermarket.

"It feels good because I try to be frugal and save. It makes me feel less stressed about money and supermarket shopping."

Christchurch based software developer Tim Hong co-founded the grocery price-comparison app Grosave in April last year, with Murray Wong and Jayon Thomas.

Christchurch based software developer Tim Hong co-founded Grosave in April last year. SUPPLIED

"There's this huge transparency issue for pricing that's why we did this first but as we expand this we want to make sure people have a healthy and affordable diet, that's our vision."

Hong said they plan to soon add a function to enable users to buy online, from the app, clicking through to the supermarket's cart.

As for scraping supermarket's data, he said Foodstuffs and Woolworths are yet to get in contact.

"We don't want to cause any trouble to their service. The data is publicly available so I think it's fine we haven't heard anything from the big players."

World.title: Māori and Pacific people have lower stigma towards mental illness  - study
World.content:
Māori and Pacific people have a lower stigma towards people with mental illness than Europeans and Asians, according to a University of Otago study.

It found integrating Māori and Pacific attitudes towards mental illness into health campaigns may result in a less judgemental New Zealand.

Using data from the long running New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study (NZAVS), the study examined more than 58,000 participants' 'ratings of warmth' towards those with mental illness.

Lead author Issac Jamieson told RNZ the study analysed the relationship between ethnicity and mental health stigma in Aotearoa.

"Stigma has many different components to it, and we focused just on one stigmatising attitude, which was how participants rated their feelings of warmth towards those with mental illness. Now, the findings challenged previous narratives held by past research and the general public to some extent that certain ethnicities or indigenous populations are synonymous with greater mental health stigma."

Jamieson said a holistic or a collective worldview that Māori and Pacific people hold might be the reason for the lower stigma findings in the study.

He also pointed to Māori health models such as Te Whare Tapa Whā, in which mental wellbeing is one of four pillars of overall health and wellbeing.

Other Māori health and wellbeing models recognise that individuals are live in wider environment systems that impact them, he said.

"One of the other things we discuss as well is how Māori have developed a language around mental health that may actually be less stigmatising than what we traditionally use today. So we talk about the example of ADHD, which stands for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, and Māori have developed the word, aroreretini, which means the mind goes to many things.

"Culture is really central to us understanding and reducing mental health stigma. And I guess to better understand the stigma associated with mental health challenges, we must better understand how different cultures define and perceive these challenges.

"For every culture has these strengths or maybe different ways of viewing mental health challenges, which may actually help us to have less stigmatising language or methods."

It was important that mental health campaigns and research not only acknowledged, but also integrated different cultural perspectives when it came to tackling mental health stigma, he said.

"So what we really want is some culturally responsive interventions that take into account these different world views."

Jamieson said despite positive shifts over the past couple of decades, the stigma of mental illness continues to be prominent in society.

"The research is still saying that there's still work to be done. And the more research we have around trying to understand what might be associated with more or less stigma or how different cultures perceive these challenges, we're gonna be better placed to try and actually reduce it, reduce the stigma of mental health and improve the livelihood of those struggling at the moment."

The study was published in Kotuitui: New Zealand Journal of Social Sciences Online, authored by Issac Jamieson, Taylor Winter, Ririwai Fox, Aaron Hapuku, Edmond Fehoko, Andre Mason, Chris Sibley and Damian Scarf.

World.title: 'Huge demand on services': North Shore ambulance patients diverted to Whāngarei
World.content:
Some Auckland ambulance patients are being taken to Whāngarei Hospital because North Shore Hospital is too full to take them.

That is despite the much smaller Whāngarei Hospital already struggling with extremely high patient numbers this winter.

RNZ understands diversions were taking place on Tuesday night which was also very busy at Whāngarei's emergency department.

Diversions were happening also last week.

Tim Malloy is a GP for Coast to Coast healthcare group which has a clinic in Auckland's most northern town Wellsford, just shy of the Northland border.

He was sent a letter by St John Ambulance last week telling him any patients from the northern part of the Rodney district who needed to go to an ED would be taken to Whāngarei. They were normally serviced by North Shore.

That was "due to the huge demand on the services at North Shore Hospital", he said.

RNZ understands Whāngarei was already under serious pressure itself. It is about half the size of North Shore.

Health NZ director of operations Brad Healy said it was a "very small number" of ambulances who were actually diverted to Whangarei.

"This practice is not unusual and used at times to manage demand and ensure patients can receive care as quickly as possible. In some instances, depending on the location of the patient, Whangārei Hospital is closer in travel time than North Shore Hospital," he said.

Malloy said the letter was the first his practice had ever received about the ambulance diversions.

Busy winter in northern Auckland

This winter was the busiest Malloy had seen in 37 years as a GP.

Patients in Coast to Coast's urgent care clinic were sometimes waiting five hours and staff have had to be brought in on their days off to help, he said

"When you have 15 people waiting for you and you have a serious illness you are trying to manage in a patient while you wait for an ambulance to arrive, and all these patients are just having to wait, it's incredibly stressful. For all of us," he said.

Most of the patients coming into urgent care had respiratory infections. The cases seemed to last longer - and there were a growing number of secondary infections, he said.

There were very high numbers of people with influenza.

Malloy wanted to see a campaign to encourage people to get vaccinated against flu - and for those vaccinations to be free.

It would help people stay healthy, in particular to avoid serious complications.

That would help the whole health system, he said.

World.title: Ex-Wallabies, league star Brian Smith dies of cancer
World.content:
Wallabies prop Angus Bell is leading the tributes for dual rugby union international and former NRL star Brian Smith, who has died aged 59.

Smith, who played six Tests for Australia in 1987 and nine for Ireland after switching allegiance, had battled cancer.

Once described by former Wallabies coach Alan Jones as one of the world's most gifted players, Smith was most recently the Head of Sport at Scots College in Sydney, where Bell and many other Wallabies graduated from.

"He was coaching at the Scots school and coached a lot of us coming through the grades and I just wanted to say it's a really sad time," Bell said from Wallabies camp in Townsville on Wednesday.

"We're wishing the best for his wife and kids. He's an avid rugby person and helped a lot of individuals in the squad and in the Wallabies today, so just sending my condolences from both the Wallabies and myself."

Australia's 999th Wallaby's Test debut Isaac Henry will run the prospect of fresh ink past his wife but is otherwise assured he can make a permanent Wallabies mark after a hard-earned debut in Osaka.

Smith, who also played 43 games for Balmain and Eastern Suburbs from 1991 to 1994, coached Bell at GPS and NSW schoolboys' level when the emerging front-rower was only 16.

"Fair to say that I wouldn't have played as good or anywhere near as good without him," Bell said.

"Me, Jeremy Williams and Will Harris from the (Western) Force were really close with him and he was a great bloke, a great father and a great coach.

"So, yeah, very sad."

After playing schoolboys' rugby for Australia, Smith made his Wallabies debut under Jones in 1987, partnering Nick Farr-Jones in the halves and bagging 18 points from a try, five conversions and a penalty in a 65-18 win over South Korea.

Australian forward Angus Bell - in Wallabies camp in Townsville - paid tribute to his former high school coach and mentor Brian Smith. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

After his playing career, Smith coached in Japan and England, where he was the national team's attack coach, and served as Australia's sevens coach.

"Brian had been very unwell in recent months and was battling an aggressive cancer," Scots College principal Dr Ian PM Lambert wrote to school colleagues.

"This is very sad news for our College community and I know it will come as a shock to many of you who knew and worked closely with him.

"Our immediate thoughts are with Brian's wife Lisa, his daughters Ruby and Santana, and his son Chilli."

AAP

World.title: Former Hurricanes cricketer jailed for abusing 15yo girl
World.content:
A former Hobart Hurricanes cricket player will serve 10 months in prison for sexually abusing a child.

WARNING: This story contains details of child sexual abuse.

Aaron William Summers, 30, pleaded guilty to two counts of penetrative sexual abuse of a young person and one count of grooming in June in the Supreme Court of Tasmania, after having previously pleaded not guilty.

In court on Wednesday, he was sentenced to two-and-a-half years in jail, suspended after 10 months, meaning he will leave prison in April next year.

Justice Helen Wood told the court that Summers met the victim at a Hobart Hurricanes cricket match in 2017.

The following month, the 15-year-old girl attended another game and spoke to Summers, who was 21 at the time.

Aaron Summers was playing for the Hobart Hurricanes when he met the 15-year-old girl. (Getty Images: Robert Prezioso)

The pair began messaging on social media, and Summers arranged to pick her up from her home later that night.

The court heard he drove her to a local primary school, laid down a blanket, and sexually abused her twice.

Justice Wood told the court that Summers knew she was under the age of 17 and at high school, but did not ask how old she was.

"She thought they were meeting to talk; in reality, she represented a sexual opportunity to him," Justice Wood said.

"She was vulnerable because of her age and innocence; he had said nothing to warn her of his real motives."

The grooming charge related to social media conversations between Summers and the girl, in which Summers sent explicit photos of himself and requested photos from her.

"As a community, we look up to sportspeople; young people are likely to admire them, see them in a positive light," Justice Woods said.

"His role as a sportsperson gave him contact with young people, and enabled the commission of his crimes; this is an aggravating factor."

In November 2021, Summers pleaded guilty to charges in the Northern Territory, including possessing and transmitting child abuse material and transmitting communication with someone under 16 with the intention of procuring the recipient to engage in, or make, sexual activity.

Summers served three years and 11 months in prison in the NT. He was arrested on the day of his release and extradited to Tasmania to face these charges.

Cricket career 'at an end'

Justice Wood said Summers had experienced social isolation, loneliness and depressive symptoms while playing cricket in Tasmania and was spending excessive time on social media.

She said once he moved to the Northern Territory, he had established a successful career playing cricket in Australia and overseas and had a high profile.

"Due to the crimes, his future as a professional cricketer is at an end," she said.

Twenty months of the sentence was suspended, meaning Aaron Summers (left) is set for release in April next year. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Justice Wood said that Summers has accepted responsibility for his crimes and understood the impact his offending has had on his victims.

In the NT, he completed an intensive sex offender treatment program, which involved over 100 sessions, in which Justice Wood told the court he engaged appropriately and gained insight into his offending.

Justice Wood said when deciding on his sentence, she considered the lengthy jail time he had already served in the NT after the Tasmanian crimes were committed, and the significant progress he has taken towards his rehabilitation.

"[The] understanding he has about the harm he has caused and he is motivated to regain his life," she said.

Justice Wood imposed a sentence of two-and-a-half years, backdated to June 28 of this year, due to the time he has spent in remand.

She suspended the last 20 months of the sentence, with strict conditions, such as obliging him to comply with his probation officers and submit to psychological treatment.

The court heard that Summers would likely return to Western Australia, where he is from and his family live, to serve out his suspended sentence once he is able to leave prison in April next year.

World.title: 'Can't compete': Super coaches weigh into PNG Chiefs debate
World.content:
Trent Robinson won't be raging about the inequality of the tax breaks afforded to the PNG Chiefs, even if he believes the NRL's open market is no longer a "level playing field".

After Penrith winger Brian To'o became the sixth player wooed by the start-up franchise's tax-free wages, Panthers coach Ivan Cleary declared clubs "can't compete" with the bounty the Chiefs can provide from 2028.

Cleary revealed he was in tears when To'o informed him he would leave Penrith to join the Chiefs, who critics — led by South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett — have said now have an unfair advantage in attracting talent.

The salary cap has been an equaliser of talent but Bennett has claimed the NRL has eroded the competition's fairness by giving the Chiefs such an upper hand.

The Chiefs' advantages are in contrast to the few concessions afforded to the Perth Bears, who will enter the NRL next season.

Chiefs sign premiership winger To'o away from Panthers Four-time premiership-winning winger Brian To'o has become the sixth player to sign with the PNG Chiefs for their inaugural NRL season in 2028.

"It's not a level playing field and I think you can see that," said Sydney Roosters coach Robinson.

"We've got (it on) one (hand) where we feel like it's not a level playing field and the other where we feel like they need more assistance.

"We're going to debate … but do we want our game to grow?

"We're not going to stop at 19 (teams) … we should own the Pacific.

"If we want more money in the game, want to expand, we need more teams, so I think it's a positive thing — players are going to go."

Penrith were the latest club to feel that pinch when they gave To'o, who enters the last 12 months of his deal in November, a seven-day window to explore his options for 2028.

Premiership-winning Panthers Jarome Luai and Brian To'o will reunite in 2028 at the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The winger signed with the Chiefs without visiting PNG, joining Jarome Luai, Connor Watson, Alex Johnston and Zac Lomax in agreeing to deals with the NRL's 19th side.

Loading Instagram content

"I had a little moment the other day, just very sad that Bizza's going to be going," the usually stoic Cleary said.

"There would've been a few (tears) … It's just hard to imagine 'Biz' playing in any other jersey. But there's a few guys out there that I thought the same."

Since their rise to premiership dominance in 2020, the Panthers have become accustomed to salary cap pressure squeezing out key players.

But they are especially vulnerable after 2027, with the cashed-up Chiefs emerging just as they battle to hold on to co-captains Isaah Yeo and Nathan Cleary, as well as premiership players Paul Alamoti, Liam Martin and Moses Leota.

"I think everyone knows with the Chiefs, it's hard to match that stuff," Cleary said.

"It's not your average club, but if players want to go there, you can't compete."

Asked whether the Chiefs had unfairly skewed the player market, Cleary recalled some wisdom from Marty Gurr, who was on the coaching staff during his early playing days at Manly.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I remember when I first played 35 years ago, my first coach said to me 'rugby league isn't fair'," Cleary said.

"I think he was right. I've worked that out along the way. Whether it's fair or not, that's what the game's gone with. I can understand it."

Since overcoming the initial emotional blow of To'o's impending exit, Cleary has turned his attention to Penrith's task of retaining their stable of stars before September.

"We're very hopeful of having a few of them done (soon), you definitely don't want to be going into the finals doing this sort of stuff," he said.

AAP

World.title: Legendary boot-studder hangs up his own after 58 years with Port Adelaide
World.content:
He's outlasted big names and seen many more games without the limelight but after nearly six decades looking after boots for Port Adelaide Football Club, Alfie Trebilcock is hanging up his own.

A young butcher from Broken Hill who came to the club during 1968, the boot-studder enjoyed 11 SANFL premierships, one AFL premiership, and watched footwear evolve from ankle-high boots with wooden knock-in sprigs, to light-weight multi-coloured fashion statements.

"I came down here [to Adelaide] in 1961. My grandparents followed Port Adelaide so I started following them and used to go to their games and all that type of thing," Trebilcock told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"I got friendly with the runner, Harry Vincent, got talking one day and said I'd like to get into the club and he said, 'I'll keep an eye out for you'."

A position opened up in the boot department and Trebilcock was told to have a "talk to the sprigger" who was also a bootmaker.

"He said, 'Are you prepared to learn?', and I said, 'Oh yeah', so I did a seven-year apprenticeship with him," Trebilcock said.

"After those seven years he got leukaemia and said, 'You're going to have to take over', and I said, 'Gee whiz, I'm a butcher'.

" But I was pretty lucky because moulded soles were coming in then and so I took it on and I've been there ever since and enjoyed every single minute of it. "

But from the day Trebilcock started looking after the players' footwear in 1968 and up to 1976, the Port Adelaide Magpies played without winning a SANFL premiership.

"I was beginning to think I was jinx," Trebilcock said.

But the club won a flag in 1977 and another 10 during Trebilcock's time, as well as a 2004 AFL premiership with its AFL side, The Power.

"The 2004 AFL premiership was mighty.

"I always pictured standing on the MCG on Grand Final day, celebrating a flag. That dream came true in 2004. I'll never, ever forget that day."

Bobby to say farewell as well

Also retiring is fellow volunteer Bob "Bobby" O'Malley after 18 years at the club mixing water barrels and player rehydration bottles, and helping set up for training sessions.

Former Port Adelaide Power player and captain Travis Boak with Bob O'Malley during a game against Carlton. (Supplied: Port Adelaide Football Club)

"I just loved being involved in this football club," he said.

"Port Adelaide was always a family club, and all my family barracked for Port Adelaide."

He will have his final home game with Port Adelaide against Melbourne on Saturday night.

Trebilcock will be saying goodbye after 58 years with the club.

He said he became "real friends" during this time with the late and great Russel Ebert OAM, who started with the Magpies the same year as him.

An Australian Football Hall of Fame member since 1996, Ebert played 392 games for the Magpies and remains the only SANFL player to win four Magarey Medals.

"He was a people's person," Trebilcock said.

"He was a player that never played a game of football in moulded sole boots. To the day he retired he still had knock-in sprigs.

"Every now and then you'd have to re-sprig his boots.

"As he got older his sprigging would change … then he got his Achilles problems and we made a [raised] heel for him."

The late Russell Ebert shares a laugh with Alfie Trebilcock at Port Adelaide Football Club. (Supplied: Port Adelaide Football Club)

Ebert once said of Trebilcock that he loved the players and the club, and the players loved him.

"He can talk to any player at any time and would have the complete respect of the entire playing and coaching group … we couldn't have had the success we had without him," Ebert said.

The AFL awarded Trebilcock the Jack Titus Award for conspicuous service to the game in 2013.

He was awarded Life Membership at PAFC in 2013 and was inducted into its Hall of Fame in 2025.

PAFC chairman David Koch said the club was what it was today because of people like O'Malley and Trebilcock.

"Nearly 60 years of turning up, asking for nothing and giving everything to the club he loves," he said.

"On behalf of every player, coach and supporter we say thank you, Alfie, and thank you, Bobby. We are the club we are today because of people like you."

World.title: 'Nowhere to hide' for Australia's under-fire batters against Bangladesh
World.content:
Former Australian Test opener Ed Cowan says some of Australia's batters are under pressure to make significant scores as the summer of cricket begins against Bangladesh in the Top End this week.

"If you're in the Australian Test team, and not performing regularly, there is just nowhere to hide," Cowan said on the ABC Cricket Podcast.

"And unfortunately, sometimes you get these weaker teams, and the expectation actually goes up. Cricket is hard enough, let alone with the weight of the world on your shoulders."

The Australian team is about to enter a 12-month period with potentially 21 Tests scheduled, including key away fixtures in India, South Africa and England.

Between June 2025 and the start of this cycle tomorrow, they played eight Tests, five of which were in Australia.

Australia played five of their eight Tests over the last 12 months at home, including the Ashes against England. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

"That's two careers, 21 Test matches. You could have two careers in that time. That's a lot of Test cricket," Cowan said.

That cycle begins in Darwin when they take on Bangladesh, a nation ranked ninth in the ICC Test rankings.

At the conclusion of the recent successful Ashes series against England, the average age of the Australian team was just under 34. This is a team that has played together and had great success for a long time.

The Test between Australia and Bangladesh starts on Thursday August 13 in Darwin, and you can hear every ball live on ABC Listen.

Cowan does not believe that playing lower-ranked opposition necessarily provides younger players with a chance to gain experience.

"I think you are trying to pick your best available team and there's always an opportunity to work through your portfolio of players, and they've done this in recent years, usually away from home and it's less opposition dependent and more condition dependent," he said.

The bowling attack has been well established for some time with the likes of Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon proving a recipe for success.

Where the questions creep in is around the batting line-up.

Jake Weatherald was given an opportunity to open the batting in the recent Ashes series but is yet to score an international century, with a top score of 72.

Jake Weatherald will be looking to impress in front of his home crowd in Darwin against Bangladesh (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Cowan expects the Northern Territory product to open in the first game, but says he remains under pressure.

"If Jake Weatherald doesn't get 100 in the next five Test matches, more than likely we'll find someone who will get an opportunity to open the batting. And so there's going to be some natural attrition over the coming months," he said.

He is not the only player who will be searching for form in this two-match series against Bangladesh. Marnus Labuschagne has averaged 26.61 with the bat in his last 20 tests and has taken time away from playing to focus on a training block in Queensland.

"After eight weeks of being able to just go back to my fundamentals and working on my game, spending hours and hours on the simple things, just my shots, working on my shapes and my technique as a whole, is something that I definitely needed," Labuschagne told reporters in Brisbane last week.

Loading Instagram content

It has been over 1,100 days since he last reached triple figures in a Test match back in 2023. Cowan believes these Tests could be a step in the right direction for Labuschagne.

"The greatest thing that you can have as a Test batsman is confidence. And confidence is only bred through performance," he said.

The youngest member of Australia's most recent Test team is Cameron Green. When the West Australian debuted in 2020, aged 21, he was touted as one of the best young talents in the country, but his recent form has some questioning his future in the side.

The now 27-year-old has played 37 Tests and has a batting average of 32.75 and a bowling average of 38.94, but Australian coach Andrew McDonald is resolute that Green remains a vital member of his side.

"We believe Cam Green is a very, very skilled player, and we believe, sometimes, his performances have been taken a little bit out of context," McDonald told SEN Radio.

"He's been contributing to this team, as have a lot of that top seven, in conditions that haven't been favourable to batters."

Cowan believes these two Tests present an opportunity for those out of form to find some form at a time when there is less pressure coming from other domestic players.

The last time Australia played a Test against Bangladesh was 2017, where Australia won the series 2-1. (Getty Images: /SOPA Images/LightRocket/Md Manik)

"They get first crack at it. And when there's no other cricket going on, there was a CA XI game that we'll come to, but there's no Shield cricket, there's no Aussie A tours, no-one's putting pressure on anyone," he said.

"It's a bit of a free swing. And in many respects, that should free the batters up to just go and play."
