After snapping a photo, I asked Gemini to build a 20-minute circuit. Within seconds, it created a workout complete with step-by-step instructions and instructional videos, which I could immediately launch on the Pixel Watch.

What impressed me wasn’t the AI-generated workout itself. Plenty of AI fitness tools can already do that. The difference is that Google’s solution bridges the gap between planning and actually exercising by pushing the routine directly to your watch, where it guides you through every rep and rest interval in real time. That’s been one of the missing pieces for AI coaching, and it’s the feature I’m most excited to test further.

Pixel Watch 5’s Health Guardian

Google is also introducing Health Guardian, an expansion of its existing emergency safety features.

Building on Loss of Pulse Detection, Health Guardian can recognize signs of breathing emergencies, including events related to choking, pneumonia or drug toxicity, as well as persistent (and potentially life-threatening) drops in blood oxygen saturation. If the watch detects one of these emergencies, it can automatically contact emergency services and share your location with your emergency contacts.

The Pixel Watch 5 has new health features that will help flag potentially serious medical conditions.

Pixel Watch 5 tracks blood pressure and insulin resistance

The watch will track blood pressure and insulin resistance trends over time.

Rather than diagnosing medical conditions, these wellness features are designed to identify longer-term trends that could signal elevated risk for hypertension or diabetes. At the time of publishing, these features have not received FDA clearance and won’t be available at launch. Google says they’re expected to arrive in a software update later this fall on the Pixel Watch 5 and Fitbit Air.

Pixel Watch 5 bottom line

Only time and real-world testing will tell just how noticeable some of these gains actually are, but for now, the Pixel Watch 5 feels like an iterative upgrade to an already well-rounded smartwatch and one of the best smartwatch experiences running Wear OS 7 in the market.

The lack of a significant battery improvement, combined with the fact that some of its best new health features and accuracy gains are also coming to older watches, makes this a less obvious upgrade, especially at $50 more.

Tech.title: The Biggest Meteor Shower Peaks Tonight. Here’s How to Watch It Live
Tech.content:
The first-ever report of the Perseid meteor shower came nearly 2,000 years ago, and the spectacular space event has enthralled observers of the night sky ever since. Tonight, the shower will hit its 2026 peak, with 50 to 100 meteors firing per hour. If you can’t make it to a viewing site, NASA is hosting a livestream.

The Perseid meteor livestream starts at 9 p.m. PT tonight (Wednesday, Aug. 12) on YouTube. NASA will broadcast real-time sky imagery from its Automated Lunar and Meteor Observatory at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. Meteoroid experts from Marshall will host the livestream, which will include several guest speakers who will discuss the meteor shower, its history and other fun facts.

Perseids began its 2026 show on July 17, and it continues until Aug. 24, so if you’ve seen a meteor in the night sky here recently, there’s a good chance it was Perseids. The meteor shower peaks on the evening of Wednesday and into Thursday, when meteors will be coming at a rate of about one per minute.

NASA hasn’t announced how long the stream will last, but the stream’s name, Up All Night, suggests it’ll last for quite a while. It may be the best way for early birds to experience Perseids after waking up.

This Perseid fireball was seen over a lake in Ontario around dusk. “It was hot and muggy even after the sun went down, with lots of haze on the horizon but this Perseid was so bright it didn’t matter,” photographer Malcolm Park said. Spaceweather.com/Malcolm Park

A full schedule of live streams for NASA

NASA typically simulcasts its streams across its YouTube channel, Twitch channel and NASA Plus, which is often also streamed on Netflix. However, Wednesday is chock-full of interesting things to look at, including a solar eclipse and even a planet parade. It seems NASA’s strategy is to divide and conquer, so the Perseids stream is only appearing on YouTube.

The agency is also hosting a livestream for the solar eclipse on NASA Plus, Netflix, X, Amazon Prime and YouTube on Wednesday. The solar eclipse lasts all day and is visible to the northern third of the US. Those outside the path can watch the eclipse online, at least.

Tech.title: The $899 Pixel 11’s Longer 30x Zoom and New Camera Bar Design Are Impressive
Tech.content:
The new $899 Pixel 11, announced Wednesday ahead of the company’s Made by Google event, has a number of meaningful improvements, like a 30x zoom and faster wireless charging, while dancing around the $100 higher starting price than last year’s Pixel 10.

The Pixel 11 shares the same 6.3-inch screen size as the Pixel 10, shaves its camera bump and extends the camera’s digital zoom range, among a few other changes, such as an ever-so-slightly larger battery. While these iterative alterations don’t seem eye-catching, I appreciated a few of the Pixel 11’s redesigned features during my brief time trying them out.

Admittedly, some of my favorite improvements are to aesthetics. The slimmer camera bar is 40% thinner than the one on the Pixel 10, making it look like a slightly raised platform on the back of the phone. While it’s not flush, it is slim enough that using Google’s PixelSnap case helps the phone lie fully flat on a table.

While the Pixel 11 supports the same 30-watt wired charging as its predecessor, it now tops out at 25-watt Qi2 wireless charging, which should let it recharge faster than last year’s version. In my story exploring CNET Lab testing for the fastest-charging phones, the Pixel 10 (which only supports 15 watts) added only 27% in 30 minutes. The Pixel 11 has a baby battery bump in capacity to 4,985 mAh, up from the Pixel 10’s 4,970 mAh.

If you’re looking for areas of improvement, don’t look at the camera hardware, as the Pixel 11 has the same cameras as the Pixel 10. The upgrades lie, as they usually do with Google phones, in the software.

The Pixel 11 now features a 30x digital zoom, up from the 20x zoom on the Pixel 10. Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Pixel 11 cameras

Lens Aperture Resolution Magnification Wide-angle f/1.7 48 megapixels 1x Ultrawide f/2.2 13 megapixels 0.6x Telephoto f/2.8 10.8 megapixels 5x Selfie f2.2 10.5 megapixels 1x

Software gives the Pixel 11’s digital zoom range a boost, now maxing out at 30x, up from last year’s 20x. During my hands-on time with the Pixel 11, I spent most of it experimenting with the improved zoom. I was impressed with how I could zoom straight into various plants in the demo room at 30x and the resulting image had sharp details — such as visible strands inside of a flower — with limited artifacting. Normally, I don’t bother with digital zoom because the resulting photos look like a pixelated mess. I still have to put the phone through more testing for my review

The Pixel 11 has Google’s new Tensor G6 processor and runs on Android 17, with a promised seven years of major OS and security updates. The Pixel 11 will also get the benefit of Google’s Pixel Feature drops that bring new functionality and refinements throughout the year between major Android overhauls.

The updated Android Switch works directly with iOS 26 for moving data from an iPhone to a Pixel phone. René Ramos/CNET Group

Google is also making it easier for iPhone owners to switch to the Pixel 11 with an update to its Android Switch app. I first tested this tool using the updated Samsung Smart Switch on the Galaxy Z Flip 8, and the Pixel 11’s process is similar: You launch it from the Pixel 11’s settings menu, the phone generates a QR code to scan with your iPhone and then you follow prompts on both devices to start the transfer.

But here’s where some of Google’s choices get messy. The barrier for entry is higher for potential Pixel buyers. Google did away with the $799 model with 128GB of storage. That means the Pixel 11 starts at $899 for 256GB, the same $899 price as last year’s 256GB Pixel 10. Even though this is a higher starting price, Google isn’t alone in raising the price of entry: Other 2026 phones like Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8 and Motorola’s Razr received $100 price increases over last year’s models without any storage bump. The Pixel 11 also now comes in a 512GB model for $1,019, which undercuts the $1,100 512GB Galaxy S26.

The Google Pixel 11 comes in Obsidian, Frost, Pistachio and Hibiscus colors. Tara Brown/CNET

This sort of price comparison is important, as we continue to grapple with the overall rising cost of electronics during an ongoing RAM shortage. This situation affects the entire industry, Google said in a press briefing, and stated that the Pixel 11’s pricing reflects this new reality.

The Pixel 11 is now available for preorder in four colors: frost, pistachio, hibiscus and obsidian. I’m personally into the greener hue of the pistachio model, but the pinker hibiscus is a bolder look that I suspect plenty of people will like.

The phone goes on sale Aug. 20, the same day as the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL, Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Pixel Watch 5.

Tech.title: I Tested the Pixel 11 Pro’s Camera in Beautiful Paris
Tech.content:
The Pixel 11 Pro has a variety of upgrades for photographers. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The Pixel 11 Pro is Google’s latest flagship phone, and I got to take it on a photo walk through the colorful streets of mid-summer Paris. Très charmant! Alongside a suite of upgrades like its Tensor G6 processor and delightful new peachy color, there are a bunch of camera updates. And, as a photographer myself, I was keen to see what was up.

So it might seem that most of the camera hardware is the same. It’s the usual trio of wide, ultrawide and telephoto lenses all at the same resolutions as last year’s model. But Google says that the main image sensor is new and generally offers better quality. And the telephoto sensor is physically larger.

But honestly, one of my favorite new features is called Camera Looks, and it’s all about the software. Similar to Apple’s Photographic Styles, Camera Looks change the colors and exposure in your images to give them a more creative look than just taking clinically accurate photos.

Lovely tones and gentle contrast from the main camera with the ‘Vanilla’ Camera Look. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Great tones and spot-on exposure from the main camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

And there’s no discernible color shift when you switch to the ultrawide lens. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I really like the looks, and I actually had them applied to the camera pretty much my whole day. You can also customize each look further, adding some warmth or adjusting the depth of shadows and even adding grain. Typically, I really like the grainy look you get from authentic analog film — it’s why I recently spent a fortune on a Leica M6 film camera — but I’ve gotta say, I don’t love the grain effect that the Pixel 11 Pro applies.

There’s a lot of grain in this picture. I know that because I specifically added loads to the scene when I shot it. I probably shouldn’t have. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

It looks very digital and not especially realistic. I shot all my photos in JPEG and in RAW, which bypasses Google’s processing, allowing me to do my own edits instead.

I’ve done this with a few shots, actually, as sometimes the Camera Looks can be a bit…much. The Black Tie effect is a very high-key black-and-white style that won’t suit every scene, but did play an absolute blinder when I got the phone low for this shot of this person carrying a plant.

It’s a lovely, punchy shot. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

And I liked it for this portrait mode shot with the 5x telephoto lens.

The amount of bokeh in the background is perfect. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Though I definitely prefer the ones we did in color using the Editorial Camera Look.

I think the colors in the ‘Editorial’ look have worked well here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

But generally, it was the “Vanilla” Look that I stuck with for most of the day.

A new feature for the phones is Magic Capture, which shoots a few seconds of video and uses AI to identify the still frame that best captures the moment, then saves that one for you.

Magic Capture really nailed the decisive moment here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I put it to use with a couple of skaters I found, and it was surprisingly effective. All I had to do was just film the action and not worry about capturing the best moment — the phone would do that for me.

I think the phone definitely highlighted the best shots for me, and while it kind of takes the skill out of nailing that decisive moment, that’s kind of the point. It’s not really for pro action photographers who know exactly when to hit the shutter; it’s more for parents who want to capture an awesome moment of their kid on their bike but don’t want to try again and again to get the shot they want.

While I initially liked the look I chose for this photo, I don’t like how blown out the sky is. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I do like the look that I created on the phone here. It’s definitely got that feel of a summer day, but I do think the sky has been blown out, arguably, a bit too much.

But because I also shot the image in RAW, I was able to do my own edit in Lightroom, and I was surprised at how much dynamic range the phone had really captured. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

But again, I shot in raw too, so a few tweaks in Lightroom and I discovered that the phone definitely had captured a lot more dynamic range than the JPEG suggested, giving me much more scope to edit the image how I wanted.

And again, I found the shadows a bit too deep in the shot using the Camera Looks. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

So I made my own edit to the raw file in Lightroom, and I really like the look I achieved. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

But otherwise, most of my images were straight out of the Pixel’s camera.

Taken with the 5x telephoto lens, I love how much background bokeh there is here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The 5x telephoto lens has been tweaked to let you focus closer, turning it into something of a macro lens. I put it to use on this shot of a padlock, and I love the shallow depth of field it produced.

But if you want to take things further, that zoom can now reach 120x magnification. That’s basically at the level of an actual telescope, though there’s an important thing to keep in mind. Once you go beyond 30x zoom, the phone uses generative AI to artificially recreate the details in your images, which is good or bad, depending on your perspective.

On the left is the raw file from the 120x zoom. It’s basically just a collection of pixels. On the right is the generative AI’s interpretation. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I shot this image of the French flag on a building that was so far away I could barely even see it. The results speak for themselves. The raw version of that shot (left) is basically just a handful of pixels, yet the AI has reconstructed it (right) with all kinds of new details.

But the problem for me is that those details aren’t real. Or at least, they might not be real. The camera is essentially seeing what’s in front of it and rebuilding that scene almost entirely using generative AI, meaning that what you’re seeing in the finished image is really more of an interpretation of what you saw.

But it’s up to you as to whether that matters. As a photographer, I don’t want generative AI anywhere near my images. I want to know that what I’ve captured in an image is actually what I saw, not simply an algorithm’s interpretation. You’ll have to draw your own ethical lines with tools like this.

Strong colors and excellent details from the main camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I love the dramatic, low-angle paired with the ultrawide lens, but I don’t love the strong grain effect applied. That’s my fault. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

A classic street photo, converted to black and white in Lightroom from the raw file. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Anyway, the afternoon rolled on, and I continued my walk with the phone, trying to indulge in some street-style photography along the way until I eventually came to an iconic spot overlooking the Eiffel Tower. I switched lenses and styles here, shooting quickly to capture some of the moments as they unfolded before me.

I think the teal of the sky is quite unnatural here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Although I think the tones work really well here, giving it a feel of a magazine fashion shoot. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I tried out what I think was the Editorial Camera Look (though it might have been called something else), and I think it goes a bit hard on the teal sky in some of these, though I do like how it looks sometimes.

It’s too early for me to give a real verdict on the cameras on the new Pixels. You’ll need to wait for my full review and for me to put them up against rivals like the iPhone 17 Pro or Galaxy S26 Ultra.

But I do really like a lot of the photos I took on this little photo walk. The overall image quality is solid, and while I’m somewhat morally opposed to the generative AI in the 120x zoom, I do think tools like Magic Capture can be genuinely helpful. I’m thrilled to see more creative shooting options with the Camera Looks tool.

Gotta love that peachy tone. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I also want to spend more time using it and do a better job of it myself — it’s really handy that the style settings you apply will remain. However, it also means that the heavy-handed grain I chose earlier in the day was still active in images I took later, and it’s…not great.

But we must all learn from our mistakes, even though experience has taught me that I never learn a damn thing.

Tech.title: I Tried Pixel 11’s New Gemini Features. One Made Me Sound Fluent in Spanish
Tech.content:
In real life, my Spanish is a little rusty. I can understand most conversations, but speaking is another story, as if the words and verb tenses are sitting on some dusty shelf I haven’t touched since high school. Right now, though, I’m hearing myself speak Spanish so rapidly and smoothly that I sound fluent.

Except I’m not. It’s Google’s Live Translate feature, dubbing one of my YouTube reviews in real time.

With the brand-new Pixel 11 Pro XL in my hand, I can tap on virtually any YouTube video and hear it translated on the fly, opening up a world of foreign-language content that I can have dubbed into English – or Spanish or Arabic, if I really want to put my language skills to the test.

Live Translate for media is just one of a handful of new Gemini Intelligence features launching on Google’s new Pixel 11 series, announced Wednesday. Along with instant translations, this suite of AI capabilities is designed to handle mundane tasks like adding something to your calendar, automatically filling out a form and sharing your flight details with loved ones. That way, you don’t have to hop between apps to track down that information yourself.

Some Gemini Intelligence features launched on Samsung’s latest foldable phones, the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra and Z Flip 8. But several new features I had the opportunity to try out last week at Google’s Mountain View, California, headquarters are arriving on Pixel 11 phones first, and will later become available on additional premium Android phones.

“We want to make sure that if you’re getting a great Android device, you should get all the great AI experiences that we’re building as well. It’s not a Pixel-only thing,” Seang Chau, vice president and general manager of Android Platform, told me. “Gemini Intelligence then becomes a brand statement that’s essentially: ‘What you have in your hand is the best that we have to offer.'”

Magic Capture snapped this shot without me hitting the shutter button. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Magic Capture

It wouldn’t be a Pixel launch without some AI camera updates. A new feature called Magic Capture lives within the camera app, next to the photo and video controls. When tapped, Magic Capture will analyze the scene and then automatically find the best shots, so you don’t have to tap the shutter button for each individual snapshot. Just hold your phone up, and your Pixel will record the scene and then pinpoint the best moments for a photo.

I tested this out while kicking a soccer ball back and forth. I pointed the Pixel’s camera at my passing partner and could focus more on playing rather than checking my framing or taking photos at the right moment. Magic Capture ended up choosing some pretty epic shots of him doing tricks, without me looking out for when to hit the shutter button.

This can be helpful if you’re trying to decide between taking a video or snapping photos, or if you just prefer to be in the moment as much as possible, rather than seeing the world through your smartphone’s viewfinder.

Rambler drafted a more touched-up text message as I yapped my way through making plans. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Rambler

Rambler takes voice-to-text to the next level by removing filler words like “um” and “uh.” You can also reverse course by saying something like, “actually, never mind,” and I’ll only take into account what it thinks you want to say.

I tested out Rambler by arranging dinner plans and stumbling through whether I wanted sushi or pizza, and if I wanted to meet at 5 or 5:30. The final text was much more cohesive than what actually came out of my mouth: “Hey, let’s get dinner today. Maybe we should get sushi. Should we meet up at 5:00?” I don’t typically use voice-to-text because I don’t like being called out for rambling, but it looks like Rambler is here to fix just that.

If someone texts you the name of a restaurant, you’ll see an option to open up a summary directly within messages. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Detailed visual cards

Choosing where to eat is one of my least favorite activities because, as my Rambler example demonstrates, I am wildly indecisive.

Now, with detailed visual cards through Gemini Intelligence, when someone texts you a restaurant suggestion, you’ll see a prompt above the text bar to open an AI overview right in messages. That way, you can get more information about that spot without opening a new window. You can also tap to open Google Maps to determine if it’s worth the trek.

You can also use this feature to quickly share your flight information. If someone texts, “What is your flight number to New York?” Gemini will pull those details from Gmail, so that person can track your arrival, and you don’t have to dig.

You can now use Circle to Search without snapping a picture. Just open up the camera and circle anything in the viewfinder. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Circle to Search in the viewfinder

Circle to Search is one of my favorite features because it lets you quickly look up anything on your phone’s screen by just circling an image, such as an outfit or accessory. I typically use this if I want to buy a product I spot online, like when I’m scrolling through Instagram.

Now, you can use Circle to Search by just launching your Pixel 11’s camera, holding down the navigation bar and circling what’s in your viewfinder – no need to actually snap the photo. That means you can eliminate one step without cluttering your Photos app with random images you don’t actually want to save.

I tried this out by holding the Pixel 11 Pro XL’s camera up to some fresh white kicks someone was wearing, and it showed me a handful of links to buy my own pair of Nike Air Force 1s. I also used Circle to Search to identify a plant, which is apparently called a California Glory Flannel Bush. I typically use Google Lens to do that, but I suppose I now have another option for quickly searching an image.

Gboard and Live Translate now work with American Sign Language. Google

Sign-language-to-text

One of AI’s most important contributions is arguably its ability to make certain features more accessible. That’s the case with Google’s new sign-language-to-text (SL2T) translation model, which allows people who are deaf to sign to their phone instead of typing. Starting with Pixel 11, people can use Gboard and Live Transcribe to translate American Sign Language to English. More devices will get this capability, and additional languages will be added soon, Google says.

People who are deaf or hard of hearing can now sign to search the web, compose messages or draft documents, or ask Gemini to execute a task using ASL. They can also use Live Transcribe to sign responses in conversations instead of typing back and forth. That can make for a faster and more natural exchange.

“Sign languages convey meaning through simultaneous movements of the hands, arms, torso, head and face,” a Google blog post reads. “Accurately tracking these at high frame rates is a difficult and computationally demanding computer vision task.”

The SL2T model is trained on over 100,000 hours of sign language data across more than 50 languages, according to Google, with around a quarter of the data in ASL. To protect people’s privacy, the company says an “on-device model tracks the location of points on the signer, and only these geometric coordinates are sent to the server for translation, allowing the original video to be discarded immediately.” That sequence is then directly translated into text.

“We spend a lot of time making sure our phones work for everybody,” said Shenaz Zack, senior director of product management at Google. “We have to solve for all our users, because this phone is not for only one user.”

Zack says practicality is at the center of all the new Gemini Intelligence features launching on the Pixel 11 series.

“How do we help our users get back to doing what they love and not worry about the cognitive load? That’s what guides us across all of these areas,” she said. “We want to make sure that we’re solving the problems that users need solving.”

Even when those problems are relatively minor, like switching the language of a YouTube video. At least now I know what to work toward as I brush up on my Spanish.

Tech.title: The Pixel 11 Pro XL Has Main Character Energy Despite a $100 Price Hike
Tech.content:
Google’s new Pixel 11 Pro flagship phones have a lot to offer, so I put them to the test in France.

If you were hoping for a fully transformed Pixel 11 Pro, then prepare to be disappointed. Google’s latest flagship Android phone stays close to its predecessors, adding a variety of upgrades across the board — including a new home-made Tensor G6 processor, some new camera tricks and a glorious new peachy color. I’ve had my hands on the phone for the better part of a day, and while it’s not a revolution, it’s certainly one of the most accomplished phones Google has made.

And while I was expecting a significant price bump due to the ongoing components shortage, Google technically made its base model cheaper and more expensive. It depends on where you live.

Pixel Pro series pricing

Model + storage Storage RAM US UK Pixel 10 Pro 128GB 16GB $999 £999 Pixel 10 Pro 256GB 16GB $1,099 £1,099 Pixel 11 Pro 256GB 12GB $1,099 £1,079 Pixel 10 Pro XL 256GB 16GB $1,199 £1,199 Pixel 11 Pro XL 256GB 12GB $1,199 £1,279

Google eliminated the $999 128GB storage option from its Pro lineup, making the $1,099 Pixel 11 Pro with 256GB of storage the new barrier for entry. If you’re lucky enough to live in the UK, like me, 256GB of storage is now marginally more affordable with the Pixel 11 Pro starting at £1,079, £20 less than the 256GB Pixel 10 Pro. The Pixel 11 Pro XL is more expensive, starting at $1,299 in the US and £1,279, a $100 and £80 price increase, respectively, over the Pixel 10 Pro XL.

Gotta love that peachy tone. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I was honestly expecting much worse. But RAM is another matter: All Pixel 11 Pro models start with 12GB of memory, compared to the Pixel 10 Pro and 10 Pro XL, which had 16GB. So while those UK prices might seem positive, it’s important to keep in mind that the starting RAM has dropped from 16GB to 12GB. If you want more, it’ll cost you. The Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL variants with 512GB and 1TB of storage come with 16GB of RAM.

But with seven years of software and security updates, the phones will still be good to use until at least 2033, as long as you look after them. The longer you keep using your phone, the more value you squeeze out of it.

As in previous generations, the only difference between the 6.3-inch Pixel 11 Pro and 6.8-inch 11 Pro XL is the screen size and a slightly bigger battery.

The Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL are now available to preorder, along with the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Pixel Watch 5. There is a Made By Google event tonight, Aug. 12, in New York, where we should learn even more about the new Pixel lineup.

I’ve not only been hands-on with the phone in Google’s Paris office, but I’ve also taken it on a lovely photowalk around the beautiful French capital, and there are a few things I like so far. So let’s dive in.

Pixel 11 Pro: Refined design with HiLight

The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL’s look isn’t a significant departure from their predecessors, with a glass-and-metal construction and a pill-shaped camera bar stretching across the back. The glass on the bar now fills the whole “island camera block,” which looks classier as a result, while Corning Gorilla Glass Victus 2 apparently makes them the most durable Pixel phones yet. Great news for clumsy people — a group in which I count myself a proud member.

A new addition in the camera bar is the revamped LED flash, which serves a deeper purpose than simply lighting up your face in the dark. Google calls it HiLight, which now functions as a notification alert. If your phone is face down on your desk, the HiLight circle will light up to tell you of an incoming call or notification — or will glow to show that Gemini has been voice-activated and is listening to your commands.

It’s a neat idea, especially as you can customize the colors according to who’s getting in touch with you (a nice calming blue for your partner and an angry red for your boss, perhaps?) but it’s hardly a cutting-edge feature. We’ve seen notification lights on phones for years — most notably in the dazzling array of LEDs on the backs of Nothing’s phones — and while I’ve found them useful, I prefer keeping my phone screen-up so I can see the notifications for real.

The phone comes in a variety of new colors, including a nice sage green and a soft pink with gold accents, called canyon, that I absolutely love. I have a thing for pink gadgets (I even turned my orange iPhone 17 Pro pink with chemicals and customized my $8,000 Leica camera with a bright pink wrap) and I think these tones are the most beautiful Google has used on its phones. Don’t want the lovely pink? Fine, there’s also a matte black option, but just know I’ll be disappointed in you. Not angry, just disappointed.

Pixel 11 Pro cameras: New color profiles for creative shooters

While it might seem that the camera hardware hasn’t changed much since last year (it’s the same trio: wide, ultrawide and telephoto, all at the same resolutions), Google reckons a lot has been done to improve camera performance. For one, the main camera uses an “all-new” 50-megapixel image sensor that will apparently deliver better dynamic range and tones in a variety of conditions, despite being the same size as the 10 Pro’s 1/1.3-inch sensor.

The 48-megapixel telephoto zoom uses a larger sensor, promising a 30% increase in light capture.

Taken with the main camera, I love the warmer tones captured with the Camera Looks. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

It looks just as good with the ultrawide camera Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Lovely tones and gentle contrast from the main camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I’ve taken a ton of photos around Paris using the Pixel 11 Pro XL and I’m impressed by what I’ve seen so far. Images are packed with detail, with evenly lit exposures that avoid looking too overprocessed. But to take my shots further, I also used the Pixel’s new Camera Looks tool, which offers a variety of color profiles designed to give your photos a more creative style than the default camera.

There’s a range to choose from — including a very high contrast black-and-white mode — and you can customize them further by tweaking the white balance, adding film grain and adjusting the intensity of the shadows. I really enjoyed playing around with these, especially the Vanilla look, which lends a warmer, almost filmic feel to the photos.

While I initially liked the look I chose when I took this photo, I don’t like how blown out the sky is. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

But because I also shot the image in raw, I was able to do my own edit in Lightroom and I was surprised at how much dynamic range the phone had really captured. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Some of the looks are too contrasty for my tastes but they’re nonetheless great fun to play around with and actually let you focus on the creative side of photography rather than it just being all about AI for a change. Don’t like the looks? You can also shoot in DNG raw and edit images to your heart’s content later on in apps like Snapseed or Adobe Lightroom.

But, yes, there’s plenty of AI going on in the cameras, too. Notably, the telephoto zoom can go up to 120x magnification, which gets you close to distant objects. Keep in mind that anything above 30x zoom uses generative AI to artificially recreate your image based on an assessment of the camera’s view. If you shoot your images in JPEG and raw you can see the wild difference between the pixellated photo of basically nothing your camera actually captured, versus the Gen AI version the phone created.

On the left is the raw file from the 120x zoom. It’s basically just a collection of pixels. On the right is the generative AI’s interpretation. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

It actually works well. I took a photo of the French flag flying above a building, and it’s honestly wild that the phone could create a usable image. On the other hand, I personally don’t want generative AI anywhere near my photos. As a professional photographer myself, I want to know that what I captured was really there, not an algorithm’s approximation. So while I’m impressed at what this tech can do, I’m morally opposed to actually using it in my own work.

I feel much better about Google’s other new tool, called Magic Capture. This essentially shoots a short video clip and then uses AI to select the best still frames from it for you. It’s aimed at parents taking photos of their kids messing around and indeed I used it to snag some cool shots of a young skateboarder hitting a ramp in the heart of Paris. And I agree that the shots it selected were the best from the set.

I didn’t press the shutter button to capture this — it was a still image highlighted by Magic Capture and it’s certainly caught the moment where the action is at its best. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I don’t mind this as it’s not using generative AI to create something that wasn’t there, it’s simply picking the best frames for you based on factors like which image is sharper, whether the whole person is in frame, if the subject has their eyes open and so on. Nothing is being altered, so you, the photographer, are still in control.

There are also new tools aimed at content creators, including an autocue mode that puts your script on-screen just below the front-facing camera, as well as the ability to group your videos into project folders for better organization. How helpful these tools really are for the creator community remains to be seen.

Pixel 11 Pro: Android 17 and AI additions

The phone launches with the latest Android 17, and as it’s a Google phone, there’s no additional manufacturer skin on top (like Samsung’s OneUI, for example). So you get a neat, fuss-free experience. It’s why the Pixels are among my favorite Android phones for everyday use.

I wasn’t allowed to swipe around the Android 17 interface during my hands-on time. I’ll save that for the review. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

There are some new AI tools thrown in, too, including deeper functionality for Gemini Intelligence to surface relevant information automatically as you go about your day (such as bringing up flight info when messaging your friend about your travel plans). Circle to Search also works within the camera for live translation and search. For example, if you circled a menu item in Japanese, it could not only translate that to English but also provide more information about the dish itself.

Speaking of translation, the phone can also translate and provide real-time dubbing for certain videos and apps. My colleague, CNET senior technology reporter, got to test the Pixel 11 Pro’s translation/dubbing feature as well as one that translates American Sign Language, and she was floored. This is likely to include YouTube, but we’ll find out more when the Pixels launch. This sounds like a genuinely useful tool, though how it really works — and how accurately — remains to be seen when we can put the phones to the test.

Pixel 11 Pro: Should you buy it?

Google certainly hasn’t overhauled its formula for its Pixel phones this time around. The 11 Pro models are best seen as iterative upgrades over the previous generation, but given how good the Pixel 10 Pro was — and the fact that price has effectively remained the same — that isn’t such a bad thing.

The soft peach of the 11 Pro and the vibrant fuchsia of the base Pixel 11. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

There are enough tweaks in the design to help it feel fresh enough, especially that soft pink color. And the new Camera Looks for your photos, the HiLight notifications alert and the new AI tools feel like they could be genuinely useful additions. Throw in the faster charging speeds (Google promises 75% in 30 mins) and the new Pixel 11 Pro range seems to have a lot to offer.

My camera test in Paris has shown me that it’s well equipped for at least casual photographers, but I’ll look forward to getting a unit in my hands for the full review later this month.

Tech.title: With the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, Google Doubles Down on Durability
Tech.content:
While many foldable phone-makers tout the sleekness of their devices, Google is once again going in a different direction.

On Wednesday, the company unveiled the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, emphasizing its increased durability over its predecessor. That might not sound very sexy, but it’s a big deal when you’re spending $1,899 on a phone.

Yes, that’s a $100 price hike over last year’s Pixel Fold, which Google acknowledged in a briefing is due to the RAM shortage that’s hiking costs across the industry. But the company clearly hopes that’s a price you’ll be willing to pay for a little more peace of mind – as well as some fresh capabilities.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold looks strikingly similar to last year’s 10 Pro Fold – which, in turn, resembled the phone before it. But beneath the surface, the latest book-style foldable is three times more durable than last year’s offering, according to Google.

The new phone lineup, which also includes the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL, arrives one month before Apple is expected to unveil its next-generation handsets and, potentially, the long-rumored foldable iPhone. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold also debuts on the heels of Samsung’s latest foldables, including the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which broke preorder records and could share a passport-style design with Apple’s anticipated foldable. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold, on the other hand, maintains the taller build of more traditional book-style phones like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

All Pixel 11 phones are open for preorder now and launch on Aug. 20. Here’s what Google says it improved with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, and what remains the same from last year.

The Pixel 11 Pro fold has a 6.5-inch cover screen made of a new glass-ceramic material that’s more resistant to scratches and cracks, according to Google. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Design and durability on the Pixel 11 Pro Fold

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a 6.5-inch display with a new glass-ceramic cover that’s more resistant to scratches and cracks, according to Google. Like most foldable phones today, that cover display is a comfortable size for scrolling, typing and browsing, and doesn’t feel awkwardly narrow or tight. The bezels have also slimmed down this year, making the display feel a little more immersive.

The Fold’s glass fiber composite back cover should be harder to crack, and an aluminum frame adds some sturdiness while keeping the phone relatively light. In fact, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is nearly 10% lighter than last year’s phone, Google says.

The 11 Pro Fold’s sprawling 8-inch inner display is also more durable, according to Google, with anti-impact film for better protection against drops. A redesigned hinge can also protect the inside display from damage if your handset takes a tumble. That offers some assurance if you like to live on the edge and go caseless like me.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is just 5mm thick when open and 10.1mm thick when closed. Rene Ramos

Google carried over one of the defining features of last year’s foldable: the IP68 rating. That means the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is protected against grains as small as dust and can be submerged in up to a meter and a half of water for 30 minutes – granting it the same level of particle and liquid resistance as most premium non-folding phones. By comparison, foldable phones like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Motorola Razr Fold are not rated for protection against dust and fine sand, so they likely wouldn’t fare well at the beach.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is slightly thinner this year, measuring 5mm thick when open and 10.1mm thick when closed. That makes it a little thicker than the Z Fold 8 Ultra (4.1mm open, 8.9mm closed) and the Razr Fold (4.6mm open, 9.9mm closed). But the differences feel rather negligible when I hold each of these phones in my hand, signaling just how far sleek foldable design has come.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold comes in two colors: olive and obsidian.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a 48-megapixel wide-angle, 10.5-megapixel ultrawide and 10.8-megapixel telephoto camera on the back. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Camera specs on the Pixel 11 Pro Fold

On paper, not much is new about the Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s cameras. This year’s phone once again has a 48-megapixel wide-angle, 10.5-megapixel ultrawide and 10.8-megapixel telephoto camera on the back. There are also 10-megapixel selfie cameras on the cover and inside displays.

Like last year’s foldable, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a more scaled-back camera system than its Pixel 11 Pro counterparts, despite the shared high-end name. But I look forward to taking it for a spin and seeing how its cameras perform.

The Fold can now take better low-light photos, according to Google. It also gets an upgrade to Super Zoom, which uses AI to sharpen zoomed-in images, going from a maximum of 20x last year to 30x this year.

The biggest new camera feature is Magic Capture, which lives within the camera app next to the photo and video controls. When you tap Magic Capture, it’ll analyze a scene and automatically find the best shots, so you don’t have to tap the shutter button each time you want to snap a picture. Just hold your phone up and your Pixel will record the scene and then pinpoint the best moments for a photo. You can read more about Magic Capture and the other Pixel 11 capabilities I tried here.

Another new feature lives within the camera bar itself. HiLight is available on all the Pixel 11 Pro devices, and will flash different customizable colors on the back to indicate that a specific person is calling, for example. That way, you can tell at a glance whether it’s worth flipping your phone over and responding, or if you’d rather keep it face down and stay in the moment.

I could see myself using HiLight to flag only the most important calls, like ones from my mom, when I want to lock in. But I also know the safest bet to avoid checking my phone is to keep it clear across the room where I can’t reach it.

Rene Ramos

Battery life and processor on the Pixel 11 Pro Fold

In slimming down, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s battery takes a slight hit (at least on paper), going from 5,015 mAh last year to 4,806 mAh this year. Still, Google says the battery should last over 24 hours, which I look forward to testing once I can use the 11 Pro Fold as my daily driver.

The new foldable is powered by a Google Tensor G6 processor and launches with Android 17. That includes a suite of Gemini Intelligence features designed to make it easier to find and share information without hopping between apps. I demoed a handful of these functions when I swung by Google’s Mountain View, California, headquarters last week, and they strike me as surprisingly helpful and time-saving.

Like last year’s foldable, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold comes with 16GB of RAM and either 256GB, 512GB or 1TB of storage. The memory shortage means you’ll pay $100 more for the same amount of storage as last year. But you can look for carrier deals to soften the blow of the $1,899 starting price.

This year, Google appears to have doubled down on the defining advantage of its foldable phone: durability. Now, the question is whether that focus will be enough to resonate with consumers – especially as competition in the foldable market continues to heat up.

Tech.title: Exclusive: New Crunchyroll Collab Brings Anime Streaming to Cars
Tech.content:
Nothing like kicking back in your car to stream Daemons of the Shadow Realm, right? But instead of watching on your phone, the in-car entertainment system lets you catch the latest episodes on your BMW’s dash. Crunchyroll and automotive app store Appning are partnering to bring the streamer’s catalog to a selection of vehicles, starting with BMW and Mini and eventually expanding to more than 40 auto brands. The companies announced the team-up on Wednesday, sharing that the anime app will soon arrive in cars.

Appning, Forvia’s app store, is an in-car platform where customers can access built-in apps for YouTube, Zoom, Spotify and more. The addition of Crunchyroll’s streaming service will make anime available to drivers around the world, including North America, Europe, Asia, Latin America and Australia. While Appning is the hub behind the experience, TiVo’s tech is surfacing titles and personalized recommendations for Crunchyroll subscribers tapping in while chilling in their cars.



Using safety-first features, the venture will allow anime fans to watch more than 50,000 episodes of TV shows and movies, plus 25,000 hours of content when the vehicle is parked. So, no streaming while driving, OK? Video playback will be blocked if you attempt to watch while the car is moving.

“Today’s consumers expect their entertainment to be available wherever they are, including in their vehicle, said Brian McGarvey, Crunchyroll’s SVP of global distribution and business development. “With Crunchyroll coming soon to global automotive partners, the anime experience will be even more accessible on every journey. Through this collaboration with Appning, we’re glad to provide another way for this passionate, global fan community to enjoy their favorite anime.”

You will still need a paid Crunchyroll subscription to watch favorites like Demon Slayer, Solo Leveling or Gachiakuta, and plans start at $10 per month in the US. Appning, which is available in car brands such as Mercedes-Benz, Lotus and Volkswagen (Latin America), is an Android-powered system that carries more than 300 apps.
